p.seg: The Origin of the Dao, First
The virtue of literature is indeed great,
coexisting with heaven and earth—how can this be?
For when the dark and yellow hues mingled,
and the square and round forms separated,
the sun and moon, like overlapping jades,
displayed the splendid images in the sky;
mountains and rivers, radiant and elegant,
spread out the patterned shapes of the earth;
these are the patterns of the Dao.
Looking up, we observe the shining luminaries;
looking down, we inspect the含蓄 patterns;
high and low take their positions,
thus the two primary forces were born;
only humanity partakes in this,
concentrating the essence of spiritual nature,
forming what is called the Three Powers.
As the finest of the Five Elements,
they are truly the heart of heaven and earth.
With the heart formed, speech is established;
with speech established, literary patterns emerge—
this is the Dao of nature.
Extending to all things,
both moving and stationary have their patterns:
dragons and phoenixes display auspiciousness with ornate designs;
tigers and leopards embody majestic postures with vivid coats;
clouds and rosy clouds carve colors,
surpassing the skill of painters;
plants and trees adorn blossoms,
needing no craftsmanship of weavers;
these are not external adornments,
but simply natural.
As for the sounds in the forest,
their melodies resemble those of the yu and se;
springs and stones striking harmonies,
their harmony is like that of jades and bells;
thus, when forms are established, patterns are completed;
when sounds are emitted, literary expressions arise.
If even inanimate things
abound with such splendor,
how could sentient beings
lack literary expression?
The origin of human culture
began from the Supreme Ultimate,
mysteriously inspired by divine intelligence,
with the "Images of the Yi" as the foremost.
Fúxī initiated it with his diagrams,
and Confucius completed it with his commentaries.
Regarding the two positions of Qián and Kūn,
he uniquely composed the "Wén Yán."
The literary quality of speech
is the heart of heaven and earth!
Thus, the Hé Tú孕育 the Eight Trigrams,
the Luò Shū contained the Nine Categories,
the reality of jade tablets and golden engravings,
the splendor of crimson scripts and green records—
who presided over these?
It was none other than the divine principle.
Since bird tracks replaced knotted cords,
writing began to shine forth;
the legacy of Yán Dì and Fúxī
was recorded in the "Three Fén,"
but the ages are remote,
and their sounds and elegance are beyond recovery.
The literature of Táng and Yú
then flourished brilliantly.
The sovereign's songs
expressed his aspirations in chant;
Yì and Jì presenting plans
also established the style of exposition.
With the rise of the Xià dynasty,
achievements were lofty and grand;
the Nine Accomplishments were sung,
and merits and virtues grew more ornate.
Reaching the Shāng and Zhōu dynasties,
literary refinement surpassed substance.
Under the influence of the "Yǎ" and "Sòng,"
brilliance renewed daily.
King Wén, in adversity,
made the "Zhòu Cí" radiant,
with layered elegance and profound subtlety,
deep and firm in essential meaning.
Moreover, the Duke of Zhōu, talented,
carried on his glorious deeds,
editing the "Shī" and compiling the "Sòng,"
adorning various writings.
When Confucius succeeded the sages,
he uniquely excelled past philosophers,
melting and harmonizing the "Six Classics,"
ensuring they resonated like gold and jade;
refining human nature,
weaving elegant language,
so that his wooden clapper aroused responses from a thousand miles,
his seated treasures flowed and echoed through ten thousand generations,
depicting the radiance of heaven and earth,
enlightening the eyes and ears of the people.
Thus, from the time of Fúxī
to that of Confucius,
the mysterious sage created the canons,
the uncrowned king transmitted the teachings;
all traced the Dao's heart to spread literary patterns,
studied the divine principle to establish education,
drew images from the Hé and Luò,
sought numbers through shī stalks and tortoise shells,
observed celestial patterns to exhaust changes,
examined human culture to accomplish transformation;
only then could they govern the world,
comprehend constant laws,
develop great undertakings,
and make literary principles shine.
Thus, we know the Dao transmits literature through sages,
and sages elucidate the Dao through literature,
permeating all without bounds,
used daily without exhaustion.
The "Yì" says:
"What stirs the world lies in the words."
The reason words can stir the world
is that they are the literature of the Dao.
Eulogy:
The heart of the Dao is subtle,
the divine principle establishes teaching.
Illuminating the mysterious sage,
shining with benevolence and filial piety.
The dragon diagram presented its form,
the tortoise script revealed its appearance.
Observing these celestial patterns,
the people all emulate them.
Evidencing the Sages, Second
Those who create are called sages,
those who transmit are called enlightened;
molding human nature,
their merit lies with the highest wisdom.
The writings of Confucius
can be heard and known,
thus the sentiments of the sage
are revealed in his words.
The teachings of ancient kings
are spread in texts;
the demeanor of Confucius
overflows in his maxims.
Therefore, praising the distant Táng era,
it was described as brilliantly prosperous;
commending the nearer Zhōu dynasty,
it was deemed richly worthy to follow.
This is evidence that governance values literature.
When the Earl of Zhèng entered Chén,
he achieved merit through establishing言辞;
when Sòng set up the broken stand,
they upheld ritual with abundant refinement.
This is evidence that deeds value literature.
Praising Zǐchǎn,
it is said, "Words to fulfill intent,
refinement to complete words";
generally discussing the noble person,
it is said, "Emotions should be sincere,
words should be skillful."
This is evidence that self-cultivation values literature.
Thus, when intent is fulfilled and words are refined,
emotions sincere and words skillful,
it constitutes the jade tablet of inner brilliance,
the golden rule of wielding literature.
For mirroring the completeness of the sun and moon,
marvelously reaching the essence of mystery;
literature forms standards,
thought aligns with tallies;
sometimes concise words convey the meaning,
sometimes rich text covers all emotions,
sometimes clarifying principles to establish form,
sometimes concealing meaning to hide utility.
Thus, the "Spring and Autumn" uses one word to praise or blame,
the "Mourning Apparel" cites the light to include the heavy—
this is concise words conveying the meaning.
The "Bīn Odes" link stanzas to accumulate lines,
the "Conduct of the Scholar" elaborates with intricate rhetoric—
this is rich text covering all emotions.
Written decisions emulate the Guài hexagram,
articles shine clearly, imitating the Lí hexagram—
this is clarifying principles to establish form.
The "Four Images" with profound meaning subtly hidden,
the "Five Examples" with delicate words gently obscure—
this is concealing meaning to hide utility.
Thus, we know abundance and brevity take different forms,
concealment and clarity employ different methods,
restraint or extension as timing requires,
adaptation and flexibility suit the occasion,
evidenced by the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius,
then literature has its masters.
Therefore, discourse must be verified by the sages,
and understanding the sages must be rooted in the classics.
The Yì Jīng states, "By distinguishing things and rectifying words,
the judgments become complete";
the Shū Jīng says, "Words value substance and essentials,
not merely a fondness for novelty."
Thus we know that rectifying words establishes distinction,
and embodying essentials completes the diction.
With diction completed, there is no fault of fondness for novelty;
with distinction established, there is the beauty of decisive judgments.
Even if the profound meaning is subtly hidden,
it does not harm the rectification of words;
even if the subtle expressions are gentle and obscure,
they do not impair the embodiment of essentials.
Embodiment of essentials and subtle expressions go hand in hand,
rectifying words and profound meanings are used together;
in the writings of the sages,
this can be seen.
Yán Hé believed that Zhòngní adorned feathers with paintings,
merely engaging in flowery rhetoric.
Though he wished to slander the sage,
he could not succeed.
Thus, the elegance and beauty of the sage's writings
inherently carry blossoms and bear fruit.
The way of heaven is hard to hear,
yet one may still delve into and admire it;
writings can be seen,
why then not ponder them?
If one establishes words by verifying the sages,
then literature may nearly achieve this.
The eulogy says:
The ultimate marvel is born of innate knowledge,
wisdom and insight alone govern.
Refined principles form the writing,
splendid spirit becomes the literary grace.
Discernment hangs like the sun and moon,
words abound like mountains and seas.
A hundred years, the shadow passes,
a thousand ages, the heart remains.
Venerating the Classics, Third
The eternal teachings of the three ultimates
are written in the "Classics."
The Classics are
the ultimate way of constancy,
the great teachings that cannot be altered.
Thus, they mirror heaven and earth,
emulate spirits and gods,
participate in the order of things,
establish human principles,
penetrate the depths of human nature,
and exhaust the marrow of literature.
The Huáng Shì's "Sān Fén,"
the Dì Dài's "Wǔ Diǎn,"
augmented by the "Bā Suǒ,"
extended by the "Jiǔ Qiū,"
their years passed in obscurity,
their branches and streams tangled and mixed.
Since Fūzǐ edited and transmitted them,
the great treasures have all shone forth.
Thus, the Yì Jīng expanded with the "Shí Yì,"
the Shū Jīng marked the seven perspectives,
the Shī Jīng listed the four beginnings,
the Lǐ Jīng rectified the "Five Classics,"
the Chūn Qiū with its five examples,
their meanings rooted in human nature,
their words crafted with literary principle,
thus they could open learning and nurture rectitude,
illuminating and blending harmoniously.
Yet the heart of the way is subtle,
the sage's plans supremely lofty,
their walls lofty and steep,
their expressions naturally profound.
Like a giant bell of immense weight,
it does not produce faint, tinkling sounds.
Now, the Yì Jīng discusses heaven,
entering the spiritual and achieving utility.
Thus, the Xì Cí praises its far-reaching meaning and elegant words,
speaking aptly with hidden matters;
the leather thongs breaking three times,
truly the deep abyss of the wise.
The Shū Jīng records speeches,
but its ancient glosses are obscure;
through the Ěr Yǎ,
the meaning becomes clear.
Thus Zǐxià praised the Shū Jīng,
bright as the alternating light of sun and moon,
scattered like the array of stars,
speaking of its brilliant clarity.
The Shī Jīng focuses on expressing intent,
its glosses similar to the Shū Jīng,
unfolding the fēng and structuring the xìng,
with ornate words and subtle metaphors,
gentle and soft in recitation,
thus most closely attaching to deep feelings.
The Lǐ Jīng establishes form,
based on events to set norms,
its articles detailed and intricate,
applied and then made clear,
gathering fragments of speech,
all are treasures.
The Chūn Qiū distinguishes principles,
a single word reveals meaning,
five stones and six waterfowl,
forming text through detail and brevity;
the pheasant gate and two towers,
showing intent through sequence;
its subtle chapters and obscure records,
truly profound.
The Shàng Shū may seem obscure at first glance,
but seeking its principles brings clarity;
the Chūn Qiū's words are immediately understood,
yet probing its meaning reveals depth.
This is the distinct character of the sage's writings,
the different forms of surface and depth.
As for their roots deep and firm,
branches lofty and lush,
words concise but meanings rich,
events near but metaphors far-reaching,
thus though past, they remain timeless,
their lingering flavor ever new,
later scholars pursuing them are not late,
earlier masters long using them are not ahead,
they may be called Tài Shān's rain reaching everywhere,
the river moistening a thousand miles.
Thus, for argumentation and discourse, prefaces and sequences,
the Yì Jīng leads the way;
for edicts, plans, memorials, and reports,
the Shū Jīng opens the source;
for rhapsodies, eulogies, songs, and praises,
the Shī Jīng sets the foundation;
for inscriptions, elegies, admonitions, and prayers,
the Lǐ Jīng summarizes the beginning;
for annals, biographies, covenants, and proclamations,
the Chūn Qiū is the root;
all set the highest standards,
open the farthest boundaries,
thus the hundred schools leap and soar,
yet ultimately remain within their sphere.
If one models on the Classics to create forms,
consults the Yǎ to enrich language,
it is like mining the mountain to cast bronze,
boiling the sea to make salt.
Therefore, if literature can venerate the Classics,
the style possesses six virtues:
first, deep emotion without deceit,
second, pure style without confusion,
third, truthful events without fabrication,
fourth, upright principles without deviation,
fifth, concise form without verbosity,
sixth, beautiful language without excess.
Yáng Zǐ compared carving jade to make vessels,
saying the Five Classics contain literary elegance.
For writing is established by conduct,
conduct is transmitted by writing,
the four teachings prioritize this,
substance and ornament complement each other,
advancing virtue and establishing reputation,
all learn from the sages;
yet in establishing words and cultivating rhetoric,
few can venerate the Classics.
Thus, the extravagance of Chǔ and the excess of Hàn,
their flaws flow unceasingly,
rectifying the end and returning to the root,
is it not admirable!
The eulogy says:
The eternal way of the three ultimates,
its teachings deep, examining antiquity.
Achieving transformation, returning to oneness,
divided teachings thus become five.
The smith of human nature,
the profound treasury of literature.
How profound and brilliant,
the ancestor of all words.
Rectifying the Apocrypha, Fourth
Now, the mystical way elucidates the obscure,
heaven's mandate subtly reveals,
the dragon-horse emerged and the "Great Yì" arose,
the divine turtle appeared and the "Great Plan" shone.
Thus the Xì Cí says, "The Hé produced the diagram,
the Luò produced the writing,
the sages took them as models,"
this is what it means.
But the age is remote, the texts obscure,
prone to generating falsities and fabrications,
though the truth exists,
the false also relies on it.
The Six Classics shine brilliantly,
while the Apocrypha are densely layered;
The Classic of Filial Piety and the Analects are clear and distinct,
yet the Hook Prophecies are lush and intricate.
Examining the Apocrypha against the Classics,
their falseness manifests in four aspects:
Now, the Apocrypha's formation from the Classics
resembles weaving,
where silk and hemp do not mix,
and only then are cloth and silk produced;
but today, the Classics are orthodox while the Apocrypha are strange,
diverging a thousand miles apart—
this is the first falseness.
The Classics are explicit,
being the teachings of sages;
the Apocrypha are obscure,
being the doctrines of spirits;
the teachings of sages should be broad,
while the doctrines of spirits should be concise;
yet now the Apocrypha exceed the Classics in volume,
with spiritual principles even more numerous—
this is the second falseness.
If a mandate comes from Heaven,
it may be called a prophetic sign,
yet the eighty-one chapters
are all attributed to Confucius;
this would mean Yáo created the Green Charts,
and King Wén composed the Cinnabar Writings—
this is the third falseness.
Before the Shāng and Zhōu dynasties,
charts and records frequently appeared,
yet by the end of the Spring and Autumn period,
the various Classics were just being completed;
for the Apocrypha to precede the Classics
violates the logic of weaving—
this is the fourth falseness.
Since the falseness is clearly exposed,
their differing meanings become self-evident;
the Classics suffice for instruction—
what need is there for the Apocrypha?
Considering the appearance of charts and records,
they are auspicious mandates of Heaven,
serving to bless sages,
not intended to match the Classics.
Thus, when the River failed to produce a chart,
the Master sighed;
if such things could be fabricated,
there would be no need for lament.
In the past, the River Chart of King Kāng
was displayed in the Eastern Hall;
hence we know that prophetic mandates of earlier ages
were treasured and transmitted through generations,
and what Confucius compiled
was merely a record and preface.
Then, practitioners of arts and techniques
attached deceitful methods,
some expounding on yīn and yáng,
others detailing disasters and anomalies,
like birds' chirping resembling speech,
or insects nibbling leaves into characters;
as chapters and条目 proliferated,
they invariably假托 Confucius.
Erudite scholars investigated and verified,
asserting that these forgeries began in the reigns of Āi and Píng,
and the secret treasures of the Eastern Hall
became confused with counterfeits.
By the time of Emperor Guāngwǔ's reign,
there was firm belief in these techniques.
Influenced by prevailing customs,
scholars emulated each other;
Prince Peì Xiàn collected the Apocrypha to understand the Classics,
and Cáo Bāo compiled prophecies to establish rituals—
deviating from the true path and distorting the canons,
this was indeed extreme.
Thus, Huán Tán denounced their falseness,
Yǐn Mǐn mocked their flaws,
Zhāng Héng exposed their absurdities,
and Xún Yuè clarified their deceptions;
these four worthies, broad and astute,
discussed the matter with precision.
As for the origins of Fúxī, Shénnóng, Xuānyuán, and Hàoxì,
the essentials of mountains, rivers, bells, and pitch-pipes,
the omens of the white fish and red crow,
the auspicious signs of yellow gold and purple jade—
these matters are rich in wonder and grandeur,
their language lush and fertile,
of no benefit to the Classics but aiding literary composition.
Therefore, later writers
gathered their finest elements;
Píngzǐ (Zhāng Héng), fearing they would mislead learning,
petitioned for their prohibition;
Zhòngyù (Xún Yuè), regretting their adulteration of truth,
did not advocate their burning;
since earlier times paired them with the Classics,
I have discussed them in detail.
The eulogy says:
The glorious River and warm Luò River
conceived the charts and Apocrypha.
Divine treasures concealed their utility,
principles hidden, yet texts valued.
Through the two Hàn dynasties,
genuine and false surged tumultuously.
Weeding out the deceitful and詭異,
harvest their ornate beauty.
Discrimination of the Lí Sāo - Part Five
Discrimination of the Lí Sāo - Part Five
Since the sounds of the Fēng and Yǎ faded,
none could continue their thread,
until extraordinary writings emerged luxuriantly—
this was the Lí Sāo!
It truly soared after the poets,
and soared high before the rhetoricians;
was it not because it was not far from the sage's time,
and the people of Chǔ were so talented!
In the past, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn loved the Sāo,
and the King of Huáinán composed a commentary,
believing that "the Guó Fēng expresses love without licentiousness,
the Xiǎo Yǎ complains without rebellion;
as for the Lí Sāo,
it may be said to combine both.
Shedding the mortal coil amidst filth,
floating beyond the dust of the world,
spotlessly pure, unblackened by dye—
it could contend in brilliance with the sun and moon."
Bān Gù considered it "flaunting talent and promoting oneself,
resentful, drowning in the river;
Yì, Ào, and the two Yáo,
inconsistent with the Zuǒ Zhuàn;
Kūnlún and Xuán Pǔ,
not recorded in the Classics' meanings;
yet its language is elegant and beautiful,
the ancestor of poetry and rhapsody—
though not from a wise man,
it may be called a work of exquisite talent."
Wáng Yì believed that "while the poets grasped ears to admonish,
Qū Yuán was gentle and顺从,
the text of the Lí Sāo
establishes meanings based on the Classics;
riding a dragon-drawn chariot with phoenix wings
parallels 'sometimes riding six dragons';
Kūnlún and the Flowing Sands
echo the Yǔ Gòng's description of taming the land;
famous scholars and writers of rhapsodies
all emulate its model,
what is called 'golden form and jade substance,'
unmatched for a hundred generations."
When Emperor Xuān of Hàn admired it,
he deemed it aligned with Classical teachings;
Yáng Xióng, reciting and savoring it,
also said its style matched the Shī and Yǎ.
Four schools compared it to the Classics,
yet Mèngjiān (Bān Gù) claimed it did not match the commentaries;
praise and blame based on hearsay,
overly exaggerated in criticism or acclaim—
this may be called discerning but not precise,
appreciative yet unverified.
To examine its arguments,
one must verify its expressions.
Thus its portrayal of Yáo and Shùn's uprightness,
and praise of Tāng and Yǔ's reverence,
embodies the style of canonical documents;
its criticism of Jié and Zhòu's arrogance,
and lament over Yì and Ào's downfall,
conveys the purpose of admonition;
using the horned dragon to symbolize the noble man,
and clouds and rainbows to represent slanderous evil,
manifests the principle of metaphorical imagery;
each glance evoking lingering tears,
sighing over the ninefold gates to the sovereign's court,
constitutes the language of loyal grievance.
Observing these four aspects,
they align with the Guófēng and Xiǎoyǎ.
As for depicting cloud-dragons,
relating fantastic tales,
Fēnglóng seeking Fúfēi,
the Zhen bird matchmaking for the Sōng maiden,
these are bizarre expressions;
Gōnggōng tilting the earth,
Yíyì shooting down suns,
the wooden man with nine heads,
the earth spirit with three eyes,
these are strange narratives;
following Péngxián's legacy,
accompanying Wǔ Zǐxū to satisfy oneself,
reflects a rigid and narrow will;
men and women mingling in seating,
disorderly and indistinguishable,
pointed to as pleasure,
endless carousing with wine,
day and night indulgence,
celebrated as joy,
conveys wanton licentiousness.
Extracting these four elements,
they diverge from classical texts.
Thus discussing its canonical aspects yields the former,
while addressing its exaggerations reveals the latter.
Hence we know the Chǔcí
embodies the models of the Three Dynasties,
yet its style blends with the Warring States period,
making it a gambler among the Yǎ and Sòng,
yet a master among poetic compositions.
Observing its structural framework
and textual embodiment,
while drawing from the essence of the Classics,
it forges its own magnificent language.
Thus the "Lísāo" and "Jiǔ Zhāng"
shine with luminous beauty while mourning aspirations;
the "Jiǔ Gē" and "Jiǔ Biàn"
display delicate elegance while grieving emotions;
the "Yuǎnyóu" and "Tiānwèn"
appear fantastically strange yet ingeniously clever;
the "Zhāohún" and "Dàzhāo"
radiate dazzling splendor with profound richness;
the "Bǔjū" marks the spirit of unfettered speech,
the "Yúfǔ" entrusts the talent of solitary independence.
Thus its energy surpasses antiquity,
its language cuts through the present,
with astonishing brilliance and peerless beauty,
none can equal its achievements.
From the "Jiǔ Huái" onward,
writers hastily followed its traces;
yet Qū Yuán and Sòng Yù's transcendent strides,
none could hope to match.
Thus in narrating sorrowful grievances,
it conveys melancholy that easily moves;
describing separation,
it expresses anguish difficult to bear;
discussing mountains and rivers,
one follows the rhythm to grasp their form;
speaking of seasonal changes,
one unfolds the text to perceive the time.
Therefore Méi Chéng and Jiǎ Yì pursued its style into elegance,
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú and Yáng Xióng followed its flow to obtain wonder,
its influence on poets
spans not merely one generation.
Thus the highly talented comprehend its grand structure,
the moderately clever hunt its beautiful phrases,
reciters cherish its landscapes,
novices gather its fragrant herbs.
If one can lean on the carriage rail to approach the Yǎ and Sòng,
yet rein in the steeds to master the Chǔ pieces,
savoring the extraordinary without losing authenticity,
admiring the blossoms without discarding the fruit;
then a mere glance can drive literary power,
a casual remark can exhaust literary essence,
no longer needing to seek inspiration from Xiāngrú,
nor borrow grace from Zǐyuān.
Appraisal:
Without Qū Yuán,
how could we have the "Lísāo"?
His astonishing talent flows like the wind,
his lofty aspirations rise like smoke.
Mountains and rivers know no bounds,
emotion and principle truly toilsome.
Golden substance and jade form,
every hair's breadth exquisitely beautiful.
Elucidating Poetry - Part 6
The great Shùn declared:
"Poetry expresses intent,
song prolongs the words."
As analyzed by the sage,
the meaning is already clear.
Thus what is in the heart becomes intent,
expressed in words becomes poetry,
unfolding literary form to carry substance,
is this not its essence!
Poetry is
sustaining,
sustaining human nature;
the essence of the Three Hundred Poems,
their meaning returns to innocence,
taking 'sustaining' as the teaching,
indeed corresponds to this.
The Music Bureau is where
tones follow chanting,
and pitch-pipes harmonize the tones.
The nine performances in the central heaven
were for the Supreme Deity;
the eight songs of Gětiān
belonged to the age of sovereigns.
Since the time of "Xián" and "Yīng,"
there is nothing more to be discussed.
As for the song of Túshān "Waiting for the Man,"
it began the southern music;
the ballad of Yǒusōng about the flying swallow
began the northern tunes;
Xià Jiǎ's lament in Dōngyáng
gave rise to the eastern music;
Yǐn Zhěng's longing by the Western River
brought forth the western melodies;
the evolution of music and sounds
is not uniform.
When common men and women
sing their local folk songs,
poetry officials collect the words,
and music masters set them to pitch,
their emotions affect the strings and bamboo,
their spirit transforms the metal and stone instruments.
Thus, Shī Kuàng observed prosperity and decline through the airs,
Jì Zhá discerned subtle signs of rise and fall,
so profound was their insight.
Since music originates from the heart,
its resonance penetrates flesh and marrow;
the ancient kings were cautious about it,
striving to curb excess and decadence.
In educating the scions,
they invariably sang of the nine virtues;
thus, emotions could move the seven beginnings,
and transformation stir the eight winds.
As the elegant music gradually declined,
decadent tunes surged forth;
the Qin burned the "Classic of Music,"
and the early Han sought to restore it,
with Zhì Shì recording its resonances,
and Shūsūn setting its ceremonial forms;
then "Wǔdé" arose under Gāozǔ,
"Four Seasons" expanded under Xiàowén,
though imitating "Sháo" and "Xià,"
they largely followed Qin's old ways,
the harmonious sounds
fell silent, never to return.
When Wǔdì revered rituals,
he first established the Music Bureau,
gathering the music of Zhào and Dài,
collecting the spirit of Qí and Chǔ,
Yánnián harmonized melodies with graceful tones,
Zhū and Mǎ composed songs in the "Sāo" style,
"Guìhuá" among the miscellaneous tunes,
beautiful but unorthodox,
"Chìyàn" in its many pieces,
exquisite yet not canonical,
though Héjiān presented elegant music, it was seldom used,
hence Jí Àn criticized the "Heavenly Horse."
By the time of Xuāndì's elegant poetry,
it somewhat imitated "Lù Míng";
reaching Yuán and Chéng's reigns,
decadent music gradually spread;
proper music clashed with popular taste,
so difficult it was.
In the Later Han's suburban and temple rites,
only mixed elegant pieces were used,
though the lyrics were classical,
the music was not like Kuí or Kuàng's.
As for the three ancestors of Wei,
their spirit was vigorous and talent brilliant,
they tailored lyrics and tunes,
resulting in melodious but placid rhythms.
Looking at their numerous compositions like "Northward March,"
and the series of "Autumn Wind" pieces,
some describe feasts and revelry,
others lament border garrison life,
their themes not beyond indulgence,
their words never straying from sorrow,
though formally correct in the three modes,
they are in essence the decadent tunes of "Sháo" and "Xià."
By the Jin dynasty,
Fù Xuán understood music,
creating and defining elegant songs
to praise the ancestors;
Zhāng Huá's new works
also filled the court.
Yet Dù Kuí adjusted the pitches,
producing舒缓雅致 music,
while Xún Xù altered the bell racks,
making the sounds mournful and urgent,
so Ruǎn Xián criticized the discordance,
later verified by the bronze ruler,
the refinement of harmonious music
indeed relies on both form and substance.
Thus, poetry is the heart of music,
sound is the body of music;
the body of music lies in sound,
so the blind musicians must tune their instruments;
the heart of music lies in poetry,
so the nobleman should correct the text.
"Love music but not to excess,"
is why the Jìn airs are praised for their depth;
"teasing each other,"
is why the state of Zhèng is said to have perished.
Thus, when Jì Zhá observed the music,
he did not merely listen to the sounds.
As for charming songs of tender love,
and plaints of severed affections,
with licentious words set to melodies,
how can proper music arise!
Yet popular tastes race ahead,
vying for novelty and strangeness,
elegant chants of warmth and reverence
inevitably induce yawns and vacant stares;
while unusual lyrics that strike home
make people slap thighs and leap like sparrows;
when both poetry and music become decadent,
it starts from this step.
Generally, lyrics for music are called shī (poetry),
chanting them is called gē (song);
when music is applied to lyrics,
complex lyrics are hard to set to rhythm;
hence, Chénsī noted, "Zuǒ Yánnián is skilled at editing ancient lyrics,
reducing them when too lengthy,"
emphasizing conciseness.
Observing Gāozǔ's "Great Wind,"
and Xiàowǔ's "Why So Late,"
when sung by choristers,
none dared not harmonize;
Zǐjiàn and Shìhéng
both had fine pieces,
yet without instructing the musicians,
they were not set to instruments,
commonly called out of tune,
perhaps unthinkingly.
As for the chariot music of Xuān and Qí,
the náo and dirge music of the Han,
though for war and mourning respectively,
all were included in the Music Bureau,
as compiled by Miù Xí,
they too are noteworthy.
In the past, Zǐzhèng classified literature,
distinguishing shī from gē,
so I briefly provide this chapter on music,
to mark the boundaries.
Summary:
The eight tones weave patterns,
establishing lyrics as the form.
Chanted in the wild fields,
resounding in the palace halls.
The sound of "Sháo" is hard to recapture,
decadent tunes easily arise.
Not only to observe music,
but also to recognize ritual therein.
Exposition on the Fǔ, Part Eight
Exposition on the Fǔ, Part Eight
The "Book of Songs" has six principles,
the second being fǔ.
Fǔ means
to spread out;
spreading colors and weaving patterns,
to embody objects and express intent.
In the past, Shào Gōng said, "Ministers present poems,
masters admonish, blind men chant fǔ."
The "Zhuàn" states:
"He who can compose fǔ upon ascending heights
may become a senior official."
The "Preface to the Songs" aligns in meaning,
while the "Zhuàn" presents a different form,
but overall,
they are like branches and trunk.
Thus, Liú Xiàng clarified that it is recited, not sung,
and Bān Gù called it a branch of ancient poetry.
As for Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng's composition of "The Great Tunnel,"
and Shì Wěi's composition of "The Fox Fur,"
they express ideas through rhymes,
with words composed by themselves.
Although they align with the style of fù,
they are clear yet not fully developed.
When Qū Yuán sang the "Sāo,"
he began to expand its sound and form.
Thus, the fù
inherited its essence from the poets
and broadened its scope through the "Chǔcí."
Subsequently, Xún Kuàng with "Rites" and "Wisdom,"
and Sòng Yù with "Wind" and "Fishing,"
were bestowed with names,
demarcating a boundary from poetry.
As a vassal of the six principles,
it flourished into a grand domain.
They used dialogues to introduce themes,
exhaustively describing sounds and appearances to the fullest in writing.
This marks the origin of distinguishing fù from poetry,
the very beginning of naming the fù.
The Qín dynasty lacked literary refinement,
yet had quite a few miscellaneous fù.
The literary figures of the early Hàn dynasty
followed this stream and composed,
with Lù Jiǎ initiating its start,
Jiǎ Yì carrying on its thread,
Méi Chéng and Sīmǎ Xiāngrú sharing its style,
Wáng Bāo and Yáng Xióng displaying its momentum.
From Gāo and Shuò onward,
all kinds of objects were fully depicted.
It accumulated abundantly by the Xuān period,
and was compiled and reviewed in the Chéng era,
with fù presented to the court
numbering over a thousand pieces.
Examining their origins and developments,
it is evident they arose in Chǔ and flourished in Hàn.
As for those on capitals, palaces, parks, and hunts,
narrating journeys and expressing aspirations,
they all embody the governance of the state and the planning of the countryside,
upholding grand and luminous principles.
They begin with an introductory recitation,
and conclude with a summarizing finale.
The preface establishes the theme,
first introducing the emotional basis;
the finale organizes the piece,
reinforcing the literary momentum.
Considering the final chapter of "Nuó,"
Mǐn Mǎ referred to it as the finale.
Thus, we know the Yīn people compiled the "Odes,"
and the Chǔ people structured the fù.
These represent the vast realm of grand compositions,
the pivotal core of elegant literature.
As for grasses, zones of birds,
and various miscellaneous categories,
they stir emotions and evoke feelings,
adapting to changes to capture harmony.
In describing their forms,
the language must be intricate and detailed;
in representing their essence,
the reasoning values subtle associations;
this is the domain of minor compositions,
the essence of ingenious craft.
Observing Xún Kuàng's use of riddles,
where events cycle back on themselves;
Sòng Yù's clever discourses,
indeed began the trend of excessive ornamentation.
Méi Chéng's "Rabbit Garden,"
highlights essentials with novelty;
Simǎ Xiāngrú's "Supreme Park,"
enriches categories with lavish beauty;
Jiǎ Yì's "Owl,"
delves into reasoning and emotion;
Wáng Bāo's "Panpipes,"
exhausts variations in sound and form;
Bān Gù's "Two Capitals,"
is brilliantly ornate and elegantly ample;
Zhāng Héng's "Two Capitals,"
swift and sharp with vast richness;
constructs a profound and majestic style;
Wáng Yánshòu's "Numinous Light,"
contains a dynamic and soaring momentum;
all these ten masters
are the outstanding talents of cí and fù.
As for Wáng Càn's delicate intricacy,
his openings are always forceful;
Xú Gàn's broad erudition,
often meets with vigorous brilliance;
Zuǒ Sī and Pān Yuè,
achieved merits in grand designs;
Lù Jī and Chéng Gōngsǔ,
succeeded in flowing styles;
Guō Pú's elegant ingenuity,
abundant in ornate reasoning;
Yuán Hóng's bold outlines,
never lacking in emotional resonance;
they are also the leading fù writers of the Wèi and Jìn dynasties.
The essence of ascending heights
lies in observing things to stir emotions.
Emotions are stirred by things,
hence the meaning must be clear and elegant;
things are viewed through emotions,
hence the words must be clever and beautiful.
Beautiful words and elegant meaning,
with inner brilliance complementing each other,
like the grading of red and purple in weaving,
or the application of black and yellow in painting.
Though the patterns may be mixed, they have substance;
though the colors may be blended, they have order.
This is the fundamental principle of composing fù.
However, those who chase the trivial
disregard its essence.
Even if they read a thousand fù,
they become more confused about the core tenets.
Thus, allowing excessive flourish to harm the branches,
and richness to injure the bones,
without valuing moral influence,
and offering no benefit for admonition.
This is why Yáng Xióng regretted pursuing such ornate carving,
and was mocked for his "mist-like gauze."
The Eulogy says:
Fù springs from poetry,
branching into different schools.
Depicting things and sketching forms,
flourishing like carved paintings.
Suppressed stagnation must be uplifted,
words, though common, should not be narrow.
Style should return to beauty with principles,
trimming words like weeding out tares.
Eulogies and Encomiums, the Ninth.
Among the four beginnings,
the Eulogy stands at the ultimate.
The Eulogy,
meaning "appearance,"
is used to praise virtuous achievements and describe forms and appearances.
In the age of Emperor Kù in ancient times,
Xiánmò composed eulogies
to sing the "Nine Sháo."
From the Shāng dynasty onward,
their literary principles became fully developed.
That which transforms one state is called "Fēng";
that which rectifies all quarters is called "Yǎ";
and that which presents appearances to inform the spirits is called "Sòng."
Fēng and Yǎ narrate human affairs,
hence they encompass both normal and altered states;
whereas the Eulogy primarily informs the spirits,
so its meaning must be purely beautiful.
Lǔ arranged theirs according to the Duke of Zhōu's order,
while Shāng retrospectively recorded former kings—
these were the proper songs for ancestral temples,
not the usual chants for feasts and banquets.
The piece "Shí Mài,"
composed by the Duke of Zhōu,
and the eulogies of the sage,
preserved the model and form.
Now, people each have their own minds,
and their mouths should not be stopped;
the Jìn carriage's reference to the fields,
the Lǔ people's criticism of fur and leather,
speaking directly without chanting,
using brief words for satire—
Qiūmíng and Zǐgāo
both recorded these as eulogies,
which are altered forms of folk eulogies,
gradually extending to human affairs.
By the time of Sānlǘ's "Jú Sòng,"
its emotion and literary grace were fragrant,
using comparisons to convey meanings,
further extending to small objects.
As for Qín Shǐhuáng's inscribed texts,
they praised his virtue;
and under Hàn's Emperor Huì and Jǐng,
there were also descriptions of appearances;
through successive generations, they were composed,
continuing over time.
As for Zǐyún's praise of Chōnguó,
Mèngjiān's preface for Dàihóu,
Wǔzhòng's exaltation of Xiǎnzōng,
Shǐ Cén's account of Xī Hòu—
some imitated "Qīng Miào,"
others modeled on "Jiōng Nuó,"
though their depth varied,
and their detail differed,
in praising virtue and displaying appearances,
their classical form was uniform.
But with Bān and Fù's "Northern Expedition" and "Western Expedition,"
they altered into prefaces and introductions—
was this not excessive praise and a distorted form?
Mǎ Róng's "Guǎngchéng" and "Shànglín,"
elegant yet resembling rhapsodies—
how they toyed with words and lost substance!
Further, Cuī Yuàn's "Wénxué,"
Cài Yōng's "Fán Qú,"
both excelled in their prefaces,
but were concise in the main text;
Zhì Yú's critiques
were quite precise,
yet when he spoke of mixing with Fēng and Yǎ
without changing the essence,
he merely spread empty theories,
resembling the false arguments about yellow and white.
By the time of Wèi and Jìn miscellaneous eulogies,
few departed from these tracks.
Chén Sī's compositions
marked by "Huángzǐ";
Lù Jī's accumulated pieces,
with "Gōngchén" as the most prominent—
their blend of praise and criticism
truly represents the corrupted style of the decadent age.
Fundamentally, the Eulogy should be dignified and elegant;
its diction must be clear and brilliant,
descriptive like the rhapsody,
yet not entering the realm of ornate extravagance;
reverent and cautious like the inscription,
but differing from the domain of admonition;
extolling to display literary grace,
vast and profound to establish meaning,
though with intricate subtleties and clever expressions,
varying with the emotion,
the essential foundation it rests upon,
is just as described.
The Encomium,
meaning "to clarify,"
and "to assist."
In the sacrifices of Emperor Shùn of Yú in antiquity,
the music master reiterated the encomium,
likely the words to initiate the singing.
As for Yì's encomium to Yǔ,
and Yīzhì's praise to Wūxián,
both were declarations to clarify matters,
and exclamations to assist the words.
Thus, the Hàn dynasty established the Court of State Ceremonial,
where chanting bows served as encomiums—
this was the legacy of ancient speech.
By the time of Xiàngrú's writings,
he first composed an encomium for "Jīng Kē."
And in the historical books of Bān Gù,
he used encomiums for praise and blame.
Condensing the text to summarize,
employing the eulogy style for discursive language;
also, the critiques after annals and biographies,
shared the same name.
Yet Zhòngzhì's "Liúbié"
mistakenly called them "accounts,"
erring greatly.
When Jǐngchún annotated the "Ěryǎ,"
he added encomiums on animals and plants,
with meanings including both good and bad—
this too resembles a variation of the eulogy.
However, based on its original meaning,
it arises from commendation and admiration,
so since ancient times, the form of the pieces
has been brief and not expansive,
necessarily concluding with four-character lines,
lingering within a few rhyming phrases,
concisely expressing to exhaust emotion,
and brilliantly conveying to present the text—
this is its form.
Though its origin is ancient,
its practical use is rather scarce;
in general, where it belongs,
is it a minor branch of the eulogy family!
Summary:
Form and substance achieve the eulogy,
meritorious deeds bequeath the encomium.
Carving shadows and arranging sounds,
the patterns of literature shine brightly.
As years accumulate and pass into distance,
their harmonious tones remain as at dawn.
Descending to the grading of things,
flaunting words becomes a diversion.
Tenth: Prayers and Covenants
Heaven and Earth have their fixed positions,
sacrifices extend to all deities.
After the six revered objects have been offered to with reverence,
and the three celestial observations are all in order,
seasonable rain and gentle breeze
give birth to millet and grain.
What the millions of people look up to
gives rise to beautiful expressions of gratitude.
Though the sacrificial offerings are fragrant,
they originate from bright virtue.
When the prayer-officers present their sincerity,
they rely on literary compositions.
In ancient times, Yìqí began the Zhà sacrifice,
to worship the eight deities.
The prayer read:
"May the soil return to its dwelling,
the waters go back to their gullies,
insects not cause harm,
and weeds go back to the marshes."
Thus, the prayer texts of the supreme sovereigns
are found here.
Shùn's prayer for the fields said:
"Carrying this long plow,
I cultivate those southern acres,
may all within the four seas share in abundance."
His intent to benefit the people
is clearly expressed in these words.
As for Shāng Lǚ (Tang of Shang),
his sage-like reverence daily ascended,
with a black bull he announced to Heaven,
taking upon himself the crimes of all regions—
this was the suburban sacrifice.
With a plain carriage he prayed for rain,
blaming himself for six faults—
this was the text of the rain sacrifice.
By the time of the Zhōu dynasty's Grand Prayer-officer,
who was in charge of the prayers for the six sacrifices,
thus all creatures flourished,
presented in the suburban ceremonies to Heaven and Earth;
solemnly assisting,
they chanted in the worship greeting the sun;
rising early and resting late,
they spoke in the prayers accompanying the temple ceremonies;
"boundless blessings"
were announced in the offering of the Shàoláo sacrifice;
for the appropriate earth and similar war sacrifices,
there were none without their texts.
All this was to show reverence to the spirits,
and respect to the ancestral temples.
From the Spring and Autumn period onward,
sacrifices became excessive and flattering,
with prayer-offerings and scribe's words
reaching every deity.
As when Zhāng Lǎo, upon the completion of his house, offered praises in his prayer of song and lament;
or Kuǎikuì, on the eve of battle,
gained protection through his plea concerning sinews and bones;
even in haste or distress,
they invariably resorted to prayers.
As for the "Summoning the Soul" in the Chǔcí,
it may be called a masterpiece of prayer literature.
The various sacrifices of the Hàn dynasty
solemnized their intent and ritual,
combining the ceremonies of great Confucian scholars
with the methods of alchemists.
Thus, the secret prayers to transfer faults
differed from the heart of Chéng Tāng;
the exorcism by child-mediums
resembled the prayers of Yuè shamans—
a gradual loss of substance.
Moreover, Huángdì had the text "Prayer Against Evil Spirits,"
and Dōngfāng Shuò had the book "Cursing Ghosts,"
whereafter later condemnations and curses
aimed at skillful invective.
Only Chén Sī's "Questioning Calamity"
was framed with correct principles.
As for the sacrificial prayers in the rites,
their purpose was merely to announce the offering;
but prayers of the middle ages
also praised the words and deeds.
Combining sacrifice with praise,
was probably to draw the spirits near.
Also, during the Hàn dynasty, for the imperial tombs,
elegies became current texts;
when Zhōu mourned Shèng Jī,
the interior scribe held the written eulogy.
Thus, the eulogy was originally a written gift,
composed out of grief.
Therefore, its meaning is similar to the lěi (funeral ode),
but the text is actually addressed to the spirits,
beginning with the lěi and ending with grief,
in the form of a eulogy but with the ceremony of prayer.
The eulogies composed by the Grand Scribe
followed the prayer texts of the Zhōu.
While ordinary writings strive for elegance,
invoking spirits requires sincerity.
Cultivating words and establishing honesty
lie in having no shame.
The model for prayers
must be sincere and respectful;
the pattern for sacrificial offerings
should be reverent and sorrowful—
this is the general idea.
Bān Gù's "Sacrifice to Zhuō Mountain"
exemplifies the reverence of prayer;
Pān Yuè's "Offering for the Woman Yǔ"
shows the respect and grief of sacrifice.
Considering these examples,
the principle is clearly evident.
As for covenants (méng), they are
about clarity.
With a red ox and a white horse,
pearl-decorated tray and jade vessel,
the words are declared under the square brightness (altar),
praying and announcing to the divine spirits.
In the times of the Three Sovereigns,
there were no sworn covenants;
occasionally there were earnest oaths,
sealed with words before parting.
With the decline of Zhōu, covenants became frequent,
leading to the abuse of coercion,
beginning with Cáo Mò
and ending with Máo Suì.
When Qín Zhāo made a covenant with the barbarians,
he set up the curse of the yellow dragon;
when Hàn Gāo enfeoffed lords,
he established the oath of the mountains and rivers.
Yet if the principle remains, the covenant is kept till the end;
if the way is abandoned, it is broken from the start.
Rise and fall lie with men;
what have curses to do with it?
As for Zāng Hóng's blood-oath,
its spirit cut through the clouds and rainbow;
Liú Kūn's iron oath,
its essence pierced the flying frost.
Yet they did not benefit Jìn or Hàn,
instead turning into enmity.
Thus it is known that if faith is not from the heart,
a covenant is of no use.
The main elements of a covenant
must describe the crisis,
encourage loyalty and filial piety,
pledge shared survival or perish,
join hearts and strength,
entreat the unseen spirits to bear witness,
point to the nine heavens as proof,
stir emotions to establish sincerity,
and express earnestness in the wording—
these are their common features.
Yet the difficulty lies not in the words,
but in abiding by them.
Later gentlemen
should keep this warning in mind:
loyalty and faith suffice,
do not rely on the spirits.
Encomium says:
Reverent sacrifices, respectful and bright,
Prayer-officers solely discourse.
Establishing sincerity requires solemnity,
Cultivating words must be pleasing.
In later ages, more adorned,
Ornate speech, vermilion and blue.
When the spirits descend,
What is valued is being without shame.
Inscriptions and Admonitions, Chapter Eleven
In ancient times, Emperor Xuānyuán inscribed warnings on carriages and tables to rectify faults,
while Great Yǔ engraved admonitions on bell frames to solicit remonstrance.
Chéng Tāng's basin
bore the rule of daily self-renewal;
King Wǔ's inscriptions on doors and mats
carried exhortations to constant vigilance.
The Duke of Zhōu cautioned against careless speech through the bronze figure,
and Confucius showed reverence before the tilted vessel:
thus, the exemplars and warnings of the ancient sages
have a long history indeed.
Hence, "inscription" (míng)
means "naming,"
for observing an vessel requires correct naming,
and examining its use values noble virtue.
As Zāng Wǔzhòng's discourse on inscriptions states:
The Son of Heaven extols virtue,
feudal lords record achievements,
and ministers proclaim their service."
The Xià dynasty cast the Nine Provinces' bronze tripod,
and the Zhōu inscribed the Sùshèn tribe's arrowheads:
these are matters of extolling virtue.
Lǚ Wàng's merits engraved at Kūnwú,
and Zhòngshān's accomplishments carved on ceremonial vessels:
these signify recording achievements.
Wèi Kē's merit recorded on the Jǐng Bell,
and Kǒng Kuī's diligence displayed on the Wèi tripod:
these represent proclaiming service.
As for Fēilián receiving a stone outer coffin as reward,
and Duke Líng getting a posthumous title from his burial mound:
such inscriptions emerging from hidden stones
are indeed strange!
Zhào Líng carving his footprint on Pānwú,
and Qín Zhāo inscribing his gaming board on Huà Mountain:
such boastful displays to posterity
are truly laughable!
Examining these various examples,
the meaning of inscriptions becomes clear.
As for the First Emperor's mountain inscriptions,
though his rule was tyrannical, the writing was elegant,
possessing a certain lucid beauty.
Like Bān Gù's inscription at Yānrán Mountain,
and Zhāng Chǎng's stele at Huáyīn:
their prefaces are also magnificent.
Cài Yōng's conception in inscriptions
stands uniquely supreme across ages.
His inscription on Qiáo's battle-axe
embodies the style of canonical documents;
his inscription for Zhū Mù's tripod
fully adopts the form of a stele text:
this shows his indulgence in his strengths.
As for Jìng Tōng's inscriptions on miscellaneous objects,
though modeled on warning inscriptions,
the content mismatches the objects,
with inappropriate elaboration and concision.
Cuī Yīn's catalog of objects
contains more praise than warning;
Lǐ Yóu's accumulated writings
show meager meaning and fragmented language.
To place divination stalks and tortoise shells—sacred objects—
alongside dice and board games;
and put steelyards and standard measures—exemplary vessels—
after mortars and pestles:
when even naming and categorization are neglected,
how can one master principles of affairs?
Wèi Wén's "Nine Treasures"
have sharp objects but dull words.
Only Zhāng Zǎi's "Jiàngé Inscription"
possesses clear talent and elegant style.
Like a swift runner galloping,
arriving later but surpassing others,
his inscription at Mín-Hàn
achieves perfect appropriateness.
"Admonition" (zhēn)
means "needle,"
used to attack ailments and prevent harm,
metaphorically like acupuncture stones.
The rise of this genre
flourished during the Three Dynasties.
The two admonitions of Xià and Shāng
survive only in scattered phrases.
By Zhōu times, Xīn Jiǎ
had officials write admonitions for oversight,
with only the "Yú Admonition" piece
fully preserving the form and meaning.
Through the Spring and Autumn period,
it declined but did not vanish.
Thus, Wèi Jiǎng admonished his ruler using Hòu Yì's story,
and the Chǔ viscount instructed his people on diligence.
Since the Warring States era,
with virtue abandoned and merit pursued,
inscriptions rose to prominence,
while admonition texts nearly vanished,
until Yáng Xióng, studying antiquity,
first modeled on the "Yú Admonition,"
composing twenty-five pieces for ministers and regional governors.
Then Cuī and Hú supplemented them,
collectively titled "The Hundred Officials,"
matching content to positions,
serving as a mirror for reflection:
truly this pursued ancient purity,
following Xīn Jiǎ in later times.
As for Pān Xù's "Tallies and Credentials,"
concise but shallow;
Wēn Qiáo's "Attending Officials,"
broad but overly elaborate;
Wáng Jì's "National Officers,"
extensive but cluttered;
Pān Ní's "Imperial Carriage,"
correct in meaning but chaotic in form:
all these subsequent works
rarely achieve balance.
As for Wáng Lǎng's "Miscellaneous Admonitions,"
placing turbans and shoes
achieves caution
but misplaces their application.
Though concise and essential in style,
modeled on warning inscriptions,
his discussions of fire, water, wells, and stoves
become endlessly wordy:
a case of skewed focus.
Now admonitions are recited by officials,
while inscriptions are marked on vessels,
differing in name and category,
but identical in warning purpose.
Admonitions purely defend against error,
hence requiring precise substance and form;
inscriptions combine praise with commemoration,
thus valuing grand and polished style;
their content must be verified and clear,
their expression must be concise and profound:
these are the essential points.
Yet the way of straightforward speech has faded,
and the tradition of commemorative vessels long declined,
hence admonitions and inscriptions see sparse use,
rarely applied in later ages.
May literary gentlemen
consider their enduring significance.
Summary:
Inscriptions manifest vessels' worth,
admonitions guide virtue's path.
Let words be worn as adornments,
not merely water-reflected images.
Holding this steadfast vigilance,
heedful in every step.
Noble meaning brings grandeur,
concise writing embodies beauty.
Lěi and Bēi: Part Twelve
In the prosperous era of the Zhōu dynasty,
there existed the genres of inscription and eulogy.
The talent of a nobleman
enabled him to compose eulogies during mourning.
A eulogy,
is an accumulation;
it gathers the virtues and deeds
to commemorate them for eternity.
Before the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
details are scarcely heard of.
Although eulogies existed in the Zhōu period,
they were not applied to common scholars.
Moreover, the lowly did not eulogize the noble,
nor the young the elder.
For the sovereign,
heaven was invoked to eulogize him.
Reading the eulogy to determine the posthumous title
was a grand ceremonial practice.
Starting from the battle of Chéngqiū under Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ,
it began to extend to scholars.
Upon the death of Confucius,
Duke Āi composed a eulogy.
Observing the words of lament and remembrance,
the sighs of "alas,"
though not from a sage's work,
preserved the ancient form.
By the time of Liǔ's wife eulogizing Huìzǐ,
the language was sorrowful and resonant.
Reaching the Hàn dynasty,
the tradition continued.
Yáng Xióng's "Eulogy for Empress Yuán,"
was verbose and cluttered;
though Shālù summarized its essence,
Zhì suspected it as a complete piece.
How could one accumulate virtues and honor the revered
with merely four brief lines?
Dù Dǔ's eulogies
were praised in earlier times.
Though his "Eulogy for Wú" was skillful,
his other works were rather crude;
could fame from Emperor Guāngwǔ turn a glance into gold?
Fù Yì's compositions
were orderly in style,
while Xiào Shān and Cuī Yuàn
combined clarity and conciseness.
Their narratives resembled biographies,
with smooth language and rhythmic tone,
truly skilled in eulogy.
Pān Yuè's构思
drew heavily from Xiào Shān,
adept at conveying grief;
easily achieving novelty and precision,
thus across generations,
he earned his renown.
As for Cuī Yīn's "Eulogy for Zhào"
and Liú Táo's "Eulogy for Huáng,"
both followed the rules,
excelling in brevity.
Chén Sī, though famed,
had a verbose and sluggish style;
at the end of his "Eulogy for Emperor Wén,"
he added a hundred words about himself,
a grave misstep.
Like the Yīn ministers praising Tāng,
extolling the auspiciousness of the dark bird;
or the Zhōu historians singing of Wén,
elucidating the achievements of Hòujì.
Eulogizing ancestors
was the poets' principle.
As for expressing sorrow,
it expanded through related themes.
Fù Yì's "Eulogy for Běihǎi,"
saying "the bright sun dims,
mist and fog loom dark,"
began with evoking emotion,
setting a model for later times;
those who imitated it
gained much from its merit.
Examining the structure of eulogies,
they select words and record deeds,
adopting the form of biography and the style of ode,
starting with glory and ending with sorrow.
In portraying the person,
they should feel vivid and tangible;
in conveying grief,
they should evoke deep sorrow.
This is their essence.
A stele,
is for support.
In ancient times, emperors
recorded their titles and held fēngshàn ceremonies,
erecting stones by the mountains,
hence called steles.
King Mù of Zhōu recording his traces on Yǎnshān's rocks
also embodied the idea of steles.
Moreover, ancestral temples had steles,
placed between two pillars,
used only for tethering sacrificial animals,
not inscribed with achievements;
as ceremonial vessels declined,
later generations used steles,
replacing metal with stone,
equally enduring,
from temples to graves,
akin to sealing tombs.
Since the Eastern Hàn,
steles proliferated like clouds;
in literary prowess,
none surpassed Cài Yōng.
Observing his stele for Yáng Cì,
its backbone drawn from classical texts,
and the works for Chén and Guō,
every phrase impeccable.
The steles for Zhōu, Hú, and others,
all clear and fitting.
His narratives were comprehensive yet concise,
his language elegant and polished;
fresh phrases flowed endlessly,
clever ideas stood out distinctly;
assessing his talent,
it came naturally.
Kǒng Róng's creations
imitated Cài Bójiē;
his pieces for Zhāng and Chén,
eloquent and richly adorned,
were also commendable.
When Sūn Chuò wrote,
he aimed at steles,
but those for Wēn, Wáng, Xī, and Yǔ
were often verbose and杂乱;
only his piece for Huán Yí
was most concise and well-structured.
The nature of stele writing
relies on historical talent,
its narrative akin to biography,
its text like an inscription,
highlighting great virtues,
it must show the brilliance of pure character;
recording grand achievements,
it must reveal lofty and mighty deeds;
this is the form of a stele.
The stele is the vessel for inscriptions,
the inscription is the text of the stele,
naming based on the vessel,
predating eulogies.
Thus, engraving stones to praise merits
falls into the realm of inscriptions;
erecting steles to recount the deceased
belongs to the domain of eulogies.
Summary:
Recording reality and chasing the intangible,
steles and eulogies are established.
Inscribing virtues and compiling deeds,
literary elegance gathers duly.
Viewing their aura feels like facing the person,
hearing their words as if weeping.
Ink and stone carve their splendor,
how can their fading shadows cease?
Mourning and Condolence, Chapter Thirteen
The constitution of posthumous titles decrees,
that premature death is called "āi" (lamentable).
Āi (哀) means
to depend on.
Grief truly depends on the heart,
hence it is called "āi."
Using words to dispel grief
is generally the mourning of the lower stream,
thus it does not apply to the hoary-haired elderly,
but must be bestowed upon those who die young or prematurely.
In the past, the three good men were buried alive with the ruler of Qín,
and a hundred men could not redeem them;
their cases were equivalent to untimely and violent death.
The "Huáng Niǎo" (Yellow Bird) expresses grief,
isn't it also the lamentation of the poet?
When Emperor Wǔ of Hàn performed the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
and Huò Shàn suddenly died,
the emperor, grieving, composed a poem,
which also belongs to the category of哀辭 (lamentations).
Descending to the later Hàn,
when the King of Rǔyáng died,
Cuī Yuàn wrote a lament,
beginning to alter the previous form.
However, "treading abruptly at the ghost gate"
is bizarre and not fitting in language,
"driving dragons and riding clouds"
is immortal-like but not sorrowful;
moreover, the final stanza in five-character lines,
rather resembles folk songs,
also somewhat reminiscent of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
As for Sū Shùn and Zhāng Shēng,
both composed mourning writings,
although they expressed their emotional brilliance,
they did not fully convey the sincerity of their hearts.
The lamentations of the Jiàn'ān period,
only those of Wěichǎng (Xú Gàn) are relatively good,
his piece "Xíng Nǚ" (The Dying Girl),
at times evokes compassion.
When Pān Yuè continued the创作,
he truly gathered their beauty.
Observing his ample thoughts and varied diction,
his emotions deeply immersed in sorrow and bitterness,
narrating events like a biography,
and composing words imitating the Shījīng,
with concise four-character rhythms,
rarely are there lax lines;
thus he could achieve righteous straightforwardness with elegant writing,
a form that is ancient yet with novel charm,
his "Jīn Lù" (Golden Deer) and "Zé Lán" (Marsh Orchid),
none have succeeded them.
Examining the main form of lamentations,
the emotion is primarily pain and injury,
and the words exhaust love and tenderness.
As the young have not yet established virtue,
praise is limited to observed intelligence;
as the weak cannot bear duties,
mourning is added for complexion and appearance.
When the heart, harboring grief, composes the text, then the matter is satisfying;
when one views the text and then attaches the heart, the style becomes excessive.
Using an extravagant style for writing,
then even if beautiful, it is not sorrowful;
one must let emotion go forth to meet grief,
and the text come to induce tears,
that is its value.
Diào (condolence) means
to arrive.
The Shījīng says:
"The spirits have diào (arrived)."
This means the spirits have come.
When a gentleman ends well and is assigned a posthumous title,
the event is ultimate and the principle mournful,
so the guest comforting the host
uses words of arrival and reaching.
Those crushed or drowned deviate from the Way,
therefore they are not condoled.
Also, when Sòng suffered floods and Zhèng fires,
envoys offered words,
as state disasters and people's deaths
are similarly condoled.
When Jìn built the Sītái palace,
and Qí attacked the city of Yān,
Shǐ Zhào and Sū Qín
turned congratulations into condolences,
for oppressing the people and creating enemies
is also a path to perish.
All such examples
are where condolence is established.
Some, arrogant and noble, perish;
some, resentful and biased, deviate from the Way;
some have ambition but no opportunity;
some have fine talent but also burdens;
to reflect upon and comfort them,
all are named diào.
Since Jiǎ Yì floated on the Xiāng,
and vented his indignation in "Diào Qū" (Condoling Qū Yuán),
its style comprehensive and events verified,
its diction clear and reasoning mournful,
it is likely the pioneering work.
As for Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Diào Èrshì" (Condoling the Second Emperor),
it is entirely in the fù style;
Huán Tán considered its words poignant and sad,
making readers sigh;
and its final chapter is essential and incisive,
decisive yet able to evoke grief.
Yáng Xióng's "Diào Qū"
has accumulated thoughts but little achievement,
its intent deep in "Fǎn Sāo" (Countering the Lament),
thus the diction and rhythm are heavy and cumbersome.
Bān Biāo and Cài Yōng,
both adept in expressive language,
yet shadowing Jiǎ Yì,
find it hard to keep pace.
Hú and Ruǎn's "Diào Yí Qí" (Condoling Bó Yí and Shū Qí),
what Zhòngxuān (Wáng Càn) composed
is truly skillful in reproach and blame.
Thus, Hú and Ruǎn admired their purity,
while Prince (Wáng Càn) lamented their narrowness,
each according to their own will.
Mí Héng's "Diào Píng Zǐ" (Condoling Zhāng Héng)
is ornate and elegant yet frivolous;
Lù Jī's "Diào Wèi Wǔ" (Condoling Emperor Wǔ of Wèi)
has a clever preface but verbose text.
Descending from this onward,
none are worthy of mention.
Although condolence has ancient meaning,
elaborate diction had not yet developed;
if too ornate and rhythmically slow,
it transforms into fù.
Thus, one should rectify meaning to measure principle,
illuminate virtue and block transgressions,
dissect with praise and blame,
mournful yet correct,
then there will be no loss of order.
The eulogy says:
What the words mourn
lies in those young and playful.
Sprouts that do not blossom,
since ancient times, this is the grief.
Though there may be versatile talents,
they lose direction and control.
A thousand years can be mourned,
entrusted words to send them off.
Miscellaneous Writings, Chapter Fourteen
Those skilled in wisdom and methods,
and men of broad elegance,
have literary splendor overflowing in their words,
and words filled with spirit.
Cultivating literary emotions,
thus daily renewing with unique expressions.
Sòng Yù, endowed with talent,
was also somewhat burdened by vulgarity,
first created "Duìwèn" (Response to Queries),
to express his will,
releasing his mind into the vastness,
his spirit truly driving it.
When Měi Chéng displayed his brilliance,
he first composed "Qī Fā" (Seven Stimuli),
with rich phrases constructed like clouds,
extravagant and beautiful as the wind startles.
As the seven orifices emit,
they arise from desires,
beginning with depravity and ending with correctness,
thus warning the sons of luxury.
Yáng Xióng deeply pondered in the realm of literature,
profound in the craft of synthesis,
with fragmented texts and trivial phrases,
initiated "Liánzhū" (Linked Pearls),
pearls linking his words,
though small, they are bright and smooth.
All these three
are branches and offshoots of literature,
the lesser creations of leisurely ease.
Since "Response to Queries,"
Dōngfāng Shuò emulated and expanded it,
titled "Guest's Objection,"
using antiquity to console his aspirations,
sparse yet discerning.
Yáng Xióng's "Dispelling Ridicule,"
mixed with humor and jest,
circling back to explain himself,
is also quite skillful.
Bān Gù's "Guest's Jest,"
contains the splendor of elegant diction;
Cuī Yīn's "Expressing Intent,"
exudes the refinement of classical language;
Zhāng Héng's "Responding to Criticism,"
dense yet elegant;
Cuī Shí's "Guest's Mockery,"
orderly yet slightly plain;
Cài Yōng's "Explaining Admonitions,"
profound in substance and brilliant in style;
Jǐngchún's "Guest's Pride,"
reveals emotion with lush ornamentation;
though they successively followed tradition,
they are among the finest compositions.
As for Chén Sī's "Guest's Inquiry,"
its language is lofty but reasoning sparse;
Yǔ Ái's "Guest's Consultation,"
ambitious in intent but feeble in style.
Such examples abound,
with little talent to commend.
The purpose of this genre
is to express indignation and convey aspirations.
Personal setbacks rely on moral triumph,
times of hardship rest on emotional composure;
all anchor their hearts like abysses and peaks,
their style like qílín and phoenixes—
this is the essence of its form.
Since "Seven Stimuli,"
authors have followed in succession.
Observing Méi's pioneering work,
it truly stands out as magnificent.
As for Fù Yì's "Seven Exhortations,"
it achieves clarity and conciseness;
Cuī Yīn's "Seven Analogies,"
displays erudition and elegance;
Zhāng Héng's "Seven Discernments,"
weaves intricate and delicate ornamentation;
Cuī Yuàn's "Seven Admonitions,"
upholds pure and upright principles;
Chén Sī's "Seven Revelations,"
excels in grandeur;
Zhòngxuān's "Seven Explanations,"
distinguishes itself in logical reasoning.
From Huán Lín's "Seven Arguments" onward
to Zuǒ Sī's "Seven Satires,"
imitators multiplied like branches and shadows,
numbering over ten.
Some ornate in style but contradictory in meaning,
others sound in reasoning but uneven in diction.
Examining their general tendencies,
none fail to extol palaces and pavilions,
or boast of grand hunts.
They exhaust rare garments and delicacies,
indulge in seductive sounds and sights.
Sweet words shake the marrow,
alluring phrases pierce the soul;
though beginning with extravagance,
they end with moral rectitude.
Yet satirizing one to admonish a hundred,
inevitably fails to reverse the trend—
as Yún said, "first indulge in frivolous tunes,
concluding with classical elegance."
Only "Seven Admonitions" narrates worthiness,
guiding back to Confucian principles,
though not unparalleled in style,
its intent truly stands eminent.
Since "Stringed Pearls,"
imitators emerged intermittently.
Figures like Dù Dǔ and Jiǎ Kuí,
Liú Zhēn and Pān Xù,
sought to thread bright pearls,
but often strung fish eyes.
They resemble the Shòulíng cripple crawling,
no longer walking the Hándān gait;
or the village ugly clutching her chest,
unrelated to Xīshī's frown.
Only Shìhéng's构思,
fresh in reasoning and agile in style;
structuring chapters and phrasing,
expanded beyond older works.
Did he envy Zhū Zhòng's four-inch ear adornments?
Brief writings are easily concise,
leisurely thoughts can be ample.
Enough to make meaning clear and diction pure,
content rounded and sounds smooth,
rolling naturally,
worthy of being called pearls.
Examining miscellaneous writings since Hàn,
their names and types are many.
Some are edicts, proclamations, oaths, queries,
others overviews, summaries, chapters, sections,
some songs, airs, ditties, preludes,
others chants, satires, ballads, odes.
Collecting their names,
all fall under miscellaneous writings;
distinguishing their meanings,
each enters the realm of discussion;
grouped systematically,
thus not elaborated in detail.
Eulogy:
Great were the former masters,
learned and richly talented.
Bearing literature with spare effort,
they wielded elegance and artistry.
Skillful phrases clustered brightly,
glimmering like the Pleiades.
Hearts that mimic frowns,
only stir confusion herein.
XV. Humor and Enigma
XV. Humor and Enigma
Ruì Liángfū's poem says:
"With their own hearts and guts,
they drive the people mad."
Hearts perilous as mountains,
mouths blocked like rivers,
feelings of resentment vary,
words of jest know no bounds.
When Huá Yuán abandoned his armor,
wall guards sang of his bulging eyes;
when Zāng Hē lost his army,
the state composed a dwarf's song.
Both mocked physical appearances,
internal resentment becoming jest.
Again, rustic proverbs of silkworms and crabs,
lewd tunes of "Lí Shǒu,"
if they could admonish,
were recorded in classical rites.
Thus, humorous and enigmatic words
are not to be discarded.
Humor (xié) means universal (jiē).
Language shallow, suited to customs,
all laugh joyfully.
When King Qí Wēi indulged in revelry,
Chúnyuán spoke of sweet wine;
when King Chǔ Xiāng feasted,
Sòng Yù composed "The Libertine;"
intending subtle satire,
worth observing.
As Yōu Zhān satirized lacquering walls,
Yōu Mèng admonished on burying horses,
both used cunning words adorned,
to restrain folly and tyranny.
Thus, Zǐcháng compiled history,
including "Jesters" biographies,
for though their words were devious,
their intent upheld righteousness.
But the form itself is inelegant,
prone to corruption.
Hence Dōngfāng Shuò and Méi Gāo,
fed on dregs and drank thin wine,
offering no correction,
but slandering, mocking, and toying,
so even calling their works "rhapsodies,"
they were still jesters.
Viewed as entertainers,
they had regrets.
To Wèi Wén composing "The Book of Laughter" from jests,
Xuē Zōng launching jests at banquets,
though amusing the feast,
they benefited nothing practical.
Yet even elegant writers
could not avoid straying;
Pān Yuè's "The Ugly Woman" series,
Shù Xī's "The Cake Seller" kind,
excessively imitated,
numbered nearly a hundred.
In Wèi and Jìn, humor
flourished and spread.
Thus, Yìng Yáng's nose
was likened to a stolen half-egg;
Zhāng Huá's shape
compared to a pounding pestle.
Such were worthless words,
marring virtuous discourse.
Is it not the drowning man's wild laugh,
the convict's mad song?
Yǐn (enigmatic language) means concealment;
it conceals meaning through evasive expressions,
and points to matters through allusive analogies.
In the past, when the State of Huán sought rescue from the Chǔ army,
they alluded to a dry well and spoke of wheat yeast;
when Shū Yí begged for grain from the people of Lǔ,
he sang of jade pendants and called out for gēngguǐ (provisions);
Wǔ Jǔ admonished the King of Jīng with the metaphor of a great bird,
and a Qí guest criticized Lord Xuē with the image of a sea fish;
Zhuāng Jī conveyed her message through the metaphor of a dragon's tail,
while Zāng Wén sent a disguised letter mentioning a sheepskin coat.
The use of enigmatic language
is recorded in historical annals.
At its best, it can revive governance and benefit one's person;
at the next level, it can correct errors and enlighten the confused.
Its intent arises from tactical cunning,
and its application stems from urgent circumstances.
Together with humorous rhetoric,
it can function as complementary.
During the Hàn dynasty, the "Book of Enigmas"
comprised eighteen chapters,
compiled by Liú Xīn and Bān Gù,
and placed at the end of the section on rhapsodies.
In earlier times, King Zhuāng of Chǔ and King Wēi of Qí
had a fondness for enigmatic language.
By the time of Dōngfāng Shuò (Mànqiàn),
his skill in verbal expression was especially clever.
However, his absurd words and mocking jests
offered no benefit for admonition or improvement.
Since the Wèi dynasty,
there has been considerable criticism of court jesters,
and the gentlemen's satirical enigmas
evolved into riddles.
Riddles
involve intertwining words
to baffle the listener.
Some focus on dissecting characters,
others on depicting objects;
they employ intricate cleverness to play with ideas,
and superficial scrutiny to parade rhetoric.
Their meaning should be subtle yet upright,
their wording concealed yet clear.
Xúnzǐ's "Rhapsody on the Silkworm"
already foreshadowed this style.
By the time of Wèi Wéndì and Chén Sīwáng (Cáo Zhí),
it became more concise and refined;
Duke Gāoguìxiāng
broadly enumerated various objects—
though exhibiting minor cleverness,
its application strayed from grand purposes.
Observing the enigmatic language of antiquity,
its principles addressed essential affairs;
how could it be mere child's play,
slapping thighs in laughter!
Yet the presence of humor and enigma in literature
is like the inclusion of minor tales among the Nine Schools;
they are collected by petty officials
to broaden perspectives.
But if imitated incessantly,
one might end up like Kūn undressing and entering the chamber,
or become a steadfast friend of Zhān and Mèng!
Eulogy says:
The mockery and enigma of old
could rescue perils and relieve weariness.
Though there are silk and hemp,
do not discard the coarse grasses.
When aligned with righteousness and timely applied,
they quite benefit satire and admonition.
But if merely frivolous and滑稽,
noble virtue is greatly harmed.
Historiography, the Sixteenth
Since the dawn of primitive chaos,
the chronicles of years stretch far and remote.
To understand antiquity while dwelling in the present—
is it not through written records?
In the age of Xuānyuán (the Yellow Emperor),
there was the historian Cāng Jié.
The duty of overseeing writings
has a long history indeed.
The "Qǔ Lǐ" says:
"The historian carries the brush."
Shǐ (historian) means envoy;
holding the brush at the ruler's side,
he is charged with recording.
In ancient times, the left historian recorded speeches,
the right historian recorded events.
The classic of speeches is the "Shàng Shū",
the classic of events is the "Chūn Qiū".
The Táng and Yú eras flowed into the Canons and Counsels,
the Xià and Shāng were covered by Announcements and Oaths.
When the Zhōu received the Mandate anew,
the Duke of Zhōu established laws,
coordinating the three correctors to promulgate the calendar,
threading the four seasons to connect affairs.
The feudal lords established their states,
each having its own state history,
to manifest goodness and censure evil,
and establish customs and reputation.
Since King Píng's decline and weakness,
government fell short of the elegant standards,
regulations scattered into disorder,
and constant principles were corrupted.
Of old, Confucius grieved over the decline of the kingly way,
lamented the fall of this culture;
in quiet residence he sighed for the phoenix,
at the crossroad he wept for the qílín.
Thereupon, he approached the Grand Master to correct the "Yǎ" and "Sòng",
and based on the Lǔ history, composed the "Chūn Qiū",
enumerating successes and failures to indicate demotion and promotion,
demonstrating survival and demise to mark encouragement and warning.
A single character of praise
could be more valued than high office;
a phrase of censure
cut deeper than axe and halberd.
Yet the profound meaning is hidden and deep,
the text of the Classic subtle and concise.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng, his contemporary,
truly grasped the subtle words;
thus, tracing origins and seeking ends,
he created the commentary style.
Zhuàn (commentary) means to transmit;
it transmits and receives the meaning of the Classic,
conveying it to posterity.
It is truly the wings of the sage's writings,
the crown of historical records.
When it came to the era of the Warring States,
the office of historian still existed.
After Qín unified the seven kings,
the Warring States period had the "Strategies."
It recorded events without narrative structure,
hence it was named after the bamboo slips.
When Hàn destroyed the Yíng and Xiàng lineages,
military achievements accumulated over years,
Lù Jiǎ examined antiquity,
and composed the "Spring and Autumn Annals of Chǔ and Hàn."
Then came Grand Historian Tán,
whose family for generations held the writing slips;
Zǐcháng continued his aspiration,
compiling and narrating imperial achievements.
Compared to Yáo's canon,
the positions were mixed with mediocrity;
modeling after Confucius' classics,
the writing fell short of profound sagacity.
Thus, adopting the style of "Lǚ's Annals,"
he generalized the designation as "Annals,"
a title for outlining essentials,
which was also a grand appellation.
Hence, "Basic Annals" recounted emperors and kings,
"Biographies" summarized feudal lords and earls,
"Eight Treatises" elaborated on governance systems,
"Ten Tables" chronicled years and ranks—
though differing from ancient forms,
they achieved proper sequence of events.
As for its purpose of truthful recording without concealment,
the talent for broad elegance and grand discourse,
the flaw of favoring novelty over classical norms,
and the errors in organizational inconsistencies,
Shūpí discussed them in detail.
When Bān Gù recorded Hàn history,
he followed previous works;
reviewing Sīmǎ Qiān's writings,
he grasped more than half the substance.
His "Ten Treatises" were comprehensive and rich,
the evaluations and prefaces grand and elegant,
cultured and refined,
truly leaving a lasting flavor.
As for modeling on classics and sages' canons,
the achievement of abundant and orderly presentation,
the fault of omitting relatives and appropriating merits,
the transgression of accepting bribes in writing—
Gōnglǐ examined these thoroughly.
Observing Zuǒ Qiūmíng's compilation of events,
attached to the classics intermittently,
the text was concise,
but clan lineages were unclear.
With Sīmǎ Qiān's various biographies,
people began to be distinctly detailed and easy to review,
becoming models for later writers.
When Emperor Huì of Hàn relinquished power,
and Empress Lǚ assumed regency,
Sīmǎ and Bān established annals for her,
both contradicting classical truth—
why?
Since Fú Xī's time,
no female emperor had been heard of.
It was a circumstance of Hàn's fate,
hard to serve as a model for later times.
"A hen does not herald the dawn,"
King Wǔ of Zhōu first vowed;
"Women shall not participate in state affairs,"
Duke Huán of Qí explicitly pledged;
Queen Xuān disrupted Qín,
