the Lǚ clan endangered Hàn—
not only is governance difficult to delegate,
but titles must also be carefully considered.
Zhāng Héng, overseeing history,
sometimes aligned with Qiān and Gù,
proposing annals for two empresses in the Yuánhé era,
intending to establish their records—
a grave error indeed.
Considering Zǐ Hóng, though illegitimate,
was still Emperor Huì's heir;
the Infant Ruler, though insignificant,
truly succeeded Emperor Píng's line—
these two could have annals,
so why include the two empresses?
As for the "Later Hàn" annals and biographies,
they originated from the "Records of the Eastern Lodge."
Those by Yuán and Zhāng,
were biased and inconsistent.
Works by Xuē and Xiè,
were careless and unreliable.
As for Sīmǎ Biāo's detailed accuracy,
and Huà Qiáo's precision and appropriateness,
they were the best.
In the Wèi era's three rival states,
records and biographies emerged variously.
Works like "The Wèi Spring and Autumn Annals" and "Wèi Lüè,"
or "Jiāngbiǎo Records" and "Wú Lù,"
were either overly contentious and hard to verify,
or too broad and lacking focus.
Only Chén Shòu's "Records of the Three Kingdoms,"
balanced in style and substance, clear and thorough,
was compared by Xún and Zhāng to Qiān and Gù—
not undeserved praise.
Regarding Jìn dynasty records,
they depended on official compilations.
Lù Jī began but did not complete them,
Wáng Sháo continued the later period but did not finish,
Gān Bǎo narrated the annals,
achieving order through careful correction;
Sūn Shèng's "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
excelled in concise presentation.
According to the "Spring and Autumn Annals" and its commentaries,
examples and guidelines were established.
After the "Records of the Grand Historian" and "Hàn History,"
none had a clear standard.
Until Dèng Càn's "Jìn Annals,"
rules and examples were first set.
Moreover, discarding Hàn and Wèi styles,
he modeled on Yīn and Zhōu,
though a provincial scholar from Xiāngzhōu,
he also aspired to classical principles.
When Ān Guó established his rules,
he followed Dèng's framework.
The essence of historical records
must connect various schools,
spanning millennia,
revealing signs of prosperity and decline,
providing lessons from rise and fall,
so that a dynasty's institutions
endure as long as the sun and moon,
and the deeds of kings and hegemons
last as vast as heaven and earth.
Thus, in early Hàn times,
the historian's role flourished;
documents from commanderies and states
were first gathered at the Grand Historian's office,
to ensure thorough understanding of state affairs.
Reviewing stone chamber archives,
opening metal cabinet records,
unrolling torn silk scrolls,
examining fragmented bamboo slips—
all to achieve broad knowledge through studying antiquity.
Therefore, establishing principles and selecting words
should follow classics as the standard;
guidance, warnings, approvals, and rejections
must align with sages as the foundation;
only then can evaluation be clear and orderly,
avoiding harshness and excess.
Yet the annals-biographies format,
arranging events by years,
is not vague discussion
but records based on facts.
With distant years, inconsistencies are hard to avoid;
with accumulated events, beginnings and ends easily become vague—
this is the difficulty of comprehensive compilation.
Sometimes one event involves multiple people;
recording it twice causes repetition,
while partial recording lacks completeness—
this is the challenge of balanced allocation.
Thus, Zhāng Héng pointed out errors in Sīmǎ and Bān's works,
and Fù Xuán criticized the "Later Hàn" for excessive detail—
all fall into these categories.
As for recounting distant eras,
distance often brings falsehoods.
Gōngyáng Gāo said:
"Accounts vary in retelling."
Xún Kuàng noted:
"Distant records are brief, recent ones detailed."
When in doubt, omit—
valuing credible history.
Yet common taste favors novelty,
disregarding truth.
Hearing tales, they exaggerate events;
recording the past, they elaborate details—
thus abandoning consensus for peculiarities,
forcing far-fetched interpretations.
What old histories lack,
their books propagate—
this is the root of distortion and excess,
the great flaw in recounting antiquity.
As for recording contemporary times,
contemporaneity often brings deceit.
Even with subtle criticism like for Dìng and Āi,
worldly interests and biases prevail.
Families of merit and glory,
even if mediocre, are fully praised;
those in adversity,
even virtuous, are ridiculed or ignored—
blowing frost or breathing dew,
cold and heat flow from the pen tip.
This is the injustice of contemporaneous records,
truly lamentable.
Thus, recounting the distant leads to such falsification,
recording the near results in such distortion—
to analyze principles and uphold integrity,
only an unbiased mind can achieve it!
As for honoring the worthy and concealing their faults,
this was indeed the sage intent of Confucius,
for minor flaws cannot taint a precious gem;
punishing the wicked and warning against evil,
this is the straightforward brush of a good historian,
just as a farmer seeing weeds
must surely hoe them out;
such principles
remain the standard for all generations.
Regarding methods for organizing complex materials,
the essence of prioritizing truth over novelty,
clarifying the sequence from beginning to end,
and evaluating examples with discernment—
once one grasps the main principles,
all reasoning can be interconnected.
Yet the historian's task
encompasses an entire era,
bearing responsibility before the world,
while incurring blame for judgments of right and wrong.
Wielding the brush and carrying this burden—
nothing is more laborious than this.
Though Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù were comprehensive,
they have been criticized by later ages.
If one follows personal bias and loses objectivity,
how perilous would such writing be!
Eulogy says:
Historiography began with Xuānyuán and Huángdì,
its form perfected by the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius.
Ages pass through these compiled records,
where good and evil are gathered together.
Soaring in praise and decisive in condemnation—
it stirs souls across millennia.
In literary excellence, it follows Qiūmíng;
in integrity, it belongs to Nánshǐ and Dǒng Hú.
The Masters, Part Seventeen
The writings of the masters
are books that penetrate the Way and express aspirations.
The highest achievement is establishing virtue,
the next is establishing words.
When common people live in crowds,
they suffer from chaos and obscurity;
when noble persons dwell in the world,
they grieve that fame and virtue remain unknown.
Only those of outstanding talent and insight
can radiate brilliance through their writings,
making their names soar
and hang them like the sun and moon.
Ancient figures like Fēnghòu, Lì Mù, and Yī Yǐn
all belonged to this tradition.
Their compiled discourses
preserve ancient sayings
recorded during the Warring States period.
When Yù Xióng understood the Way,
King Wén consulted him;
his remaining words and deeds
were recorded as *The Master Yù*.
The beginning of "Master" texts
starts with none earlier than this.
When Lǎo Zǐ (Bó Yáng) understood rites,
Confucius visited and questioned him;
thus he composed the Dàodé Jīng,
standing foremost among the Hundred Schools.
Thus, Yù was a friend to King Wén,
while Lǐ Zǐ (Lǎo Zǐ) was truly a teacher to Confucius—
sage and wise man coexisting,
yet Classics and Masters flowing differently.
By the time of the Seven Warring States exercising force,
outstanding talents swarmed forth.
Mèng Zǐ upheld Confucianism with bowed reverence;
Zhuāng Zhōu expounded the Way in soaring freedom;
Mò Dí held fast to ascetic teachings;
Yǐn Wén examined the correspondence of name and reality;
the Old Man of the Fields governed states through land benefits;
Zōu Zǐ nurtured governance with astronomy;
Shēn Bù Hài and Shāng Yǎng used punishments to enforce order;
Guǐ Gǔ exercised eloquence to achieve merit;
Shī Jiǎo synthesized various arts;
Qīng Shǐ meticulously recorded street talk—
those who followed their streams and branched from them
were too numerous to count.
All debated brilliantly and spread their doctrines,
satisfied with emoluments and lasting glory.
When the violent Qín dynasty set its fires,
flames raged like burning Mount Kūnlún,
yet the scorching poison of the blaze
did not reach the Masters' texts.
By Hàn Emperor Chéng's broad-minded reign,
Liú Xiàng collated and edited them;
then the *Seven Summaries* bloomed fragrantly,
the Nine Schools gathered like scales,
and the finalized editions compiled
amounted to over 180 schools.
Up to Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
authors emerged intermittently,
preserving both rambling words
and recording trivial sayings—
classified and assembled,
they filled chests and illuminated carriages.
Though accumulated texts were abundant,
their essence could be easily summarized:
expounding the Way and discussing governance,
they branch out from the *Five Classics*.
The pure ones fit the square,
the inconsistent stray from the compass.
*Yuè Lìng* from the *Book of Rites*
adopts its framework from *Lǚ's Spring and Autumn Annals*;
the "Three-Year Mourning" inquiry
copies from the writings of *Xún Zǐ*—
these are examples of the pure.
As for Tāng's question to Jí,
claiming a mosquito's eyelash holds thunder's roar;
Huì Shī's reply to King of Liáng,
saying a snail's horn witnessed a deadly war;
*Liè Zǐ*'s tales of moving mountains and crossing seas;
*Huáinán Zǐ*'s discourse on toppling heavens and breaking earth—
these are examples of the inconsistent.
Thus the world criticizes the Masters
as chaotic, empty, and absurd.
Yet consider the *Guīcáng* classic,
greatly illuminating far-fetched marvels—
it tells how Yì shot down ten suns
and Cháng'é fled to the moon.
If the *Yīn Yì* is like this,
how much more the Masters!
As for *Shāng Jūn Shū* and *Hán Fēi Zǐ*,
with "six lice" and "five vermin"—
rejecting filial piety and discarding benevolence—
the calamity of being torn by chariots
did not come without cause.
Gōngsūn Lóng's "white horse" and "orphaned calf" arguments,
clever in wording but flawed in logic—
Wèi Móu comparing them to owls
was no groundless criticism.
When King Dōngpíng requested the Masters and *Records of the Grand Historian*,
the Hàn court refused.
For the *Records* contained much military strategy,
and the Masters mixed in deceptive arts.
Yet the well-informed scholar
should extract their essentials,
admiring the blossoms but consuming the fruit,
rejecting the deviant and gathering the upright—
surveying their diversity to the fullest,
this too is a magnificent vista for the learned.
Examining the works of Mencius and Xunzi,
their principles are profound and their language elegant;
the chapters of Guanzi and Yanzi,
present verified facts with concise words;
the book of Lie Yukou,
is grand in spirit and extraordinary in literary grace;
the theories of Zouzi,
are ambitious in thought and vigorous in expression;
Mo Di and Sui Chao,
convey clear ideas in plain language;
Shi Jiao and Wei Liao,
offer comprehensive methods but blunt writing;
He Guanzi flows continuously,
frequently expressing profound insights;
Gui Guzi is subtle and vast,
always circling around its core meaning;
clear in emotion and rich in expression,
Wenzi excels in this ability;
concise and precise in wording,
Yin Wenzi captures the essence;
Shen Dao skillfully analyzes intricate reasoning,
Han Feizi displays a wealth of broad analogies,
Lüshi Chunqiu shows foresight and comprehensive structure,
Huainanzi gathers extensive sources with elegant prose.
These represent the brilliant aspects of the Hundred Schools,
and the general characteristics of their style and tone.
As for Lu Jia's New Discourses,
Jia Yi's New Book,
Yang Xiong's Exemplary Sayings,
Liu Xiang's Garden of Stories,
Wang Fu's Comments of a Recluse,
Cui Shi's Correct Discourses,
Zhongchang Tong's Propitious Words,
Du Yi's Seeking the Profound,
all narrate classical works,
or elucidate principles of governance.
Although they bear the name of "discourses,"
they belong to the category of various masters.
Why is that?
Because broadly illuminating all matters defines a master,
while appropriately arguing a single principle defines a discourse.
These works all extend into miscellaneous theories,
hence they fall into the stream of various masters.
Before the Six States period,
the distance from the sages was not far,
thus they could discuss lofty topics beyond their time,
and open their own schools of thought.
the vigor of the style gradually weakened,
although they understood the clear path,
they mostly relied on borrowing and selection.
This is the gradual change over distant and recent times.
Alas!
Though their lives were at odds with their times,
their aspirations were expressed through the Way.
They set their hearts above the ancient past,
and sent their thoughts down through the millennia.
Even metal and stone may decay,
but how could their voices ever vanish!
The Encomium says:
A great man stands in the world,
bearing treasure and displaying excellence.
His arguments carve all things,
his wisdom encompasses the universe.
Why conceal the establishment of virtue?
Embracing the Way, he must impart it.
Different branches and varied approaches,
as if within distinct gardens.
On Discourse and Argument: Part 18
The enduring teachings of sages are called classics,
while expositions that elucidate classics and principles are termed discourses.
The term "discourse" (lùn)
signifies order;
when ethical order is without error,
the sage's intent remains undiminished.
In the past, Confucius's subtle words
were recorded by his disciples,
who thus modestly titled the classic
as the "Analects" (Lúnyǔ);
indeed, the naming of various discourses
originated from this.
Before the Analects,
no classic contained the character for discourse;
works like "Liù Tāo" and "Èr Lùn"
were titles added by later generations!
A detailed examination of the discourse form
reveals multiple branches and categories:
In presenting governance, it aligns with deliberations and persuasions;
in interpreting classics, it complements commentaries and annotations;
in debating history, it parallels eulogies and critiques;
in evaluating literature, it shares principles with prefaces and introductions.
Thus, deliberation involves appropriate speech;
persuasion entails pleasing language;
transmission passes down teachings from masters;
annotation focuses on explanation;
eulogy clarifies intent;
critique balances principles;
preface sequences events;
introduction extends rhetoric;
these eight names are distinct,
yet all adhere to the essence of discourse.
A discourse
synthesizes myriad viewpoints
to meticulously investigate a single principle.
Hence, Zhuāng Zhōu's "On the Equality of Things"
used "discourse" in its title;
Lǚ Bùwéi's "Spring and Autumn"
clearly presented six discourses;
up to the discussions at the Stone Canal Pavilion
and the White Tiger Hall gatherings,
where sagely teachings were conveyed through classics,
representing the orthodox form of discourse.
Later, Bān Biāo's "On the Mandate of Kings"
and Yán Yóu's "On Three Generals,"
with their clear emotional expression,
skillfully incorporated historical style.
In the early hegemony of Wèi,
methods combined School of Names and Legalism;
Fù Gǔ and Wáng Càn
examined and refined names and principles.
By the Zhèngshǐ era,
the emphasis was on preserving texts;
figures like Hé Yàn
began to promote metaphysical discourses.
Thus, Lǎo Dān and Zhuāng Zhōu dominated the path,
contending with Confucius for influence.
A close look at Fù Gǔ's "On Talent and Nature,"
Wáng Càn's "On Abandoning Boastfulness,"
Jī Kāng's debates on music,
Xiàhóu Xuán's "On Fundamental Mystery,"
Wáng Bì's two "Examples,"
and Hé Yàn's two "Discourses"
all reveal independent thought and unique insights,
with sharp and precise reasoning,
making them outstanding among human exemplars.
As for Lǐ Kāng's "On Fate and Fortune,"
it resembles "Discourses Weighed" but surpasses it;
Lù Jī's "Debate on the Fall of Wú,"
imitates "On the Faults of Qín" yet falls short;
still, they possess their own merits.
Next, Sòng Dài and Guǒ Xiàng
focused their sharp thoughts on subtle mysteries,
while Wáng Yǎn and Péi Wěi
debated in the realm of existence and non-existence,
both unmatched in their time,
their reputations enduring posterity.
However, those stuck in existence were wholly tied to form and function,
and those valuing non-existence clung solely to emptiness,
merely sharpening biased understandings
without reaching true principles.
To move to the ultimate divine source,
is that not the transcendent realm of prajñā?
When it came to the discussions in the Eastern Jìn,
they solely pursued metaphysics;
though there were innovations,
most drew from previous threads.
As for Zhāng Héng's "Satire on the Age,"
its tone resembled comic tales;
Kǒng Róng's "On Filial Piety and Integrity,"
merely engaged in jest and mockery;
Cáo Zhí's "Debate on Dao,"
was structured like a copied compilation;
if talent cannot sustain discourse,
it were better to stop.
Fundamentally, the nature of discourse
is to distinguish right from wrong,
exhausting the finite,
pursuing the formless,
tracing the solid to seek understanding,
probing the profound to grasp the ultimate;
it is the trap and snare of all thoughts,
the balance of all matters.
Thus, its principles value comprehensiveness and coherence,
its wording avoids fragmentation;
it must ensure the mind aligns with reason,
seamlessly without gaps;
words closely following the mind,
so opponents find no opening;
this is its essence.
Therefore, discourse is like splitting firewood,
valuing the ability to follow the grain.
If the axe is too sharp,
it cuts across the grain arbitrarily;
if the rhetoric is too clever,
it twists meaning for coherence;
though the text may appear skillful,
examining its traces reveals fallacy.
Only the gentleman can penetrate the world's will—
how can biased discourse be acceptable?
As for explanatory annotations,
they dismantle the discourse form,
and though miscellaneous writings differ,
their collective purpose is the same;
like Qín Yánjūn's annotation on the "Canon of Yáo,"
spanning over a hundred thousand characters;
or Zhū Pǔ's interpretation of the "Shàng Shū,"
reaching three hundred thousand words—
thus the learned detest such verbosity,
ashamed to study mere chapter and verse.
In contrast, Master Māo's glosses on the "Shī Jīng,"
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary on the "Shū Jīng,"
Zhèng Xuán's explanations of the "Lǐ Jì,"
and Wáng Bì's interpretations of the "Yì Jīng"
are concise and clear,
serving as exemplary models.
Persuasion is about delighting;
the Dui trigram represents the mouth and tongue,
hence speech relies on delight and joy;
excessive delight must be false,
so Shun was alarmed by slanderous talk.
Among the skilled in persuasion:
Yǐ Yīng used discussions on flavors to elevate Yīn,
Tài Gōng employed discernment in fishing to revive Zhōu,
and when Zhú Wǔ acted, he relieved Zhèng,
Duānmù went forth and preserved Lǔ,
these are also their merits.
By the time of the Warring States' struggle for supremacy,
debaters swarmed like clouds;
vertical and horizontal alliances were strategized,
strengths and weaknesses vied for advantage;
"Turning the Pearl" displayed their clever rhetoric,
"Flying the Tongs" concealed their refined techniques;
one person's argument
outweighed the treasure of the Nine Tripod Cauldrons,
a three-inch tongue
proved stronger than a million-strong army;
six seals hung impressively from their belts,
five cities were enfeoffed with hidden wealth.
Until Hàn stabilized after Qín and Chǔ,
debaters restrained their pace,
Lì Jīng perished in Qí's cauldron,
Kuǎi Zǐ nearly entered Hàn's tripod;
although Lù Jiǎ was highly renowned,
Zhāng Shì adeptly adapted,
Dù Qīn eloquent in debate,
Lóu Hù skilled in speech,
they vied at the steps of the sovereign,
and clashed in the seats of high officials;
all rode the wind to leverage their positions,
none could swim against the current upstream.
Persuasion values seizing the moment,
relaxation and tension following each other,
not solely relying on smooth talk,
but also in written words.
Fàn Jū's presentation of affairs,
Lǐ Sī's halt to the expulsion of guests,
both channeled genuine feelings into opportunity,
their moving words hit the core of matters;
though they touched the reverse scales,
they achieved success and their plans aligned,
these are exemplary submissions of persuasive discourse.
As for Zōu Yáng's persuasions to Wú and Liáng,
his metaphors were clever and reasoning sound,
thus, though in peril, he incurred no blame.
Jìng Tōng's advice to Bào and Dèng,
was slow in action and verbose in text;
hence, despite his extensive efforts, he rarely met success.
The crux of all persuasion
must ensure timeliness and righteous integrity;
advancing, it aligns with accomplishing tasks,
retreating, it does not hinder personal honor.
Unless deceiving the enemy,
it should only embody loyalty and trust.
Baring one's heart to serve the ruler,
wielding swift and sharp writing to aid speech;
this is the foundation of persuasion.
Yet Lù Jī directly stated, "Persuasion dazzles with deceit and trickery,"
why is that?
Commendation says:
Reason takes form in words,
narrating reason completes discourse.
Words delve into human and heavenly matters,
reaching far from the heart's depth.
Neither yin nor yang can cause doubt,
even ghosts and spirits cannot hide.
Persuade with the "Flying Tongs,"
in a breath, you may deter or urge.
Edicts and Strategies, Chapter Nineteen.
The Eulogy states:
When emperors and kings issue decrees,
They solemnly proclaim their sacred edicts.
My silken words,
Are cherished by the myriad people.
Resplendent tones soar high,
Vast influences spread afar.
Rising in righteousness, soaring in rhetoric,
They disseminate the great proclamations.
20. Admonitions and Transmissions (Xí Yí)
Thunder begins with dazzling lightning,
Deploying troops is preceded by intimidating声势.
Thus, seeing lightning makes one fear the thunder's might,
Hearing the声势 makes one dread the military power.
Military action being preceded by声势,
Has been a practice since ancient times.
In the past, Yǒu Yú first issued warnings to the state,
Xià Hòu initially made oaths to the army,
Yīn pledged outside the military gate,
Zhōu would swear before engaging in battle.
Thus we know that in the age of emperors, warnings were for military discipline,
The three dynastic kings swore in their troops,
To instruct their own masses,
Not yet targeting the enemy.
By the time of King Mù of Zhōu's western expedition,
Jì Gōng Móufù stated, "In ancient times, there were commands of威严谴责,
And proclamations of written admonition,"
Which are the origins of the admonition (xí).
During the Spring and Autumn period's campaigns,
Initiated by the feudal lords,
Fearing the enemy would not submit,
They needed a justification for出兵,
To bolster their own威风,
And expose the enemy's folly and chaos.
As Liú Xiàngōng said, "Admonish them with written words,
And oversee them with martial forces."
When Duke Huán of Qí chastised Chǔ,
He questioned the shortage of offering grass;
When Duke Lì of Jìn attacked Qín,
He condemned the burning of Jī and Gào;
Guǎn Zhòng and Lǚ Xiàng,
Bore the admonitions as vanguards;
Examining their meaning,
They were the admonitions (xí) of today.
By the Warring States period,
It began to be called "xí."
Xí means
Clarity (jiǎo).
It is revealed outwardly,
Clear and evident.
When Zhāng Yí issued an admonition to Chǔ,
It was written on a foot-two-long tablet,
A clear text,
Sometimes called "exposed proclamation."
Exposed proclamation
Refers to an unsealed wooden board,
Broadcast for all to see and hear.
War is to quell chaos,
None dare act on their own authority;
When the Son of Heaven leads the army personally,
It is called "reverently executing Heaven's punishment;"
When feudal lords command troops,
It is said "solemnly carrying out the king's execution."
Thus, entrusted with authority beyond the border,
They uphold the charge to punish crimes,
Not only achieving resolution through firmness,
But also wielding sharp words as martial power.
Making the声势 like a gale's impact,
The aura like a comet's sweep,
They unleash their martial fury,
Gather accusations against the offenders,
Cite the time when their evils ripened,
Reveal the extent of their accumulated crimes,
Shake the traitors' courage,
Steady the faithful and cautious hearts,
So that a hundred-foot assault vehicle
Crumbles before a short document,
A walled city of ten thousand fathoms
Falls by a single admonition.
Observing Wěi Xiāo's admonition against the usurper Wáng Mǎng,
Listing three perversities,
The language is unadorned,
Yet the words are incisive and the facts clear;
The scholars of Lǒngyòu
Grasped the essence of the admonition.
Chén Lín's "Admonition to Yùzhōu,"
Vigorous and firm-boned,
Though detailing the eunuch's adopted lineage,
Is excessively harsh in exposure,
Accusing of tomb-robbing and gold-plundering,
Exaggerating beyond truth;
Yet its defiant recording of faults
Is clearly revealing of the circumstances.
Daring to point at Cáo Cāo's sharp edge,
He was fortunate to escape execution as Yuán's partisan.
Zhōng Huì's admonition to Shǔ,
With very clear evidence;
Huán Wēn's admonition to the Hú,
Observing faults with particular acuity,
Both are powerful writings.
Generally, the main form of an admonition
Either proclaims one's own virtue and brightness,
Or describes the enemy's harsh cruelty,
Points to celestial timing,
Examines human affairs,
Calculates strength and weakness,
Measures authority and power,
Cites milfoil and tortoise shells with prior proofs,
Hangs the mirror of warning over past events,
Though rooted in state credibility,
It truly involves military deception.
Using cunning to convey the intent,
Employing brilliance to promote the argument,
All these points
Must not be violated.
Thus, in establishing meaning and proclaiming words,
The aim must be robustness and vigor;
Attaching feathers signifies urgency,
Words must not be sluggish;
Using exposed boards to inform the public,
The meaning must not be obscure;
Facts must be clear and reasoning distinct,
Spirit vigorous and wording decisive,
These are the essentials.
If the approach is twisted, intricate, and clever,
It holds no merit.
Also, when regional states summon officials,
It is called an admonition,
Reflecting the principle of clear recommendation.
Transmission (yí) means
Change.
To transform customs and practices,
So that when orders go forth, the people follow.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Challenging the Shǔ Elders,"
Clear in language and broad in analogy,
Possesses the backbone of transmission and admonition.
As for Liú Xīn's "Transmission to the Tàicháng,"
Forceful in diction and discerning in meaning,
It stands as the foremost of civil transmissions.
Lù Jī's "Transmission to the Hundred Officials,"
Concise in speech and evident in facts,
Is key among martial transmissions.
Thus, the use of admonition and transmission
Spans both civil and martial affairs;
In military contexts,
Admonitions are for rebellious factions,
Transmissions guide compliant masses,
Thereby cleansing the people's hearts,
Strengthening clear agreements,
Their intents differ slightly, but their forms and principles largely align,
Intertwining with admonitions,
So they are not discussed separately here.
The Eulogy states:
Like the hunt's net laid aside on three sides,
The nine punishments are preceded by words.
The mirror reflects fortune and misfortune,
Milfoil and tortoise foretell success and failure.
Crushing the whales and monsters,
Striking down the wasps and scorpions.
Transforming treasures to change customs,
Like grass bending to the wind's passage.
21. Fēng Shàn Sacrifices
The true position is the North Star,
Facing south toward brightness,
Thus operating the pivot of heaven,
Nurturing the common and the worthy—
How could it not be by weaving the way with virtue,
To inscribe the imperial achievements!
The "Green Chart" says:
"Vast and murmuring,
Chaotic and diverse,
All things transform completely."
This speaks of the reach of ultimate virtue.
The "Cinnabar Script" says:
"When righteousness overcomes desire, there is accord;
When desire overcomes righteousness, there is calamity."
This is the utmost in caution and vigilance.
Thus, through caution and vigilance to exalt virtue,
And ultimate virtue to solidify transformation,
The seventy-two sovereigns
Performed the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
The establishment of offices and division of duties,
link affairs from high to low.
The Son of Heaven hangs pearls to listen,
feudal lords jingle jades at court.
Presenting reports through speech,
testing clearly through merits.
Thus Yáo consulted the Four Peaks,
Shùn appointed the Eight Yuán,
with firm refusals and repeated deferrals requested,
and approvals of "Go, be reverent!" bestowed,
all were declarations at the imperial court,
not relying on written documents.
Hence, presenting reports through speech
embodies the principle of zhāng and biǎo;
testing clearly through merits
constitutes the ceremony of granting ranks.
When Tàijiǎ was enthroned,
Yīyǐn wrote admonitions;
upon reflecting on constancy and returning to Bó,
he again composed writings to exhort.
The literary contributions of remonstrance
thus became evident.
Zhōu drew from two dynasties as mirror,
its cultural patterns grew more splendid,
with double bows and kowtows,
responding to and extolling gracious mandates,
receiving texts and accepting edicts,
daring to bear great brilliance—
though speech and writing were not yet distinguished,
the expression of gratitude is visible.
Descending to the Seven States,
the ancient forms remained unchanged;
addressing matters to the king
was all called "submitting writings."
Qín initially established regulations,
changing "writings" to "zòu."
Hàn defined rituals and protocols,
establishing four categories:
first called zhāng,
second called zòu,
third called biǎo,
fourth called yì.
Zhāng for expressing gratitude,
zòu for impeachment and censure,
biǎo for presenting requests,
yì for upholding dissent.
Zhāng means
clarity.
The Book of Songs says:
"Forms a pattern in heaven."
This refers to cultural brilliance.
In artifacts and designs,
red and white form a pattern.
Biǎo means
marker.
The Rites has the "Biǎojì",
meaning virtue appears in demeanor;
in instruments and models,
measuring shadows is called a marker.
The terms zhāng and biǎo
likely derive from these.
According to the Seven Summaries and Arts and Writings,
songs and poems were always recorded;
zhāng, biǎo, zòu, and yì,
pivotal to state governance,
were omitted from compilation
because each had its precedents
distributed among official duties.
Earlier Hàn gratitude biǎo
have few surviving pieces.
By Later Hàn's selection system,
zhāng and zòu were mandatory tests.
Zuǒ Xióng's zòu and yì
became models for the secretariat;
Hú Guǎng's zhāng and zòu
ranked first in the land;
both were masterpieces of their time.
Reading Bóshǐ's zhāng for imperial tomb visits,
fully reveals the beauty of his classical writing.
When Duke Wén of Jìn received edicts,
he declined thrice before complying,
hence late Hàn deferral biǎo
limited to three refusals.
Cáo Cāo stated that biǎo should not exceed three deferrals,
nor be florid.
Thus early Wèi zhāng and biǎo
addressed matters with factual basis;
seeking ornate beauty
was then insufficient for excellence.
As for Wénjǔ's recommendation of Mí Héng,
spirited and brilliantly eloquent;
Kǒngmíng's farewell to the later sovereign,
thorough in intent and smooth in writing;
though differing in ornate and substantial styles,
both are outstanding biǎo.
Lín and Yǔ's zhāng and biǎo
were praised in their time;
Kǒngzhāng acclaimed as vigorous,
exemplifies this standard.
Chénsī's biǎo
uniquely topped all talents.
Observing their full-bodied style and rhythmic harmony,
clear diction and evident intent,
skillfully adapting to situations,
generating interest through variation,
holding the reins with ease,
thus matching rhythm whether slow or urgent.
Reaching early Jìn writings,
Zhāng Huá stood as a peer.
His triple deferral of ducal enfeoffment,
logically thorough and concise in wording,
citing principles and comparing matters,
always achieving parallelism,
yet the world treasured his "Wren",
overlooking his zhāng and biǎo.
As for Yáng Gōng's "Declining the Appointment",
praised in earlier discussions;
Yǔ Gōng's "Deferring the Secretariat",
truly fine among past records.
Expressing intent and revealing categories,
they possess cultural elegance.
Liú Kūn's "Urging Advancement",
Zhāng Jùn's "Self-Narrative",
stylistically upright and principled,
are both excellent biǎo for presenting matters.
Fundamentally, the function of zhāng and biǎo
is to respond in the royal court
and illuminate innermost thoughts.
They reflect the individual's culture
and also the state's splendor.
Zhāng reaching the palace gates
should clearly manifest grace and norm;
biǎo presented to the forbidden interior
ought to shine with essential brilliance.
Examining reality against the name,
they take refinement as foundation.
Thus zhāng forms are radiant,
aiming at canonical models;
making them essential but not sketchy,
clear but not shallow.
Biǎo style encompasses much,
with genuine and feigned emotions often shifting;
must use elegant principles to fan its ethos,
and pure writing to gallop its beauty.
Yet the sincere are guided by heartfelt words,
the florid have emotions bent by ornate text.
Ensure complexity and brevity find balance,
ornament and substance complement each other,
and speech flows without stagnation,
then they hit the norm.
Zǐgòng said:
"The heart to control it,
words to bind it."
This unifies wording and meaning.
Xúnqīng believed "observing others' fine words,
adorned like embroidered patterns",
may also illustrate this!
Appraisal:
Presentations at vermilion gates,
admonitions before patterned screen.
Words must be upright and clear,
principles grand and majestic.
Reverent and respectful in ritual form,
ordered from start to end.
The noble master wields culture,
elegant in speech and command.
Zòu and Qǐ: Twenty-Three
Appraisal says:
Deliberation concerns governance,
names and realities mutually examined.
Judging principles must be resolute,
wielding words without timidity.
Responding to policy at the royal court,
contemporaries harmonize in consultation.
Upholding the essence of governance,
elegant plans spread far and wide.
Twenty-fifth: Letters and Documents
The Great Shùn said:
"Documents are for recording!"
They are used to chronicle events of the time.
The words of sages and worthies,
were compiled into the "Shàngshū",
the nature of documents
primarily lies in speech.
Yáng Xióng said:
"Speech
is the voice of the heart;
writing
is the painting of the heart."
When voices and paintings take form,
gentlemen and petty men are revealed.
Thus, writing means
to express.
Spreading forth one's words,
laying them out on bamboo slips,
taking the image from the Guài hexagram,
its value lies in clarity and decisiveness.
During the Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu dynasties, in political leisure,
literary compositions were quite sparse.
In the Spring and Autumn period, diplomatic missions were frequent,
documents and envoys became abundant:
Rào Cháo presented a strategy to Shì Huì,
Zǐjiā sent a letter to Zhào Xuān,
Wū Chén's message to Zǐ Fǎn,
Zǐchǎn's admonition to Fàn Xuān,
examining these four letters,
the words feel like face-to-face conversation.
Also, Zǐshū Jìngshū presented a condolence letter to the Lord of Téng,
thus it is known that envoys carrying messages
often employed brush and ink.
By the time of the Seven States, submitted documents
were cunningly ornate and gathered densely;
since Hàn, written correspondence
displayed varied tones and styles.
Observe Sīmǎ Qiān's "Reply to Rèn Ān",
Dōngfāng Shuò's challenge to Gōngsūn,
Yáng Yùn's response to Huìzōng,
Zǐyún's reply to Liú Xīn,
their will and spirit lingering,
each containing unique brilliance;
all woven into a foot of silk,
modulated within an inch of the heart.
By the Later Hàn, in letters and records,
Cuī Yuàn was especially skilled.
In Wèi, Yuányú (Ruǎn Yǔ),
was praised as graceful;
Wénjǔ's (Kǒng Róng) compositions,
even half a slip was worth recording;
Xiūliǎn's (Yīng Chàng) fondness for affairs,
attentive to literary expression;
these are next in rank.
Jī Kāng's "Letter Severing Friendship",
truly shows lofty ambition and magnificent writing.
Zhào Zhì's farewell gift,
is the fervor of youth.
As for Chén Zūn's dictated words,
a hundred letters each with distinct intent;
Mí Héng's drafted letters,
appropriately addressing intimacy or distance;
these are specialized talents in letter writing.
In summarizing the form of letters,
the essence is to fully express words,
words to disperse pent-up feelings,
entrusting one's demeanor,
thus they should be smooth and free-spirited,
gentle to please the heart.
Elegant and composed writing,
is also an exchange of heartfelt voices.
As for distinctions of尊贵,
then solemn with ritual restraint,
before the Warring States period,
rulers and ministers used the same form of letters,
Qín and Hàn established ceremonies,
beginning with memorials and petitions,
within the domains of princes and dukes,
also called petitions,
Zhāng Chǎng's petition to the Queen of Jiāo,
its intent was admirable.
By the Later Hàn,
gradually there were distinctions in names and grades,
with petitions to official bureaus,
and reports to commandery generals.
Records convey intent,
presenting one's own will.
Reports are,
to express,
to manifest one's feelings.
Cuī Shí's petition to the official bureau,
is a virtuous sound of reverence and deference;
Huáng Xiāng's report in Jiāngxià,
also a model of solemn respect.
Gōnggàn's (Liú Zhēn) reports,
elegant and admonitory for benefit,
Zǐhuán (Cáo Pī) did not discuss them,
thus overlooked by the world,
if overlooking names and seeking substance,
they have beauty surpassing his poetry.
Liú Yì's gratitude for grace,
metaphor apt and profound;
Lù Jī's self-justification,
emotion thorough and skillful;
these are excellent examples of reports.
The pattern of reports,
looks up to memorials above,
and glances at letters below,
making them respectful but not fearful,
concise yet not arrogant,
clear and beautiful to display talent,
brilliant and lush to adorn their resonance,
this is the distinction of reports.
The scope of letters and documents is vast,
covering all matters,
various names for writings,
many types through ages.
Thus, for governing the populace,
there are genealogies, registers, records, and lists;
for medicine, calendar, astrology, and divination,
there are prescriptions, techniques, and divination forms;
for proclaiming laws and discussing military affairs,
there are statutes, orders, legal rules;
for verification in court and market,
there are tallies, contracts, deeds, and statements;
for officials inquiring into affairs,
there are passes, inquiries, explanations, and reports;
for the people to express their will,
there are petitions, statements, complaints, and proverbs;
all articulate reasoning from the heart,
setting words to paper,
though the lowest grade of literary art,
they are the foremost task of governance.
Thus, genealogy means
universal.
Recording lineage sequences,
requires comprehensive detail,
Mr. Zhèng's genealogy of the "Shī",
draws from this.
Register means
to borrow.
Annual conscription of labor,
listed on boards,
the "Spring and Autumn" official registers,
refer to this matter.
Record book means
garden.
As plants are categorized,
documents are grouped by type,
Zhāng Tāng and Lǐ Guǎng,
were investigated by officials,
to distinguish truth from falsehood.
List means
to lead.
Ancient histories and genealogies,
compiled on bamboo slips,
recording names and numbers,
thus called lists.
Prescription means
corner.
Medicine treating illnesses,
each has its specific focus,
specializing in one area,
thus medical arts are called prescriptions.
Method means
path.
Calculating calendars and exhausting numbers,
seeing the path makes it clear,
"Nine Chapters" accumulates subtleties,
thus called methods,
"Huáinán Wàn Bì",
all belong to this category.
Divination means
to observe.
Stars' movements and positions,
watching carefully reveals them,
ascending to observe and record clouds,
thus called divination.
Form (Shì) means standard.
The waxing and waning of yīn and yáng,
the growth and decline of the five phases,
though their changes are irregular,
can be examined according to fixed principles.
Statute (Lǜ) means centrality.
From the Yellow Bell pitch standard,
the five notes are regulated;
governing the people by laws,
the eight punishments achieve fairness—
the term "statute" is used
to denote centrality and correctness.
Edict (Lìng) means command.
Issuing commands and proclaiming prohibitions
is as if from Heaven itself;
Guǎn Zhòng's orders flowed like water,
making the people follow.
Method (Fǎ) means pattern.
Military strategies have no fixed form,
yet the regular and the extraordinary have patterns—
hence it is called method.
Regulation (Zhì) means cutting.
The superior applies it to the inferior,
like a craftsman cutting material to make vessels.
Tally (Fú) means trust.
Summoning and preventing fraud
rely on inner sincerity.
The jade tokens of the Three Dynasties,
the metal and bamboo tallies of the Hàn,
were simplified in later ages,
replaced by written documents.
Contract (Qì) means tying.
In ancient simplicity,
knots were tied and contracts held;
today the Qiāng and Hú peoples count by notches,
and traders record debts—
are these not surviving customs?
Deed (Quàn) means binding.
Clearly stated restraints
prevent deceit;
the characters are split in half,
so in the Zhōu it was called split-document.
Ancient iron deeds
secured oaths with firm trust.
Wáng Bāo's "Bearded Slave"
is a humorous example of a deed.
Memorandum (Shū) means spreading out.
Arranging categories of things,
summarizing with concise meanings—
thus short documents and brief writings
are called memoranda.
Barrier (Guān) means closing.
Entry and exit pass through gates,
closing requires scrutiny;
in governance of various affairs,
openness and blockage should be detailed.
Hán Fēi said:
"Sūn Dǎnhuí was a sage minister,
yet he started at the local level."
This refers to such barriers.
Communication (Cì) means reaching.
The poets' satires,
the three inquiries in the Rites of Zhōu—
matters are narrated to reach understanding,
like needles untying knots.
Explanation (Jiě) means unravelling.
Resolving obstructions
by citing evidence in response.
Slip (Dié) means leaf.
Short strips bound into slips
are like leaves on a branch;
Wēn Shū cutting reeds
exemplifies this.
When policy debates are unsettled,
short slips consult for plans.
The most confidential slips
are called memos (Qiān).
Memos mean meticulous detail.
Account (Zhuàng) means appearance.
Describing the original form,
capturing the factual essence—
the posthumous honors for worthies of old
all included conduct accounts,
the major form of accounts.
Statement (Liè) means presenting.
Setting forth facts
makes them clearly visible.
Speech (Cí) is the writing from the tongue's tip,
communicating oneself to others.
Zǐ Chǎn's eloquence
was relied on by the feudal lords—
it cannot be dispensed with.
Proverb (Yàn) means direct speech.
Even mourning words avoid ornament,
so condolences are also called proverbs.
Marketplace plain talk
has substance without flourish.
Duke Mù of Zōu said:
"Leaking from bag into storehouse."
All belong to this category.
The Great Declaration states:
"The ancients had a saying:
'A hen does not crow at dawn.'"
The Major Odes say:
"People also have a saying:
'Worry alone brings age.'"
These are proverbs handed down from high antiquity,
which the Book of Songs and Documents can quote.
As for Chén Lín's remonstrance
using "cover eyes to catch sparrows,"
or Pān Yuè's elegy
using "palm pearl" and "devoted couple"—
both draw on common sayings for literary composition.
Now, no writing is more rustic than proverbs,
yet sages and worthies in the Poetry and Documents
adopted them for discourse;
how much more beyond this
can they be ignored!
Considering these four categories,
all encompassed by documents and letters:
some matters are fundamentally interconnected
yet differ in literary intent;
some rely entirely on plain substance,
some mix in elegant ornament—
the form is established according to the matter,
with precision and essence valued.
Missing one word voids the meaning,
one extra word mars the expression.
These are the practical affairs of officials,
often neglected for flowery rhetoric.
Yet those crowned as great writers
are often unskilled in correspondence,
like Jiǔfāng Yīn recognizing a steed's speed
while ignoring its color and gender.
Since language reflects the self,
sincerity is the state's treasure—
scholars in the literary forest
should ponder substantial principles.
Summary:
The branches of literary elegance
reside in written records.
They convey golden brilliance
and employ rustic simplicity.
Their sound is offered through ages,
their response spans a thousand miles.
Amid myriad tangled duties,
through documents they're clarified.
The Spirit and Thought, Chapter 26
The ancients said:
"The body may remain among rivers and lakes,
but the mind lingers beneath the palace gates."
This describes spiritual thought.
In literary contemplation,
the spirit travels far.
Thus in silent concentration,
thought connects across millennia;
in subtle shifts of expression,
vision penetrates myriad miles;
while chanting verses,
one breathes forth sounds like pearls and jade;
before one's very eyes,
colors of wind and clouds roll and unfold -
is this not the achievement of intellectual reasoning?
Thus the wonder of reasoning lies in
the spirit wandering with things.
The spirit dwells in the breast,
governed by will and vital energy as its pivot;
things reach us through ears and eyes,
with language managing their mechanism.
When this mechanism functions smoothly,
no aspect of things remains hidden;
when the pivot becomes blocked,
the spirit retreats inward.
Therefore, in cultivating literary thought,
emptiness and tranquility are valued,
cleansing the five viscera,
purifying the spirit,
accumulating learning to store treasures,
weighing principles to enrich talent,
studying experience to exhaust illumination,
disciplining disposition to unravel language -
only then can the understanding mind,
seek musical patterns to set ink;
the uniquely perceptive craftsman,
observe mental images to wield his axe -
this constitutes the primary technique for mastering writing,
the essential approach to planning compositions.
When spiritual thought begins to flow,
countless paths compete to sprout,
shaping emptiness into form,
carving the formless,
climbing mountains makes emotions fill the peaks,
viewing seas makes ideas overflow the waters -
whatever talent I possess
will race alongside wind and clouds.
When first grasping the brush,
energy doubles before words form;
upon completing the piece,
half the original intent is lost.
Why?
Ideas soaring through emptiness easily become marvelous,
while words grounded in reality struggle to achieve elegance.
Thus ideas derive from thought,
words derive from ideas -
when closely connected, no gap appears;
when loosely related, they miss by miles.
Sometimes truth lies within the heart,
yet we search beyond borders;
sometimes meaning rests close at hand,
yet thought remains separated by mountains and rivers.
Therefore, nurture the mind and cultivate technique -
no need for painful straining;
embrace patterns and master principles -
no requirement for laborious emotions.
People's endowed talents
differ in speed;
literary forms and styles
vary in magnitude and effort:
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú chewed his brush until it rotted,
Yáng Xióng took up writing and startled from dreams,
Huán Tán fell ill from intense contemplation,
Wáng Chōng exhausted his energy in deep thought,
Zhāng Héng researched his "Jīngfū" for ten years,
Zuǒ Sī refined his "Dūfù" for twelve -
though producing great works,
these represent slow thinking.
Huáinán composed his "Sāo" in one morning,
Méi Gāo completed fu upon imperial command,
Cáo Zhī drafted documents as if reciting,
Wáng Cán wielded his brush like preparing overnight,
Ruǎn Yǔ wrote letters leaning on his saddle,
Mí Héng drafted memorials during banquets -
though creating shorter pieces,
these represent swift thinking.
For the brilliantly inspired,
mind masters essential techniques,
quickness precedes deliberation,
deciding immediately as opportunity arises;
for the deeply contemplative,
emotions linger at crossroads,
discernment follows doubt,
determination comes only after thorough consideration.
Agility brings success in haste,
deliberation achieves results through prolonged effort.
Though difficulty differs,
both require broad learning and practice.
If learning is shallow yet one slowly produces nothing,
talent is sparse yet one rapidly achieves emptiness,
to succeed through such means -
I've never heard of it before.
Thus when facing composition and organizing thoughts,
two troubles inevitably arise:
those obstructed in reasoning suffer from poverty of ideas,
those drowning in verbiage suffer from chaotic expression.
Therefore, broad knowledge provides grain to feed the impoverished,
coherent focus offers medicine to save the chaotic -
breadth combined with unity
greatly aids mental strength.
When emotional complexities become deceitful and tangled,
when stylistic changes shift unpredictably,
clumsy phrases may contain clever meanings,
commonplace events may sprout novel ideas -
viewing cloth compared to hemp,
though fundamentally no costlier,
through loom's transformative work,
it becomes brilliantly precious.
As for subtle meanings beyond thought,
curved nuances outside the text,
where language cannot pursue,
the brush naturally knows to stop.
Only through utmost refinement can one expound its wonders,
only through supreme flexibility can one comprehend its patterns -
Yī Zhì couldn't explain the cauldron's secrets,
Lún Biǎn couldn't speak of his axe's mastery,
how subtle indeed!
Summary:
Spirit connects through images,
nurtured by emotional transformations.
Things seek expression through appearance,
mind responds through principled understanding.
Carve and engrave musical patterns,
sprout metaphors and comparisons.
Organize thoughts and master principles,
lower the curtain and achieve victory.
XXVII. Style and Nature
When emotions stir, words take form;
when principles emerge, patterns appear.
This is because we follow the hidden to reach the manifest,
matching the inner with the outer.
However, talent may be ordinary or outstanding,
disposition may be firm or gentle,
learning may be shallow or deep,
habits may be refined or vulgar.
All are shaped by innate nature
and solidified through cultivation.
Thus, the realm of writing is as varied as clouds,
and the garden of literature as unpredictable as waves.
Therefore, the mediocrity or excellence in diction and reasoning
cannot transcend one's talent;
the firmness or gentleness in style and taste
can hardly alter one's disposition;
the depth or shallowness in allusions and meanings
is never divorced from one's learning;
the elegance or vulgarity in form and style
rarely contradicts one's habits.
Each follows their own established mind,
differing as much as faces.
To summarize the paths,
they converge into eight styles:
first, the classical and elegant;
second, the profound and abstruse;
third, the concise and precise;
fourth, the clear and relevant;
fifth, the elaborate and ornate;
sixth, the majestic and splendid;
seventh, the novel and unusual;
eighth, the light and frivolous.
The classical and elegant
molds itself on the classics,
following the Confucian school.
The profound and abstruse
draws from esoteric texts,
delving into mystical doctrines.
The concise and precise
scrutinizes words and economizes sentences,
analyzing with fine detail.
The clear and relevant
uses straightforward language and smooth meanings,
fitting principles and satisfying the mind.
The elaborate and ornate
employs extensive metaphors and rich embellishments,
flourishing with branching streams.
The majestic and splendid
boasts lofty discussions and grand structures,
shining with extraordinary brilliance.
The novel and unusual
rejects the ancient and competes with the modern,
leaning towards perilous and bizarre paths.
The light and frivolous
features superficial patterns and weak foundations,
drifting ethereally to suit vulgar tastes.
Thus, the elegant opposes the unusual,
the abstruse differs from the clear,
the elaborate conflicts with the concise,
the majestic contradicts the light.
The roots and leaves of literary expression
are all encompassed within these.
As for the frequent shifts among the eight styles,
their mastery depends on learning,
with innate ability at the core,
originating from one's vitality.
Vitality充实 the will,
and the will determines the words.
The expression of brilliance
invariably reflects one's nature.
Thus, Jiǎ Yì, being brilliant and expressive,
wrote with purity and clarity;
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, being arrogant and extravagant,
produced lavish reasoning and overflowing diction;
Yáng Xióng, being deep and reserved,
conveyed hidden intentions and profound flavors;
Liú Xiàng, being straightforward and simple,
displayed clear interests and broad knowledge;
Bān Gù, being refined and virtuous,
achieved meticulous structure and elegant thoughts;
Zhāng Héng, being profound and comprehensive,
demonstrated thorough consideration and dense ornamentation;
Wáng Càn, being restless and competitive,
showed sharp insights and decisive talent;
used strong words and startling emotions;
Ruǎn Jí, being untrammeled and free,
created distant echoes and far-reaching tones;
Jī Kāng, being outstanding and chivalrous,
expressed lofty inspirations and intense brilliance;
Pān Yuè, being light and quick,
produced sharp edges and flowing charm;
Lù Jī, being dignified and serious,
wove complex emotions and obscure diction.
Applying this reasoning broadly,
the inner and outer must correspond.
Is this not the constant endowment of nature,
the general outline of talent and disposition?
Talent is innate,
but learning must be careful in initial habits.
Like carving wood or dyeing silk,
the effort lies in the initial transformation.
Once the vessel is formed and the color set,
it is hard to change.
Thus, in training the young,
one must start with elegant models,
tracing the roots to examine the leaves,
so that thoughts turn naturally and smoothly.
Though the eight styles differ,
they meet and blend in accordance with principles.
Grasping the central pivot,
they converge like spokes in a wheel.
Therefore, one should imitate styles to establish habits,
and cultivate talent according to nature.
This is the compass for writing,
the way to follow.
The encomium says:
Talents and natures differ in kind;
literary styles are varied and intricate.
Diction is the skin and root,
but will is the very marrow.
Elegance and beauty are like ornate embroidery;
excessive artifice is like garish colors.
Habits too can solidify genuineness,
achieved through gradual influence.
**Chapter 28: Wind and Bone**
The *Book of Songs* encompasses the six principles,
with Wind leading them,
for it is the source of transformative influence,
the seal of will and vitality.
Thus, in expressing emotions with depth,
one must begin with Wind;
in pondering and arranging words,
nothing precedes Bone.
For words relying on Bone
are like a body supported by a skeleton;
emotions containing Wind
are like a form enveloping vitality.
If the language is upright and direct,
then literary Bone is formed;
if the spirit is vigorous and clear,
then literary Wind is pure.
If rich rhetoric abounds,
but Wind and Bone do not soar,
then the brilliance loses its freshness,
and the sound lacks strength.
Therefore, in composing and structuring a piece,
one must ensure ample vitality is maintained.
When firmness and vigor are substantial,
the radiance becomes fresh.
Their function in writing
is like wings for a bird of prey.
Thus, those skilled in Bone
analyze words with precision;
those profound in Wind
express emotions clearly.
Words are hammered firm and hard to shift,
resonance is condensed yet not stagnant—
this is the power of Wind and Bone.
If meaning is meager and words are bloated,
tangled and lacking order,
that is a sign of lacking Bone.
If thoughts are not comprehensive,
dragging weakly without vitality,
that is evidence of lacking Wind.
In the past, Pān Xù's edict for the Wèi,
imitating the classics in thought,
made other talents sheathe their brushes—
such was the loftiness of its Bone;
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's rhapsody on immortals,
with vitality said to reach the clouds,
became a model of writing—
such was the strength of its Wind.
Those who can grasp these essentials
can produce solid writing;
if this method is neglected,
do not pursue ornate rhetoric.
Thus Emperor Wén of Wèi stated, "In literature, the vital force (qì) is paramount;
this force has its substance in clarity and turbidity,
which cannot be achieved by forceful striving."
Hence, in his appraisal of Kǒng Róng,
he said, "His substance and force are sublime and exquisite";
discussing Xú Gàn,
he remarked, "He often has the Qí-like force";
and of Liú Zhēn,
he noted, "He possesses an untrammeled force."
Gōnggàn (Liú Zhēn) also said:
"Kǒng is outstanding,
truly containing an extraordinary force;
the nature of his brush and ink,
is almost unsurpassable."

are similar to this.

it is like a bird of prey gathering in the literary grove;

and mastering the techniques of the philosophers and histories,
penetrating the changes of emotions,
and clearly understanding literary styles,
then one can generate new ideas,
and carve out extraordinary expressions.

by comprehending changes, extraordinary expressions do not become excessive.

and the wind and expressions are not yet refined,
yet one disregards old rules,
and rushes after new creations,
even if clever ideas are obtained,

avoid errors and result in frivolity?

"Words should uphold substance and essentials,

each suiting one's preferences,
the enlightened do not impart them,

making the writing clear and robust;

Emotion and vital force go together,

Thoroughness and Change - Chapter Twenty-Nine
The forms of established writing have constancy,
but the methods of changing writing are without fixed rules.
How do we know this is so?
All poetry, rhapsodies, records, and letters,
their names and principles follow each other,
this is the constancy of form;
the diction, vital force, and strength in writing,
through thoroughness and change, endure,
this is the method without fixed rules.
Names and principles have constancy,
so form must draw from past examples;
thoroughness and change have no fixed rules,
so methods must consider new voices;
thus, one can gallop on an endless path,
and drink from an inexhaustible source.
However, with a short rope, one suffers thirst,
with tired feet, one halts on the road;
it is not that the methods of literary principle are exhausted,
but that the art of thoroughness and change is neglected.
Therefore, the way of discussing literature
is like plants and trees:
roots and trunks cling to the soil, sharing the same nature,
but scents and tastes, basking in the sun, differ in quality.
Thus, through nine dynasties of song,
the intent conforms to literary principles.
The Huáng-era song "Breaking Bamboo"
is of utmost simplicity;
the Táng-era songs of the past
were broader than the Huáng era;
the Yú-era song "Qīng Yún"
was more ornate than the Táng time;
the Xià-era song "Carved Walls"
was more elaborate than the Yú dynasty;
the pieces of the Shāng and Zhōu
were more beautiful than the Xià years.

their standard is one.

it modeled after the Zhōu people;

the writings of the Jìn
gazed upon the Wèi brilliance.

the Yú and Xià were simple yet discerning,

the Wèi and Jìn were shallow and flowery,

From simplicity to distortion,
the closer in time, the more insipid.

Competing in the present and neglecting the ancient,

diligently study writing,

crimson is born from madder,

and steering between elegance and commonness,

The rhythm of literature cycles continuously,
its craft renews daily.

continuity prevents exhaustion.
Adapt to the times decisively,
seize opportunities without fear.
Look to the present to create novelty,
consult the past to establish norms.
Chapter Thirty: Determining Style
Emotional expressions vary in nature,
literary transformations differ in method,
all establish form based on emotion,
and from form emerges style.
Style
follows advantage to shape.
Like an arrow shot straight from a bow,
or a torrent winding through a curved ravine,
it is the tendency of nature.
Round shapes, by their nature,
tend to rotate;
square shapes, by their form,
tend to stabilize;
the style of literary writing
is just like this.
Thus, those who model after the classics
naturally attain the beauty of elegance;
those who emulate the "Lísāo" in composition
inevitably achieve the splendor of grace and freedom;
those who express shallow thoughts
generally lack subtlety;
those who use concise and clear language

just as rushing water has no ripples,
and withered trees cast no shade,
this is the natural tendency.
Thus, in painting, colors depict,
in writing, words convey emotions fully;
colors blend, yet dogs and horses differ in form,
emotions interact, yet elegance and vulgarity differ in style;
the molds and models one imitates,
each has its master craftsman,
though without strict boundaries,
they are hard to overstep.
However, those profound in literature
master all styles collectively;
though unconventional and orthodox oppose,
they must understand and integrate both;
though firm and gentle differ,
they must apply each as appropriate to the occasion.

then the principle of comprehensive mastery is biased,
like the Xià people arguing over bows and arrows,

requires skill in discrimination;
musical notes and colors,
each matches according to style.

aim for elegance and dignity;
rhapsodies, odes, songs, and poems,
model after clarity and beauty;
official documents and proclamations,
follow clarity and decisiveness;
historical records, discourses, prefaces, and commentaries,
learn from conciseness and essence;
admonitions, inscriptions, steles, and elegies,

linked pearls and seven-part compositions,
engage in cleverness and brilliance;
this is forming style by following form,
achieving success through adaptation.
Though agreements and meetings may intertwine,
and rhythms and patterns mix,
like a brocade of five colors,
each takes its original hue as the base.
Huán Tán said, "Literary writers each have their admirations,

tracing their form,

examining their distorted intent,

suppressing the upper word and elevating the lower,

The main road is level and broad,
yet many take shortcuts,
because they seek the near;
proper writing is clear,
yet some often pursue contrary expressions,

hold to the orthodox to驾驭 the novel;

Form begets style,
beginning and end connect.

arrows shot straight as strings.

Chapter Thirty-One: Emotion and Ornament
The writings of sages and worthies
are collectively called literary compositions—
how could they be without literary elegance?
Water, being fluid, forms ripples;
trees, being solid, produce blossoms:
this shows how pattern attaches to substance.
If tigers and leopards had no patterns,
their hides would be no different from those of dogs or sheep;
rhinoceroses have hides,
yet their color depends on vermilion lacquer:
this shows how substance depends on pattern.
As for delineating human nature
and describing objects and appearances,
carving out thoughts through writing
and weaving words on paper,
their brilliance
lies in rich coloration.
Thus, the ways of establishing pattern
follow three principles:
first, form-pattern,
which is the five colors;
second, sound-pattern,
which is the five notes;
third, emotion-pattern,
which is the five inherent natures.
The five colors interwoven create embroidered patterns;
the five notes harmonized produce the Sháo and Xià music;
the five emotions expressed become literary compositions:
this is the law of divine principle.
The Classic of Filial Piety establishes the rule
that words of mourning should not be ornate;
thus we know that in ordinary speech, a gentleman
is not necessarily plain.
Lǎozi detested falsity,
hence he said, "Fine words are not truthful";
yet his Five Thousand Characters are exquisitely subtle,
showing he did not abandon beauty.
Zhuāng Zhōu said,
"Debate carves all things,"
referring to ornate embellishment.
Hán Fēi said,
"Gorgeous is debate and persuasion,"
referring to florid beauty.
Florid beauty in elegant persuasion,
ornate embellishment in carved debate—
the variations of literary expression
reach their extreme here.
Studying the Classic of Filial Piety and Lǎozi,
we understand that substance and pattern depend on innate nature;
examining Zhuāngzǐ and Hán Fēi,
we see that flourish and substance exceed proper bounds into extravagance.
If one distinguishes between the currents of the Jīng and Wèi Rivers,
and guides along the path of deviance and rectitude,
one can then master literary elegance.
Cosmetics serve to adorn appearance,
but charming glances arise from innate beauty;
literary elegance serves to adorn language,
but persuasive brilliance stems from genuine emotion.
Thus, emotion
is the warp of literature,
and diction
is the weft of reason;
only when the warp is straight can the weft be formed,
only when reason is settled can diction flow smoothly:
this is the fundamental source of establishing literature.
In the past, the poets' compositions
created literature for the sake of emotion;
rhapsodists' odes and eulogies
created emotion for the sake of literature.
How do we know this is so?
The emergence of the Airs and Elegantiae
stemmed from pent-up thoughts and feelings,
chanting innate emotions
to remonstrate with superiors:
this is creating literature for emotion.
The various masters,
with hearts not truly stirred,
merely pursued exaggeration,
fishing for fame and worldly acclaim:
this is creating emotion for literature.
Thus, writing for emotion is concise and portrays truth,
while writing for literature is excessively ornate and redundant.
Later writers
adopted excess and neglected truth,
abandoning the ancient Airs and Elegantiae
and following recent rhapsodies;
hence, works embodying true emotions dwindled,
while pieces chasing literary form flourished.
Thus, some deeply desire high office,
yet idly chant about rustic life;
their minds entangled in worldly affairs,
they fictitiously describe transcendence.
With no true essence within,
their words turn contrary.
Peach and plum trees do not speak, yet paths form beneath them,
because there is fruit;
a man plants orchids, but they lack fragrance,
because he has no genuine feeling.
If even slight plants
rely on feeling and depend on substance,
how much more should literature,
which takes expressing intent as fundamental?
When words contradict intent,
how can such writing be trusted?
Thus, connecting phrases and weaving colors
aims to clarify principle;
if colors are excessive and phrases deceptive,
the mind's principle becomes more obscured.
We know well that emerald fishing lines and cassia bait
instead cause loss of fish.
"Words are obscured by flourish"
probably refers to this.
Therefore, wearing brocade covered by a plain gown
shows dislike for too glaring patterns;
the Bì hexagram's image ends in pure white,
valuing return to fundamentals.
To establish a model for positioning principle
and prepare a ground for placing the heart,
first settle the heart, then compose the melody;
first correct the principle, then spread the ornament,
ensuring pattern does not overshadow substance,
and breadth does not drown the heart,
so true colors like vermilion and blue shine forth,
and mixed colors like pink and purple are set aside.
Only then can we speak of carving and polishing one's work,
becoming a refined gentleman.
The Encomium says:
Words, through pattern, endure;
truly, this is proven.
When the heart's method takes form,
splendid bloom flourishes.
Wú brocade easily fades;
hibiscus flowers are vainly bright.
Excessive colors with little feeling,
when savored, must cause disgust.
Molding and Cutting: Thirty-Second
When emotion and principle are set in place,
literary elegance moves among them.
Firmness and softness establish the foundation,
adaptation and flexibility follow the times.
Establishing the foundation has its form,
but ideas may be uneven;
following the times has no fixed method,
so phrases may become cluttered.
The crucial task
lies in molding and cutting:
rectifying emotion and principle,
and adjusting literary elegance.
Regulating the main substance is called molding;
trimming excessive words is called cutting.
Cutting prevents rank growth;
molding makes the outline clear and smooth,
like the marking line's precise division,
or the axe's hewing and carving.
Webbed toes or extra fingers
are excesses of nature;
attached warts and hanging tumors
are excesses of form.
One idea appearing twice
is a webbed branch in meaning;
repeated phrases and redundant sentences
are tumors and warts in writing.
When thoughts first emerge,
verbal ornament tends to be杂乱;
the mind is no scale,
so imbalance is inevitable.
Thus, in drafting a great work,
first set three standards:
beginning at the start,
establish emotion to position the form;
setting the norm in the middle,
select events for their relevance;
completing the end,
gather phrases to highlight essentials.
Then unfold blossoms and display fruit,
adopt or reject with rhythmic pattern,
beyond the marking line,
fine timber is hewn,
so head and tail can blend smoothly,
orderly and coherent.
If the method is not set beforehand,
but one follows whims and chases phrases,
heterodox thoughts will swarm,
and redundant excess will abound.
Once the three standards are established,
one proceeds to examine the words and sentences.
If a sentence can be pruned,
it reveals its looseness;
if a word cannot be reduced,
then its density is known.
Refined arguments and essential phrases
represent the extremely concise style;
wandering thoughts and scattered sentences
represent the extremely elaborate style.
As for elaboration and conciseness,
they suit individual preferences.
Extending and expanding them,
two sentences can be elaborated into a chapter;
condensing and unifying them,
a chapter can be trimmed down to two sentences.
Those with abundant ideas excel at elaboration,
while those with precise talent excel at pruning.
Skillful pruning removes words but retains meaning;
skillful elaboration uses varied expressions to make the meaning clear.
If words are cut and meaning is lost,
it is brevity due to deficiency, not precision;
if expressions are elaborated and words are repetitive,
it is冗杂 due to verbosity, not richness.

literary scholars from Xīhé,
were regarded by Zhāng Jùn as "Ài's elaboration cannot be pruned,
Jì's conciseness cannot be added to."
These two men
can be said to have mastered refinement and understood elaboration and conciseness.
As for Lù Jī, whose talent was superior,
his compositions were particularly elaborate;
while Lù Yún, whose thinking was inferior,
had a fondness for clarity and conciseness.
When Yún discussed Jī,
he repeatedly regretted his verbosity,
yet praised the continuous freshness,
not considering it a flaw,
likely out of respect for brotherly affection.
Just as fine brocade is made into clothing,
its length has a measure;
though one may admire its color,
the collar and sleeves should not be doubled.
Even the skillful find it hard to handle elaboration,
let alone the clumsy.
Yet the "Wén Fù" suggests not pruning brambles and thorns,
and that mediocre notes suffice for a melody.
This is not due to lack of discernment,
but rather a reluctance to cut away excess.
A body with a hundred joints
relies on the circulatory system;
myriad ideas converge in writing,
never departing from expression and emotion.
If emotions are thorough without being冗杂,
and expressions flow without excess,
without refinement,

The encomium says:
Chapters and sections are like windows and doors,
positioned to face each other.
Words are like river currents,
overflowing leads to flooding.
Weighing gains and losses,
balancing density and lightness.
Pruning冗杂 and cutting away the superfluous,

Sound and Rhythm, Thirty-Third
The origin of musical tones
lies in the human voice.
Sounds contain the gōng and shāng notes,
arising from one's vitality.
The ancient kings followed this
to create music and songs.
Thus, we know instruments imitate the human voice,
not the voice learning from instruments.
Therefore, speech
is the pivot of spirit in writing,
emitting the musical tones
through the lips alone.
In ancient teaching of singing,
methods were first applied,
making swift calls match gōng,
and slow calls match zhǐ.
Now zhǐ and yǔ notes resonate high,
while gōng and shāng notes sound low;
differences in raising the throat and adjusting the tongue,
variations in pursing lips and striking teeth,
balanced between sharp and full,
are clearly distinguishable.
If a zither is out of tune today,
one knows to readjust the strings;
but if writing is discordant,
one does not know how to tune it.
The resonance lies in those strings,
achieving harmony;
the sound arises in my heart,
yet loses harmony and rhythm.
What is the reason for this?
Truly, external listening is easy to master,
while internal listening is hard to make acute.
Thus, the ease of external listening
lies in strings being fixed by hand;
the difficulty of internal listening
lies in sounds and mind being entangled;
it can be sought through rules,
but hard to capture with words.
All sounds have rising and falling,
resonances have movement and stillness.
Alliterations separated by characters often clash,
rhyming words mixed in sentences inevitably conflict;
falling sounds cause the resonance to break off,
rising sounds make the tone float away unreturned.
They should interact like a well-pulley,
or scale-like patterns fitting together.
If their meeting is obstructed,
then progress is hindered and regress tangled.
This ailment
is like a writer's stammer.
The problem of stammering in writing
arises from a fondness for the bizarre,
chasing novelty and strangeness,
thus tangling the throat and lips.
To unravel the knot,
one must be resolute and decisive.
If blocked on the left, seek the right;
if stuck at the end, examine the front.
Then sounds flow on the lips,
tingling like jade pendants shaking;
words smooth to the ear,
continuous like strung pearls.
Thus, the beauty or ugliness of sound patterns
lies in recitation;
flavor flows from phrasing,
and vigor depends on harmony and rhyme.
Different tones following each other is called harmony;
similar sounds responding to each other is called rhyme.
Once rhyme's tone is fixed,
the remaining sounds are easy to arrange;
as harmony's form has rises and falls,
the leftover resonances are hard to match.
Composing is easily skillful,
but selecting harmony is extremely difficult;
writing is hard to refine,
yet creating rhyme is very easy.
Though subtle ideas and intricate variations
cannot be detailed in full,
grasping the main principles,
does not go beyond this discussion.
As for the great harmony of gōng and shāng,
it is like blowing the yuè panpipes;
adjusting to achieve balance,
somewhat resembles tuning the sè zither.
The sè relies on moving bridges,
so sometimes it goes out of tune;
the yuè has fixed pipes,
thus never fails to be consistent.
Chén Sī and Pān Yuè
exemplify the harmony of the yuè;
Lù Jī and Zuǒ Sī
represent the tuning of the sè.
Generalizing and extending,
one can see by analogy.
Moreover, poets who composed rhymes
mostly achieved clarity and precision.
The "Chǔ Cí" used Chǔ dialect,
so erroneous rhymes were indeed plentiful.
When Zhāng Huá discussed rhymes,
he said Lù Jī used much Chǔ influence,
and the "Wén Fù" also mentioned it's hard to avoid this.
This can be said to inherit Qū Yuán's vocal remnants,
but lose the correct tone of the huáng zhōng pitch.
Generally, the movement of precise rhymes
is as smooth as turning a circle;
the occurrence of erroneous sounds
is worse than fitting a square peg into a round hole.
Avoiding such misfits,
then there are no major faults.
Those with cultivated talent and deep insight
analyze characters and delve into sounds;
the negligent and粗略
follow wherever the sound leads,
like the wind blowing through hollows,
or the man of the eastern suburb blowing the yú.
In ancient times, people wore jade pendants,
with gōng on the left and zhǐ on the right,
to regulate their steps,
so the sounds never lost order.
Using sound to rhythmize writing,
how can one forget this!

Expressing emotions strives for depth,
Comparing sounds draws near.
Blowing pitch-pipes from the chest,

Chapter Thirty-Four: Sentences and Paragraphs

Placing words has their positions;

The position of words is called a sentence.
Thus, a paragraph
Clarifies;

Delimits.

Joins characters to define boundaries,

Synthesizes meanings to encompass form,
Distinct regions differ,

When people establish discourse,

Lies in flawless paragraphs;

Lies in unblemished sentences;

Shake the root and the branches follow,
Understand one and all becomes clear.

Works vary in size;
Dividing paragraphs and combining sentences,
The rhythm may be slow or urgent,
Adapting to changes and occasions,
No fixed standard is seen.

Awaiting connection to function;
A paragraph synthesizes one meaning,

Guiding emotions and principles,
Welcoming and sending off at junctions,

Yet with fixed positions on stage;
Or the lingering beauty of song,
Yet with rising and falling rhythms.

Are like drawing thread from a cocoon,
From beginning to end,
The structure must be orderly like fish scales.
The opening words
Foreshadow the meaning of the middle section;
The concluding remarks
Echo the intent of preceding sentences;
Thus, the external text is intricately woven,
The internal meaning flows like veins,
As calyx and petals interlock,
Head and tail form one body.

Four-character lines are the norm,
Except for "Qífǔ" and "Zhàoyīn",
Which use two-character lines.
Trace two-character lines to the Huáng era,
As seen in the "Zhúdàn" ballad;
Three-character lines arose in the Yú period,
As in the "Yuánshǒu" poem;
Four-character lines expanded in the Xià years,
As in the "Luòruì" song;
Five-character lines appeared in the Zhōu dynasty,
As in the "Xínglù" chapter;
Six and seven-character lines
Occur sporadically in Shī and Sāo,
But as complete forms,
They matured in the two Hàn dynasties,
As emotional complexity evolved,
Usage adapted with the times.
As for changing rhymes to follow melody,
It regulates literary expression and tone;
Jiǎ Yì and Méi Chéng
Changed rhymes every couplet;
Liú Xīn and Huán Tán
Kept the same rhyme for a hundred lines;
Each had their own rationale.
Formerly, Wèi Wǔ discussed fù,
Disliking accumulated rhymes,
And praised shifting changes.
Lù Yún also said, "For four-character turning lines,
Four lines are best."
Observing their rhyme schemes,
Their intent aligned with Méi and Jiǎ.
Yet changing rhymes every couplet
Makes the sound slightly hasty;
Keeping the same rhyme for a hundred lines
Makes the lips and mouth weary;
Though talented writers inspire,
And even if thoughts flow smoothly,
How better to balance with moderation,
To ensure no fault remains?
Moreover, poets incorporate "xī" within lines,
As in Chǔcí usage,
Placing the word outside the line.
Consider "xī" continuing a line,
It is a auxiliary trailing sound.
Shùn chanting the "Nánfēng",
Used it long ago,
Yet Wèi Wǔ disliked it,
Perhaps finding it added no literary meaning!
As for "fú", "wéi", "gài", "gù",
They initiate beginnings;
