"Zhī", "ér", "yú", "yǐ",
Are the conventional structure for linking sentences;
"Hū", "zāi", "yǐ", "yě",
Also common endings.
Seemingly incidental in context,
They are crucial in application.
Skillful writers deftly employ them,
Mending literary form,
So beyond several sentences,
They gain the aid of a single word.
If auxiliary words are hard to misuse,
How much more so for sentences and paragraphs!
Eulogy says:
Structuring paragraphs has its rules,
Accumulating sentences follows no constant.
Principles rely on matching the theme,
Words dread losing companions.
Circling emotions and drafting tones,
They waltz and soar in turn.
Separating similarities and uniting differences,
To exhaust their potential.
Parallel Prose Chapter Thirty-Five
When nature endows forms,
limbs invariably come in pairs;
when divine principle functions,
nothing stands in isolation.
When the mind generates literary expressions,
organizing and refining myriad thoughts,
high and low complement each other,
naturally forming parallels.
In the era of Táng and Yú,
language had not yet reached literary extremes,
yet Gāo Yáo proclaimed:
"When guilt is doubtful, treat it lightly;
when merit is doubtful, reward it heavily."
Yì set forth counsel saying:
"Fullness invites loss,
modesty receives gain."
Were these deliberately crafted parallel phrases?
They emerged spontaneously as counterparts.
The "Wén Xì" of the Yì Jīng
embodies the sage's marvelous thinking.
In presenting the four virtues of Qián,
eight lines interlock;
in describing the mutual response of dragon and tiger,
every character forms a couplet;
in explaining the simplicity of Qián and Kūn,
meaning turns and continues;
in depicting the alternation of sun and moon,
separate lines distantly correspond;
though the phrasing may differ,
the parallel intent remains constant.
As for the poets' parallel stanzas
and officials' linked expressions,
the use of singular and parallel adapted to circumstance
without laborious contrivance.
Since Yáng, Mǎ, Zhāng, and Cài,
parallel diction has been highly esteemed,
like Sòng painting and Wú metalwork,
carving shapes and engraving methods,
where elegant lines flow with profound brilliance,
and parallel meaning emerges with transcendent charm.
By the time of Wèi and Jìn talents,
phrase analysis became increasingly meticulous,
connecting characters to unite meaning,
splitting hairs and analyzing minutiae.
Yet only those who grasp the essence achieve skill,
while the superficial and artificial gain nothing.
Thus parallel diction, as a form,
generally comprises four types of antithesis:
verbal antithesis is easy,
factual antithesis is difficult,
contrasting antithesis is superior,
complementary antithesis is inferior.
Verbal antithesis
involves pairing empty phrases;
factual antithesis
juxtaposes human experiences;
contrasting antithesis
unites different principles in shared meaning;
complementary antithesis
employs different facts to express identical meaning.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Shàng Lín" states:
"Cultivate demeanor in the garden of rites,
soar freely in the park of books."
This exemplifies verbal antithesis;
Sòng Yù's "Shénnǚ Fù" says:
"Máo Qiáng shielding her sleeves
cannot serve as standard,
Xī Shī covering her face
appears colorless in comparison."
This exemplifies factual antithesis;
Wáng Càn's "Climbing the Tower" states:
"Zhòng Yí imprisoned yet playing Chǔ melodies,
Zhuāng Xì prominent yet singing Yuè songs."
This exemplifies contrasting antithesis;
Zhāng Zǎi's "Seven Sorrows" says:
"Hàn Gāozǔ yearning for Fényú,
Guāngwǔ Dì longing for Báishuǐ."
This exemplifies complementary antithesis.
Generally, parallel expressions from the heart
make verbal antithesis easy;
drawing on others' learning
makes factual antithesis difficult;
sharing purpose despite different circumstances
makes contrasting antithesis superior;
equal emphasis on similar thoughts
makes complementary antithesis inferior.
Moreover, both verbal and factual antithesis
have contrasting and complementary variations—
follow these categories to seek examples,
and countless instances will become clear.
Zhāng Huá's poem states "Wandering wild geese fly wing to wing,
returning swans know to join pinions."
Liú Kūn's verse says "Confucius grieved at capturing the qilin,
wept for the western hunt's Confucius."
Such repetition
constitutes superfluous parallelism.
Therefore, the beauty of verbal antithesis
lies in exquisite refinement;
the priority in factual antithesis
rests on perfect appropriateness.
If two facts are paired
with unequal quality,
it's like placing a steed as left trace-horse
with a nag as right shaft-horse.
If a fact stands isolated
with nothing to pair,
it's like the one-legged Kuí
hopping along.
If the spirit lacks extraordinary quality,
the writing wants distinctive brilliance,
then mediocre parallel phrases
will only dull the ears and eyes.
One must ensure logical coherence and factual precision,
linking jade-like compositions,
alternating singular and parallel,
tempering with varied ornaments—
this is what's valuable.
Reflecting along these lines,
the principle becomes evident.
Summary:
Forms inherently come in pairs,
expressions naturally find matches.
Lifting left while supporting right,
essence and flavor both carried.
Brilliantly gleaming connected blossoms,
mirror-still yet containing postures.
Jade-smooth dual flow,
like those paired pendants.
Bǐ and Xìng: Chapter Thirty-Six
The Poetry's texts are vast and profound,
encompassing the six principles,
yet Master Máo, composing the Commentary,
singled out the Xìng style—
was this not because Fēng flows freely while Fù remains uniform,
Bǐ is evident while Xìng is subtle!
Thus Bǐ
means to attach;
Xìng
means to arise.
Attaching to principle uses close analogy to indicate matters;
arousing emotion follows subtle cues to suggest meaning.
Arousing emotion establishes the Xìng form;
attaching to principle generates the Bǐ pattern.
Bǐ accumulates emotion for direct expression,
Xìng employs circular analogies for implicit criticism.
As circumstances vary endlessly,
so poets' approaches diverge.
Observe how Xìng conveys meaning through allusion,
subtly yet coherently composed,
naming small things
to represent large categories.
The separated ospreys
symbolize the queen's virtue;
the chaste dove
represents the lady's constancy.
The meaning values chastity,
regardless of the bird being common;
the virtue prizes distinction,
unbothered by the bird being fierce;
clear yet not fully transparent,
thus requiring commentary for understanding.
And what constitutes Bǐ?
It describes objects to convey meaning,
using elevated language to sharpen matters.
Thus gold and tin metaphorize bright virtue,
jade tablets illustrate outstanding people,
caterpillars exemplify teaching,
cicadas depict crying out,
washing clothes suggests heartache,
rolling mats symbolizes steadfast will—
all these close images
represent Bǐ's meaning.
As for "hempen garments like snow,"
"two side-horses like dancing,"
such examples
all belong to Bǐ's categories.
When Xiāng of Chǔ trusted slander
and Qū Yuán demonstrated loyalty,
he created the "Lí Sāo" following the Poetry,
blending criticism through Bǐ and Xìng.
Though the mighty Hàn flourished,
writers became obsequious,
the way of criticism was lost,
so Xìng's meaning faded.
Then Fǔ and Sòng took precedence,
and Bǐ forms proliferated like clouds,
numerous and disorderly,
truly departing from classical tradition.
The principle of analogy
embraces diverse comparisons:
some liken sounds,
some describe appearances,
some convey emotions,
some illustrate events.
Sòng Yù in "Gāotáng" wrote:
"Slender branches wail mournfully,
their sound resembling reed pipes."
This exemplifies sound analogy;
Méi Chéng in "Tù Yuán" wrote:
"Swirling and scattering,
like dust mingling with white clouds."
This exemplifies appearance analogy;
Jiǎ Shēng in "Fú Niǎo" wrote:
"Misfortune and fortune
differ no more than twisted ropes."
This uses objects to illustrate principles;
Wáng Bāo in "Dòng Xiāo" wrote:
"Gentle and warm,
like a kind father loving his son."
This uses sound to convey emotion;
Mǎ Róng in "Cháng Dí" wrote:
"Intricate and continuous,
like the arguments of Fàn Jū and Cài Zé."
This uses resonance to depict debate;
Zhāng Héng in "Nán Dū" wrote:
"The Zhèng dance begins,
like cocoons yielding silk."
This uses manner to describe objects.
Such methods
are prioritized in rhymed prose,
daily employing analogy
while neglecting evocation,
mastering minor techniques while abandoning major ones,
hence falling short of the Zhōu dynasty writers.
As for writers like Yáng Xióng and Bān Gù,
and those after Cáo Zhí and Liú Zhēn,
depicting mountains and rivers,
portraying clouds and objects,
all weave analogy into their meaning,
displaying literary flourish,
startling ears and captivating eyes,
relying on this for achievement.
Again, Pān Yuè in "Yíng Fù" wrote:
"Flowing gold in sand."
Zhāng Hàn in "Zá Shī" wrote:
"Green twigs like clustered jade."
Both exemplify this principle.
Thus analogies, though varied,
should value precision;
if carving a swan results in a duck,
it is worthless.
Appraisal:
The poet's analogy and evocation
respond comprehensively to things encountered.
Things may be as distant as Hú and Yuè,
yet united as closely as liver and gall.
Imitate appearances, capture essence;
decisive diction must be bold.
Gather diverse songs
like a river's flow.
Exaggeration and Embellishment, Thirty-Seventh
What is beyond form is called Dào,
what has form is called object.
The divine Dào is hard to depict,
refined words cannot capture its limit;
physical objects are easy to describe,
vigorous language can convey their truth;
it's not a matter of talent's length,
but principle's inherent difficulty.
Since heaven and earth began,
involving sound and appearance,
wherever literary expression reaches,
exaggeration constantly exists.
Even in the elegant words of the "Shījīng" and "Shūjīng",
serving as models to instruct the world,
matters require breadth,
and language likewise exceeds.
Thus speaking of height, Sōng Mountain reaches the sky;
discussing narrowness, the river cannot hold a boat;
describing multitude, descendants number thousands of millions;
referring to scarcity, not a single person remains;
flooding hills raise the term 'inundating heavens',
fallen weapons establish the saying 'floating pestles',
though the phrasing is extreme,
the meaning suffers no harm.
Moreover, the owl's harsh cry
could not become pleasant in a school's woods;
the sowthistle's bitter taste
would not turn sweet on Zhōu's plains;
both cases deeply intend praise,
thus creating deliberate embellishment,
recorded by the great sage
to establish models.
As Mèng Kē said, "Interpreting the 'Shījīng' should not let wording obscure the phrase,
nor phrasing obscure the meaning."
From Sòng Yù and Jǐng Chā onward,
exaggeration began to flourish.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú rode this trend,
becoming increasingly extravagant.
Thus in the Shànglín Park's lodge,
shooting stars and arched rainbows enter the windows;
in the abundance of hunting,
Fēilián and Jiāomíng are both captured.
When Yáng Xióng wrote "Gānquán",
drawing from this tradition,
he described marvels by borrowing jade trees,
and spoke of extreme heights by invoking falling deities.
As for the "Dōngdū"'s paired fish,
and the "Xījīng"'s sea god Ruò,
examining principle finds no basis,
yet exhaustive embellishment remains unfinished.
Again, Yáng Xióng in "Jiàoliè"
whipped Fú Fēi to feed Qū Yuán;
Zhāng Héng in "Yǔliè"
trapped Xuánmíng in northern wilds.
That lovely Luò River goddess
was no demon;
this water creature
was no monster;
yet they used empty descriptions recklessly
—was this not careless?
They wished to exaggerate majesty,
but contradicted factual meaning.
As for depicting mountains and seas' spirit,
palaces' grandeur,
towering and majestic,
glittering and brilliant appearances,
radiant colors about to blaze,
precarious forms about to move—
all achieve description through exaggeration,
gaining wonder through embellishment.
Thus later talents,
encouraged and emboldened,
soar aspiring to fly high,
leap proudly, ashamed of small steps,
language becomes dazzling,
spring flora cannot match its brilliance;
words describing withering,
barren valleys cannot equal its desolation;
speaking of joy, characters laugh with meaning;
discussing sorrow, tone weeps with sound;
truly capable of releasing pent-up feelings,
enlightening the blind and startling the deaf.
Yet if embellishment captures essence,
hearts' voices surge sharply;
if exaggeration exceeds reason,
name and reality diverge.
If one can blend the "Shījīng" and "Shūjīng"'s broad intent,
trim Yáng and Sīmǎ's excess,
making exaggeration measured,
embellishment truthful,
this may be called excellence.
Appraisal:
Exaggeration's use
cannot follow rigid rules.
Words must soar like Péng,
spirit surpassing wild geese's flight.
Overturn seas for pearls,
topple Kūnlún for jade.
Vast but not overflowing,
lavish yet flawless.
Allusion, Thirty-Eighth
Allusion means
beyond the text itself,
citing events to categorize meaning,
invoking antiquity to prove modernity.
When King Wén composed the "Yìjīng",
analyzing hexagram positions,
"Jì Jì"'s third nine
remotely cited Gāozōng's campaign;
"Míng Yí"'s fifth six
recently recorded Jīzǐ's steadfastness;
these briefly cite human affairs
to demonstrate meaning.
As for "Yìn Zhēng" mentioning Yì Hé,
presenting canonical instruction;
"Pán Gēng" addressing the people,
narrating Chí Rèn's words;
these fully quote established phrases
to clarify principle.
Thus clarifying principle through established phrases,
demonstrating meaning through human affairs
constitutes sages' great design,
classics' universal standard.
The "Dà Xù" hexagram image states:
"The gentleman extensively remembers past words and deeds."
This also encompasses literature.
Observing how Qū Yuán and Sòng Yù composed their works,
they were said to follow the poets of the Shījīng,
and though they alluded to ancient events,
they never borrowed old expressions.
Only in Jiǎ Yì's "Fú Fù",
did he begin to employ theories from the Hè Guànzǐ;
in Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Shàng Lín",
he extracted passages from Lǐ Sī's writings;
these were but one in ten thousand instances of convergence.
By the time of Yáng Xióng's "Liù Guān Zhēn",
he substantially drew from the Shījīng and Shūjīng;
Liú Xīn's "Suì Chū Fù",
narrated through historical records;
gradually they synthesized and adopted more broadly.
As for Cuī, Bān, Zhāng, and Cài,
they then gathered from classics and histories,
adornments and substance spreading widely,
achieving merit through these writings,
all becoming models for later generations.
Ginger and cinnamon from the earth,
their pungency lies in their innate nature;
literary compositions stem from learning,
but capability depends on natural endowment.
Talent emerges from within,
learning is acquired externally,
some have ample learning but meager talent,
others abundant talent but impoverished learning.
Those poor in learning
struggle with matters and meanings;
those lacking in talent
labor over expressions and emotions;
this is the distinction between internal and external.
Therefore in conceiving and establishing writing,
when mind and brush conspire,
talent serves as the sovereign,
learning as the assistant,
sovereign and assistant united in virtue,
literary elegance will surely dominate;
if talent and learning are narrow,
though beautiful, achieve little.
With Yáng Xióng's talent,
he himself confessed to lacking learning,
until he studied in the stone chamber,
then achieved magnificent elegance.
Inner and outer qualities complement each other,
this principle holds true from ancient to modern times.
Thus Cáo Cāo criticized Zhāng Zǐ's writing as clumsy,
for his learning was shallow,
his knowledge not extensive,
merely picking up minor works of Cuī and Dù,
his writings cannot withstand thorough questioning,
when questioned, he wouldn't know their origins,
this is the malady of limited exposure.
The classics are profound and deep,
records vast and extensive,
truly the abstruse region of all expressions,
and the divine marsh of talent and thought.
From Yáng Xióng and Bān Gù onward,
none have not drawn from these resources,
exerting effort in plowing and weeding,
following their will in fishing and hunting,
wielding the knife to cut,
they surely carve out fertile lands;
thus to nourish one's talent,
one must strive for broad exposure,
a fox's armpit cannot be warmed by one pelt,
chicken feet must number thousands to satisfy.
Therefore comprehensive learning lies in breadth,
selecting matters values conciseness,
examination and refinement must be precise,
gathering principles requires verification,
all beauties converging like spokes,
inner and outer qualities shining forth.
Liú Shào's "Zhào Dū Fù" says:
"The guest of the prince,
scolded mighty Chǔ to make them swear alliance;
the warehouse servant,
rebuked powerful Qín to make them drum pottery."
Using allusions like this,
can be called grasping principles and capturing essence.
Thus when matters capture the essence,
even small achievements,
like an inch-long linchpin controlling the wheel,
a foot-long pivot operating the gate.
Sometimes subtle words and fine matters,
placed in trivial positions,
is like adorning ankles with gold and jade,
applying powder and mascara to the chest.
Whenever using old references appropriately,
they appear as if from one's own mouth;
if citing events erroneously,
even after millennia it remains a flaw.
Cáo Zhí stands as the finest among talents,
yet in his "Letter in Reply to Chén Lín" he wrote:
"The music of Gě Tiānshì,
with a thousand singing,
ten thousand harmonizing,
listeners thereby despised Sháo and Xià."
This citation is factually mistaken.
Checking the songs of Gě Tiān,
only three people sang and harmonized.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Shàng Lín" says:
"Performing the dance of Yáo,
listening to the songs of Gě Tiān,
a thousand singing,
ten thousand harmonizing."
Singing and harmonizing by thousands,
was Xiàngrú's exaggeration,
thus extravagantly magnifying Gě Tiān,
inflating three into ten thousand,
believing the rhapsody's reckless writing,
led to this error.
Lù Jī's "Garden Mallows" poem says:
"Sheltering feet shares one wisdom,
living principles embrace different ends."
The mallow's ability to protect its roots,
alludes to the criticism of Bào Zhuāng;
the vine sheltering its roots,
comes from Lè Yù's expression;
if comparing vine to mallow,
then the allusion is mistaken;
if claiming 'shelter' surpasses 'protect',
then altering the event loses truth;
this again is the fault of imprecision.
Despite Cáo Zhí's clarity and proficiency,
Lù Jī's depth and meticulousness,
they could not avoid errors.
How then can Cáo Hóng's mistake about Gāotáng
be worth mocking!
Just as mountain timber is measured by skilled craftsmen,
classical texts are selected by literary scholars,
fine wood determined by the axe,
fine matters shaped by the brush,
those who refine their thoughts
need not feel ashamed before the master carpenter.
Encomium says:
Classics and texts profound and rich,
language and principles far-reaching and enduring.
Vast as rivers and seas,
lush as Kūnlún and Dèng Forest.
Ornamental catalpa jointly gathered,
jasper pearls exchanged as gifts.
Using others' words as one's own,
since ancient times, none have been ignorant.
Chapter 39: Refining Characters
The movements of the mind's techniques are profound,
and the transformations of literary emotions run deep;
from an abstruse source, streams branch out,
with vigorous roots, the tips soar high.
Thus, in the flowering of literature,
there are both the outstanding and the implicit.
The implicit refers to
the layered meanings beyond the text;
the outstanding refers to
the uniquely exceptional within the篇章.
The implicit excels through multiple meanings,
the outstanding through卓越 and uniqueness;
these are the splendid achievements of classical works,
the fine convergence of talent and emotion.
The nature of the implicit
is that meaning arises beyond the text,
with secret resonances echoing laterally,
and hidden brilliance emerging subtly,
like the transformations of hexagram lines in mutual bodies,
or rivers and streams concealing pearls and jade.
Thus, through mutual bodies and changing lines,
the four images of transformation are formed;
with pearls and jade submerged in water,
ripples manifest as squares and circles.
"The cool breeze stirs the autumn grass,
the frontier horse yearns to return,"
the chill air and the sorrowful event
make this a lament of the traveler's woes.
Among all literary collections, masterpieces
do not exceed one in ten;
chapters with outstanding lines
are barely one or two in a hundred;
both arise when thoughts align spontaneously,
not through deliberate calculation.
Some use obscurity to feign depth,
but though abstruse, it is not implicit;
others carve and polish for cleverness,
but though beautiful, it is not outstanding.
Thus, natural convergence achieves subtlety,
like flowers and trees shining in splendor;
embellishment for beauty
is like dyeing silk with red and green.
Red and green on silk,
deep and vividly rich;
splendor adorning trees,
light yet brilliantly radiant;
outstanding lines illuminate the literary garden,
precisely for this reason.
Summary:
Profound writing,隐蔚 with depth,
lingering flavors intricately wrapped.
Words arise from mutual bodies,
resembling changing lines.
The outstanding in speech
meets but once in myriad thoughts.
Stirring the heart, startling the ear,
like the ethereal sounds of shēng and páo.
Pointing Out Flaws: Chapter Forty-One
Guǎn Zhòng once said:
"What flies without wings is sound,
what stands firm without roots is emotion."
Thus, sound needs no wings
to fly with ease;
emotion requires no roots
to stand firm without difficulty;
yet when conveying them through writing,
must one not be cautious!
Throughout history, literary talents
have vied across eras:
some with unbridled talent, swift and sharp,
others with meticulous thought, fine and detailed,
yet their considerations often lack completeness,
rarely free from flaws.
The writings of Chén Sī,
the finest among many talents,
yet in his "Elegy for Wǔdì" he wrote:
"The revered spirit eternally hibernates."
In his "Ode to Míngdì" he said:
"The sacred body floats lightly."
Floating lightly resembles a butterfly,
eternal hibernation suggests insects;
applied to the most尊极,
is it appropriate!
Zuǒ Sī's "Seven Satires,"
advocating filial piety yet not following it,
such reversal of the Way
renders the rest unworthy of notice.
Pān Yuè, as a talent,
excelled in哀文,
yet mourning his elder cousin,
he spoke of sensing his breath;
grieving his young son,
he said his heart was as if in doubt.
The Lǐ texts apply to the尊极,
yet he used them for inferiors;
though the words are sorrowful enough,
the meaning is thus lost.
When a gentleman compares people,
it must be to their peers,
yet Cuī Yuàn in his "Elegy for Lǐ Gōng"
compared his conduct to Huángdì and Yúshùn,
and Xiàng Xiù in his "Rhapsody for Jī Shēng"
equated his faults with Lǐ Sī;
though it is said,
"rather err in excess than in deficiency,"
yet Gāo Hòu's poem
was utterly incongruous.
Generally, clever words are easily noticed,
clumsy phrases hard to conceal;
the flaws in speech
cut deeper than a white jade disc's flaw;
numerous examples are hard to list,
so I briefly cite four cases.
As for the way of establishing writing,
it lies in words and meanings.
Words are corrected by explanation,
meanings clarified by principle;
yet in late Jìn篇章,
their intent became vague,
with phrases like "appreciating the extraordinary arrival,"
and later, "stroking and knocking in response,"
often singling out one word
to convey emotion.
Now, "appreciate" means to bestow rewards—
how does it relate to understanding?
"Stroking" means to grasp—
what has it to do with emotion and reason?
Unheard in the "Yǎ" and "Sòng,"
unused in Hàn and Wèi,
vaguely grasped as if discernible,
yet in textual scrutiny,毫无意义;
this is truly a distortion of emotion,
a flaw of literary decline.
Since Sòng, talented minds
have not changed this;
old habits became customs,
not in a single day.
Modern writers
often indulge in suspicion,
even to the point of picking faults through homophones,
or finding flaws in reverse pronunciations;
though not esteemed in antiquity,
it is practiced today.
Also, composing what matches others' texts
should rightly be revised;
if appropriating others' fine phrases
as one's own effort,
like the precious jade and great bow,
they are never truly theirs.
Full copying is like lifting a chest,
partial borrowing like probing a bag;
yet copying from antiquity is too lightly taken,
while from contemporaries is a greater fault.
As for annotations in books,
they aim to clarify truths;
yet errors in research
or rash judgments occur.
The "Xījīng Fù" mentions warriors like Zhōng Huáng and Yù Huò's peers,
but Xuē Zōng erroneously annotated,
calling them eunuch officials—
this shows ignorance of those who tame雕虎.
Also, in the "Zhōu Lǐ," land tax
traditionally included a "pǐ" of horses,
but Yìng Shào explained "pǐ"
by counting heads or hooves—
is this the essence of discerning things?
Originally, in ancient correct naming,
chariots came in "liǎng," horses in "pǐ,"
the terms "pǐ" and "liǎng"
denoted pairing in use.
For chariots had secondary supports,
horses paired as cān and fú,
neither ridden nor driven singly,
so names were necessarily dual;
once naming was correct,
even alone, it was called "pǐ."
"Pǐ" for man and woman
also implies pairing.
Though a minor point on chariots and horses,
no era grasped it through the ages;
in the near matter of rhyme-prose,
errors spanned a thousand miles;
how much more in delving into classics,
could they avoid mistakes?
To debate words by counting heads and hooves,
or select bravery yet drive eunuch officials—
too grossly unreasonable,
so I cite this as a warning.
Vivid colors blaze at first but later fade,
writings grow brighter with passing years;
if one can correct flaws in a single day,
they may face millennia without shame.
Eulogy says:
Even Yì the Archer could err in shooting,
And Dōngyě's charioteering ended in failure.
Though possessing outstanding talent,
Mistakes bring much regret.
Once a word is flawed,
For millennia it remains unchanged.
Elegant writings free from fault
Are next to perfection.
Chapter Forty-Two: Nurturing Vital Energy
In the past, Wáng Chōng composed writings
And created the chapter "Nurturing Vital Energy,"
Based on his own experience—
How could it be mere fabrication!
The ears, eyes, nose, and mouth
Are servants of life;
Mental deliberation and verbal expression
Are functions of the spirit.
Following one's will with ease
Brings coherence to principles and fluency to emotions;
Grinding oneself excessively
Leads to mental fatigue and depletion of vital energy—
This is the nature of human disposition.
The language of the Three Sovereigns was plain,
Their minds detached from ornate elegance;
In the era of the Five Emperors, writing began,
With speech valued for its elaborations;
Through the Three Dynasties and the Spring and Autumn period,
Though styles grew increasingly ornate over time,
All expressed what fit within their capacities,
Without straining talents beyond their limits.
The Warring States era branched into deceit,
Promoting cunning and embellished arguments;
From the Hàn dynasty to the present,
The pursuit of novelty in writing daily intensifies,
Vying for brilliance and flaunting literary flair,
Exhausting all mental efforts.
Thus, comparing simple words with flowery rhetoric,
The gap in substance spans millennia;
Contrasting following one's will with draining one's emotions,
The difference in ease and toil is vast as ten thousand miles;
This is why the ancients had ample leisure,
While later scholars find no respite.
Generally, the young have shallow insight but abundant ambition,
The elderly have firm knowledge but waning energy;
Those with strong ambition think sharply and endure labor,
Those with fading energy ponder deeply but harm their spirit—
These are common traits of average people,
A general pattern across the ages.
If one's innate capacity is limited,
Yet the use of intellect knows no bounds,
Some may, like a duck trying to match a crane's height,
Strain their words and carve their thoughts,
Thereby depleting their vital energy within,
Like the waves at the Wěilǘ drain;
Injuring their spirit outwardly,
Similar to the trees on Niú Mountain;
The severe illnesses born of anxiety
Can thus be inferred.
As for Zhòngrèn setting out his inkstone to compile works,
Shūtōng carrying his brush to specialize in writing,
They were not only worn by the passing years,
But also tormented by each day and hour—
Hence, Lord Cáo feared that writing could harm life,
Lù Yún lamented how thinking wearies the spirit—
These are not empty words.
While diligence is key in scholarly pursuits,
As seen in pricking one's thigh to stay alert;
In literary endeavors,
One should express pent-up thoughts;
Thus, it is fitting to follow emotions leisurely,
Gently adapting to the moment.
If one melts away essence and courage,
Constricts harmonious energy,
Grasping tablets to hasten aging,
Wielding the brush to assault one's nature—
Is this the original intent of sages and worthies,
Or the true principle of literary composition?
Moreover, thoughts have their sharp and dull moments,
Times when they flow freely or are blocked;
Even when washing, the heart may turn upside down,
Leading to反常 behavior;
When the spirit is in turmoil,
Repeated efforts only deepen confusion.
Therefore, in expressing literary art,
One must focus on moderation and release,
Purifying and calming the mind,
Regulating and smoothing the energy;
When vexed, set it aside,
Avoiding congestion and stagnation;
When inspiration strikes, wield the brush with ease,
When logic hides, lay it down and withdraw—
Use leisure to counteract fatigue,
Conversation to cure weariness;
Often hone the edge of talent in idleness,
Sell surplus literary courage,
Keeping the blade sharp as new,
With no blockages in the texture—
Though not the myriad techniques of fetal breathing,
This is one method to preserve vital energy.
Eulogy says:
Multitudinous are all phenomena,
Wearying are a thousand thoughts.
The mysterious spirit should be treasured,
The primal energy needs nurturing.
Water, when still, reflects clearly;
Fire, when calm, burns brightly.
Do not disturb literary contemplation—
Cultivate this essence and clarity.
Chapter Forty-Three: Organization and Coherence
What is meant by organization and coherence?
It refers to unifying the literary structure,
Integrating the beginning and end,
Deciding what to include and exclude,
Joining the edges together,
Weaving the entire piece into one,
So that it is varied yet not disjointed.
Like building a house requires a foundation and framework,
Or making clothes awaits sewing and stitching.
When talented youth learn writing,
They should correct the form and style,
Taking emotions and intent as the spirit,
Events and meanings as the bones and marrow,
Literary embellishment as the skin and flesh,
And tonal patterns as the voice and breath;
Only then can they evaluate the colors,
Resonate like metal and jade,
Advocate the good and reject the bad,
To achieve balance—
This is the constant rule of composing thoughts.
Generally, most writings
Resemble branches and tributaries;
To organize tributaries, follow the source,
To manage branches, adhere to the trunk.
Thus, in attaching words and assembling meanings,
One must grasp the main outline,
Guiding all paths to the same destination,
Aligning countless thoughts into unity,
So that numerous principles, though complex,
Have no disorder in arrangement,
And many phrases, though abundant,
Avoid the tangles of tangled silk.
Support the yang to let branches sprout,
Follow the yin to conceal traces;
Make the beginning and end thorough,
The surface and core integrated as one—
This is the technique of organization and coherence.
A painter focusing on hairs may miss the likeness,
An archer aiming at hairs may lose the wall;
Sharpening precision and detail
Often neglects the overall structure.
Hence, it's better to sacrifice an inch to gain a foot,
Forgo a foot to straighten a fathom,
Abandon partial cleverness,
Learn the skill of achieving complete beauty—
This is the strategy for composing a piece.
Literary changes know no fixed rules,
Opinions float in diversity;
Being too concise leaves meaning isolated,
Too broad makes words rebellious;
Hastiness often brings blame,
Delay can harm the task.
Moreover, talents differ,
Trains of thought vary;
Some plan from start to finish,
Others patch inch by inch—
Yet those who master the whole are few,
While those who piece together are many.
If the main thread loses its core,
The flavor of words will surely chaos,
The flow of meaning stalls,
And the literary style becomes paralyzed.
Only by discerning the underlying texture
Can the sections and words naturally cohere,
Like glue bonding wood,
Or beans matching their yellow hue.
Thus, though four steeds differ in strength,
Six reins harmonize like a qín;
The method of steering literature
Is much like this.
Deciding what to keep or discard lies with the heart,
Lengthening or shortening rests in the hand;
To synchronize the steps,
Just hold the reins steadily.
Thus, those skilled in connecting ideas can harmonize different themes as intimately as liver and gallbladder,
while clumsy assemblers make even similar tones seem as distant as the Hú and Yuè peoples.
Revising a chapter is harder than composing a new piece,
altering a word more arduous than replacing a sentence—
this is a proven fact.
In the past, Zhāng Tāng's memorial was questioned and repeatedly rejected,
and Yú Sōng's draft report faced constant reprimands,
both due to unclear reasoning and events,
and a lack of harmony in wording and intent.
When Ér Kuān revised the draft
and Zhōng Huì changed the wording,
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn marveled at its uniqueness,
and Jǐng of Jìn praised its excellence,
because the reasoning was sound and the events clear,
the mind sharp and the wording appropriate.
From this perspective,
we see that the skill or clumsiness in connecting ideas
makes a vast difference!
As for concluding the writing and closing the chapter,
it is like rowing a boat with oars;
to achieve final success,
it relies on the momentum to send it far.
If the opening is flourishing,
but the following sentences are withered,
then the remaining force is stifled,
and the lingering wind cannot flow freely.
This is what the "Zhōu Yì" means by "the buttocks have no skin,
and the walking is unsteady."
Only when the beginning and end support each other
can the form of connection
truly reach its peak.
The eulogy says:
The structure of the piece is intricate,
the emotions layered and dense.
Trace the origin and seek the end,
arrange the branches and spread the leaves.
When the essence of the Dao adheres,
scattered threads naturally connect.
Like the harmony of music,
the voice of the heart achieves concord.
Chapter 44: The Overall Method
In common parlance today,
there is wén and bǐ,
considering unrhymed writing as bǐ,
and rhymed writing as wén.
Now, wén enhances speech,
encompassing both poetry and prose in principle,
but distinguishing them into two categories
is a recent practice.
Yán Yánnián believed that "bǐ as a form
is the refinement of speech;
classics are speech but not bǐ,
while commentaries are bǐ but not speech."
Let us take his spear
to attack his shield.
Why?
The "Wén Yán" of the "Yì Jīng",
is it not refined speech?
If bǐ is indeed refined speech,
one cannot say classics are not bǐ.
To establish such a theory,
I see no solid ground for it.
I believe that spoken words are speech,
while written composition is termed hàn;
eternal principles are called classics,
and expositions on classics are called commentaries.
The forms of classics and commentaries
transition from speech to writing,
with writing serving speech,
which can be strong or weak.
The "Liù Jīng" are revered for their profundity and timelessness,
not for the distinction between speech and writing.
In the past, Lù Jī's "Wén Fù"
was hailed as exhaustive;
yet it broadly discusses details
without covering the essence of forms.
Thus, we know the thread of myriad changes is endless,
and selecting those who understand speech is difficult to perfect.
All who meticulously craft writings
strive for novelty and beauty,
mostly focusing on refining diction,
but few are willing to study method.
Scattered jade
may be confused with stones;
common stones
sometimes resemble jade.
The refined is concise,
the impoverished is also scant;
the erudite is comprehensive,
the cluttered is also verbose;
the eloquent is clear,
the shallow is also obvious;
the profound is intricate,
the deceptive is also twisted.
Some have splendid meaning but poor rhythm,
others clumsy reasoning but polished text.
Knowing that tuning bells is not easy,
and stringing a qín is truly hard.
When musicians declare harmony,
it need not capture every subtle nuance;
in waving a fan,
why exhaust all initial and final rhymes?
Wèi Wén compared writing to music,
and there is evidence for this.
Without cutting gnarled roots,
one cannot test a sharp tool;
without dissecting literary depth,
one cannot discern a versatile talent.
For talent to be versatile,
it must rely on understanding method;
unless one comprehensively assesses the domain,
and broadly judges the principles,
how can one control the source of emotion
and triumph in the literary realm?
Therefore, applying method to steer writing
is like a skilled chess player mastering all tactics;
abandoning method to follow whim
is like a gambler relying on chance.
Thus, writings like gambling
borrow accidental cleverness;
though they may achieve initial success,
subsequent support is hard to maintain;
with little, there is nothing to connect,
with much, one does not know what to cut,
leading to confusion in quantity,
how can one control beauty and ugliness?
As for writings like skilled chess,
the method has constant principles,
organizing sections and aligning ranks,
awaiting the convergence of emotion,
adapting to the moment and seizing opportunity,
never straying from correctness.
When tactics reach their peak,
and opportunity meets skill,
then meaning and flavor surge forth,
and wording and energy arrive in abundance.
Visually, it is like brocade and embroidery;
audibly, like strings and reeds;
in taste, rich and sweet;
in wearing, fragrant and aromatic;
the achievement of crafting a piece
reaches its zenith here.
Though the steed's hooves are swift,
the reins fear being too long;
a single burden in ten thousand
can hinder a thousand-mile journey.
Moreover, literary forms involve many methods,
all intertwined and supporting each other;
if one element is discordant,
the whole structure may collapse.
Therefore, compiling them in one chapter
comprehensively captures emotional variations,
like thirty spokes
uniting to form a hub,
though it may not be fully admirable,
it is the humble view of this commoner.
The eulogy says:
In the fields of wén and gardens of bǐ,
there are methods and gates.
Focus first on the overall structure,
discern to the very source.
Master one to command ten thousand,
grasp essentials to manage complexity.
Though thoughts have no fixed pattern,
principles remain constant.
Chapter 45: The Sequence of Times
As times and fortunes shift and change,
substance and ornament alternate in transformation.
The principles and sentiments of ancient and modern times,
how can they be spoken of!
In the past, during the era of Yáotáng,
when virtue flourished and transformation was uniform,
the old rustic uttered the words "What strength?",
and the village child sang the song "I do not know."
When Yǒuyú succeeded,
governance was abundant and the people were at leisure,
the "Southern Breeze" poem was composed by the sovereign,
and the "Brilliant Clouds" song was chanted by the assembled ministers.
In expressing their beauty,
how could it be but that their hearts were joyful and their sounds serene!
By the time of Dàyǔ's regulation of the land,
the "Nine Orders" celebrated his achievements;
Chéngtāng, sage and reverent,
inspired the "How Majestic!" eulogy.
When Jīwén's virtue flourished,
the "Zhōunán" reflected diligence without resentment;
under Tàiwáng's pure influence,
the "Bīnfēng" expressed joy without excess;
under the darkness of Yōu and Lì, the "Bǎn" and "Dàng" seethed with anger,
and with Píngwáng's decline, the "Shǔlí" lamented in sorrow.
Thus we know that the patterns of songs and odes
evolve with the age;
as the wind stirs above,
the waves tremble below.
After the Spring and Autumn period,
heroes contended in warfare,
the "Six Classics" were buried in obscurity,
and the Hundred Schools surged like a gale.
At that time,
Hán and Wèi emphasized military governance,
Yān and Zhào relied on stratagems,
the "Five Vermin" and "Six Lice"
were severely prohibited by Qín's decrees,
only the two states of Qí and Chǔ
had considerable literary culture;
Qí opened mansions on the broad avenues,
Chǔ expanded the palaces of Lántái,
Mèng Kē was hosted in guesthouses,
Xún Qīng served as a district magistrate,
thus at Jìxià, a fresh breeze was fanned,
and at Lánlíng, a rich custom flourished,
Zōu Zǐ gained fame for discussing the heavens,
Zōu Shì achieved renown for his ornate rhetoric,
Qū Píng linked his literary splendor to the sun and moon,
Sòng Yù intertwined his colors with the wind and clouds.
Observing their elegant discourse,
it overshadowed the "Yǎ" and "Sòng."
Thus we know that their dazzling and extraordinary ideas
emerged from the cunning customs of the Vertical and Horizontal Schools.
Then came the Hàn dynasty,
whose fortune followed the burning of books,
Gāozǔ esteemed military prowess,
mocked Confucians and neglected learning,
although rituals and laws were roughly established,
there was no leisure for the "Odes" and "Documents,"
yet the songs "Great Wind" and "Swan"
were also divinely inspired masterpieces.
Extending to Xiàohuì,
and up to Wén and Jǐng,
classical studies somewhat revived,
but literary men were not employed;
Jiǎ Yì was suppressed, and Zōu, Mèi sank into obscurity,
this too can be understood.
When Xiàowǔ revered Confucianism,
he adorned the grand enterprise,
rituals and music vied in splendor,
and literary embellishments competed in flourish:
at Bóliáng, court banquet poems were displayed,
at Jīndī, compassionate odes for the people were composed,
Méi Chéng was summoned in a cushioned carriage,
Shēn and Zhǔfù were honored with tripod feasts,
Gōngsūn's policy responses were promoted,
Ní Kuān's doubtful memorial was admired,
Mǎi Chén, once a wood-gatherer, donned brocade,
Xiàngrú, a washer of vessels, wore embroidery;
then, figures like Sīmǎ Qiān and Shòu Wáng,
and the likes of Yán, Zhōng, Méi, and Gāo,
though their responses were not always measured,
their literary compositions were never lacking,
their lingering influence and remaining brilliance
had no equal in splendor.
Passing through Zhāo and reaching Xuān,
they indeed continued the martial achievements,
galloping through the Shíqú Pavilion,
leisurely enjoying literary gatherings,
gathering extraordinary talents in ornate writing,
issuing lofty metaphors like fine silk;
thus, Wáng Bāo and his peers
awaited appointment with secured salaries.
From Yuán to Chéng,
they condescended to attend to books and records,
admiring the talk of jade dust,
clearing the path to the Jīnmǎ Gate,
Zǐyún sharpened his thoughts with a thousand pieces,
Zǐzhèng collated the "Six Arts,"
this too was splendid.
From the Hàn house,
up to Chéng and Āi,
though the era spanned nearly a century,
and literary men underwent nine transformations,
the general tendency of their return
was to follow the "Chǔcí,"
the lingering shadow of Língjūn
was thus present.
Since Āi and Píng declined,
and Guāngwǔ restored the dynasty,
he deeply cherished prognosticative texts,
and somewhat neglected literary elegance,
yet Dù Dǔ presented a eulogy and escaped punishment,
Bān Biāo participated in memorials and was made a magistrate,
though not extensively sought,
they were not entirely cast aside.
When Míng and Zhāng shone successively,
they revered and loved Confucian arts,
practiced rituals in the Bì Hall,
discussed literature at the Hǔ Pavilion,
Mèngjiān wielded his brush for the state history,
Jiǎ Kuí was supplied with paper for auspicious eulogies,
Dōngpíng excelled in refined writings,
Pèi Wáng promoted his comprehensive discourses,
imperial models and princely norms
shone upon each other.
From Hé and Ān onward,
up to Shùn and Huán,
there were the three Bāns, Fù, and Cuīs,
Wáng, Mǎ, Zhāng, and Cài,
outstanding great Confucians,
their talents never lacking for the times,
but the selection of literary works
remains unremarked upon.
However, after the restoration,
the many talents slightly altered their former paths,
where ornament and substance adhered,
they斟酌 classical phrases,
for through successive reigns of scholarly gatherings,
they gradually were imbued with Confucian style.
Descending to Língdì's time,
when there was a fondness for literary composition,
he created the script of Fúxī,
opened the Hóngdū Academy for rhapsodies,
but followers like Yuè Sōng
gathered shallow and vulgar men,
so Yáng Cì labeled them as Huāndōu,
Cài Yōng compared them to jesters,
their remaining influence and writings
are thus negligible.
Since Xiàndì was displaced,
literature drifted like tumbleweed,
by the end of Jiàn'ān,
the realm was just being stabilized.
Wèi Wǔ, with the dignity of a chancellor and king,
greatly loved poetry;
Wèi Wén, bearing the weight of heir apparent,
excelled exquisitely in rhapsodies;
Chén Sī, with the nobility of a prince,
wrote with gem-like brilliance;
together, they esteemed the talented and extraordinary,
thus outstanding talents gathered like clouds.
Zhòngxuān submitted from south of the Hàn,
Kǒngzhāng pledged allegiance from north of the river,
Wěicháng followed office in Qīngtǔ,
Gōnggàn offered his service by the seaside,
Déliǎn synthesized his striking thoughts,
Yuányú displayed his graceful joy.
Wénwèi, Xiūbó, and their peers,
Zǐchù, Dézǔ, and their companions,
proudly elegant before the wine cups,
dignified and composed upon the mats,
they wielded brushes to complete hearty songs,
mixed ink to accompany talk and laughter.
Observing the writings of that time,
they had a refined fondness for fervor;
truly, it was due to an age accumulated with chaos and separation,
where customs decayed and grievances prevailed,
all with profound intent and enduring strokes,
thus they were resolute and full of spirit.
When Míngdì succeeded to the military legacy,
he composed poems and set them to music,
summoned masters of literary pieces,
established the Chóngwén Observatory,
Hé, Liú, and the host of talents
shone in turn.
With young emperors in succession,
only Gāoguì was intelligent and refined,
his glances contained literary grace,
his every word formed a discourse.
At that time, the remaining style of Zhèngshǐ,
made the literary form light and tranquil,
yet Jī, Ruǎn, Yìng, and Miù
all raced along the literary path.
When the Jin Dynasty's foundation was laid by Xuān Dì,
and Jǐng Dì and Wén Dì continued the construction,
they all submerged traces of Confucian elegance,
and delved deeply into strategic methods.
By the time of Wǔ Dì's renewal,
who received the mandate in a time of peace,
the writings of schools and academies
did not attract imperial consideration.
Descending to Huái Dì and Mǐn Dì,
they were but dangling ornaments.
Yet, though Jin lacked literary refinement,
its talents were truly abundant:
Mào Xiān waved his brush scattering pearls,
Tài Chōng moved his ink laying out brocades,
Yuè and Zhàn shone with the splendor of paired jades,
Jī and Yún displayed the brilliance of two outstanding talents,
figures like Yìng, Fù, and the three Zhāngs,
and the likes of Sūn, Zhì, and Chéng Gōng,
all wove clear and exquisite literary embellishments,
flowing with elegant and delicate charm.
Previous historians believed that as fate touched the end of an era,
men could not fully realize their talents,
truly this saying
is worthy of a sigh!
With Yuán Huáng's restoration,
he promoted literature and established learning,
Liú and Diāo, as ritual officials, were honored and glorified,
Jǐng Chún, literary and sharp, was excellently promoted,
and when Míng Dì, endowed with wisdom,
had a refined love for literary gatherings,
ascending from heir to the throne,
he diligently pursued the arts,
honing his skills in edicts and policies,
and revitalizing literary grace in poetry and prose,
Yǔ, with his writing talent, grew closer,
Wēn, with his literary thought, became more esteemed,
extolling the cultured and elegant,
he was the Hàn Wǔ Dì of that time.
With Chéng and Kāng's brief reigns,
Mù and Āi's short rules,
Jiǎn Wén rose vigorously,
profound and pure in his severity,
subtle words and refined principles,
filled the seats of profound discourse,
serene thoughts and rich colors,
often sprinkled the literary garden.
By the time of Xiào Wǔ, with no heir,
Ān and Gōng came to an end;
in literature and history, there were the likes of Yuán and Yīn,
and the group of Sūn and Gān,
though their talents varied in depth,
they were sufficiently valuable like jade tablets.
Since the central court valued the mysterious,
it was especially praised in Jiāng Zuǒ,
carried on the remaining spirit of discourse,
it flowed into a literary style.
Thus, though the world was extremely troubled, the words and meanings were calm and peaceful,
poetry necessarily echoed the tenets of the Zhù Xià,
and prose became commentaries on the principles of the Qī Yuán.
Hence, we know that literary change is dyed by the sentiments of the age,
its rise and fall tied to the sequence of times,
tracing the beginning to grasp the end,
even a hundred generations can be understood.
Since Sòng Wǔ loved literature,
and Wén Dì was refined and elegant,
upholding the virtue of literature,
Xiào Wǔ was multi-talented,
with outstanding brilliance constructed like clouds.
From Míng Dì onward,
literary principles declined.
Among the ranks of officials,
they surged like rosy clouds and whirlwinds;
Wáng and Yuán, united in clan, displayed dragon-like elegance,
Yán and Xiè, through generations, showed phoenix splendor,
and the likes of Hé, Fàn, Zhāng, and Shěn,
were too numerous to count.
Having heard of them in the world,
I briefly outline the general picture.
With the imperial Qí steering the treasure,
fortune gathered in splendid brightness:
Tài Zǔ, with divine prowess, received the mandate,
Gāo Zǔ, with wise literature, continued the enterprise,
Wén Dì, with dual brilliance, contained elegance,
Zhōng Zōng, with superior wisdom, raised the fortune,
all with civilization from heaven,
securing the distant and glorious legacy.
Now the sacred calendar is just rising,
literary thought abundantly spreads,
gods descend from seas and mountains,
talents and heroes bloom forth,
riding flying dragons in the heavenly thoroughfare,
driving noble steeds across ten thousand miles,
classical rites and regulations,
surpass Zhōu and overtake Hàn,
the literature of Táng and Yú,
is it not at its peak!
Grand style and beautiful colors,
my short brush dares to present;
to proclaim and praise the times,
I entrust to the wise and discerning.
The Eulogy says:
Lushly reflecting through ten dynasties,
literary grace changes in nine ways.
When the pivot within moves,
it flows circularly without weariness.
Substance and style follow the times,
rise and fall lie in selection.
Though ancient times are far,
they feel as vivid as facing us.
On Physical Appearance, Forty-Six
As spring and autumn alternate in sequence,
darkness and light bring gloom and ease,
the stirrings of physical appearance,
also sway the heart.
For when the yang energy sprouts, the black ant marches,
and the yin tone congeals, the red bird stores food,
even tiny insects are stirred,
so deep is the effect of the four seasons on beings.
As for the noble heart that stands out like jade,
and the pure spirit that blooms with excellence,
when physical appearances summon,
who can remain unmoved?
Thus, at the year's start, spring emerges,
feelings of joy and comfort flow freely;
in the swelling early summer,
pent-up emotions congeal;
when the sky is high and the air clear,
somber thoughts reach far;
when sleet and snow are boundless,
solemn reflections run deep;
each season has its features,
each feature its appearance;
emotions shift with the scenes,
words emerge from the emotions.
A single leaf may invite reflection,
the sound of insects enough to draw the heart.
How much more when clear winds and the bright moon share the night,
and the white sun with spring woods grace the morn!
Thus, poets, stirred by scenes,
associate endlessly with kinds;
lingering at the edge of myriad images,
pondering in the realm of sight and sound;
depicting the essence and sketching the form,
they follow the scenes in their twists and turns;
attaching colors and matching sounds,
they also wander with the heart.
So "blazing" describes the freshness of peach blossoms,
"clingingly" captures the appearance of willow trees,
"brightly" serves for the look of the rising sun,
"flurrying" mimics the shape of falling snow,
"chirping" chases the sound of yellow birds,
"chirring" learns the rhythm of grass insects.
"Glistening sun" and "twinkling stars,"
with one word exhaust the principle;
"uneven" and "luxuriant,"
with two words link the form.
All use little to encompass much,
leaving no遗漏 of emotion and appearance.
Though one may ponder for a thousand years,
how can it be easily replaced?
When the "Lí Sāo" rose to prominence,
it touched on kinds and expanded,
the appearances of things being hard to exhaust,
so it layered and extended descriptions,
hence clusters like "towering"
and accumulations like "lush" emerged.
And with followers like Cháng Qīng,
who pursued bizarre postures and rare sounds,
modeling mountains and imitating waters,
words marching like fish in a row,
this is what is called poets being beautiful yet restrained in words,
while prose writers are excessively ornate with verbose lines.
As in the "Yǎ" ode singing of pear blossoms,
some yellow, some white;
the "Sāo" describing autumn orchids,
with green leaves and purple stems;
whenever displaying the five colors,
value lies in timely appearance,
if blue and yellow repeatedly emerge,
they become numerous but not precious.
Since the modern era,
literature has valued verisimilitude,
peering into emotions above the scenery,
delving into the appearances of plants and trees.
The expressions of chanting
aim solely for profundity;
the skill in embodying things
lies in close adherence.
Thus, clever words precisely depict forms,
like a seal imprinting clay,
without additional carving,
yet minutely rendering the finest details.
Hence, one can see the appearance through the words,
and discern the season from the phrasing.
However, things have constant postures,
but thoughts lack fixed standards;
some effortlessly reach the pinnacle,
while others, despite deep contemplation, become more distant.
Moreover, the standards set by the "Shī" and "Sāo"
both grasp the essential points,
so later writers with sharp pens
hesitate to contend with them.
None fail to borrow skill based on established forms,
seize momentum to converge with the extraordinary;
excelling at capturing the essential,
then even the old becomes ever new.
Thus, the four seasons whirl in succession,
yet inspiration values leisure;
though the aspects of things are diverse,
the analysis of diction still prizes simplicity;
making the flavor drift lightly upward,
and emotions shine with renewed freshness.
Throughout history, literary figures,
generations following one another,
all interweave and transform,
achieving merit through adaptation and reform;
those who exhaust the description of things yet have emotions to spare
understand the fusion of traditions.
As for mountains, forests, and marshlands,
they are indeed the profound treasury of literary thought,
omitting words leaves gaps,
while detailed explanation becomes verbose.
Yet the reason Qū Yuán could deeply perceive the sentiments of the "Fēng" and "Sāo"
was perhaps also due to the aid of rivers and mountains!
Eulogy says:
Mountains layered, waters encircling,
trees intermingled, clouds converging.
As the eyes wander back and forth,
the heart too breathes in and out.
The spring day lingers long,
the autumn wind soughs and sighs.
Emotions sent forth are like gifts,
inspiration coming is like a reply.
Summary of Talents Forty-Seventh
The literature of the nine dynasties
is rich and abundant;
its elegance and brilliance in language
can be summarized in detail.
The writings of Yú and Xià
include Gāo Yáo's six virtues,
Kuí's arrangement of the eight tones,
Yì had his eulogies,
the five sons composed songs,
their diction and meaning gentle and refined,
exemplars for ten thousand generations.
In the times of Shāng and Zhōu,
then Zhòng Huī handed down admonitions,
Yī Yǐn expounded teachings,
followers like Jí Fǔ
all composed "Shī" and "Sòng",
their meanings solid as classics,
their writings also models.
By the time of the Chūnqiū great officers,
they refined rhetoric and convened assemblies,
magnificent like a garden of precious stones,
resplendent as a market of brocades;
Wěi Áo selected the fine statutes of Chǔ,
Suí Huì discussed the rites and laws of Jìn,
Zhào Cuī with literary prowess attended feasts,
Guó Qiáo used refined rhetoric to defend Zhèng,
Zǐ Tàishū elegant and cultured,
Gōngsūn Huì skilled in discourse,
all are benchmarks of literary fame.
The Warring States era employed martial means,
yet literary scholars did not cease;
the various masters gained support through their doctrines,
Qū and Sòng displayed brilliance with the "Chǔcí",
Yuè Yì's reply letter was reasoned and righteous,
Fàn Jū's memorial was meticulous and thorough,
Sū Qín's successive persuasions were vigorous and effective,
Lǐ Sī's personal petitions were elegant and moving;
had they lived in a literary age,
they would rank with Yáng and Bān.
Xún Kuàng, master of learning, depicted things and named fu,
form and substance well-matched,
truly the sentiment of a great Confucian.
In the Hàn court, Lù Jiǎ
first displayed extraordinary brilliance,
composed "Mèng Chūn" and selected canonical admonitions,
his arguments were rich indeed.
Jiǎ Yì, talented and sharp,
surpassed even the flying hare,
his discussions apt and fu pure,
how could this be without substance!
Méi Chéng's "Qī Fā",
Zōu Yáng's "Shàng Shū",
their pens richly moistened,
their spirit shaped in words.
Dǒng Shū, a dedicated Confucian,
Zǐzhǎng, a pure historian,
yet composed elegant and ornate writings,
also like the poets' expression of sorrow.
Xiàngrú loved books,
modeled himself on Qū and Sòng,
deeply immersed in exaggeration and beauty,
achieved fame as a master of cí.
Yet examining his essential ideas,
reason does not surpass diction,
so Yáng Zǐ considered "Wén Lì Yòng Guǎ Zhě Chángqīng",
truly apt words!
Wáng Bāo constructed brilliance,
aiming for meticulous skill,
attuning to sounds and gauging appearances,
refreshingly admirable;
Zǐyún focused on meaning,
his diction and thought deepest,
observing his profound scope,
searching for strange beauty,
and exhausting his talent in deep thought,
thus able to have ample reason and firm diction.
Huán Tán's discourses
were rich, called Yī Dùn,
Sòng Hóng praised and recommended him,
comparing him to Xiàngrú,
but his fu like "Jí Líng"
were shallow and lacking talent,
thus knowing he excelled in satire,
not matching ornate writing.
Jìng Tōng had a refined love for rhetoric,
yet stumbled in a flourishing age;
"Xiǎn Zhì" and "Zì Xù"
were like pearls from a clam's ailment.
The two Bān and two Liú,
generations continuing the brilliance,
old accounts say Gù's writing surpassed Biāo,
Xīn's learning excelled Xiàng's,
yet "Wáng Mìng" was clear and reasoned,
"Xīn Xù" comprehensive and practiced,
as jade discs from Kūngāng,
it is hard to surpass the origin.
Fù Yì and Cuī Yīn,
their radiance shoulder to shoulder,
Yuàn and Shí followed their steps,
able to perpetuate their style.
Dù Dǔ and Jiǎ Kuí
also had literary reputations,
tracing their talents,
they are the later strain of Cuī and Fù.
Lǐ Yóu's fu and inscriptions
aspired to grand composition,
but his talent was heavy and sluggish,
wings drooping, unable to fly.
Mǎ Róng, a great scholar,
thought comprehensively, ascended heights,
expounding classical models,
blossom and fruit supporting each other.
Wáng Yì, broad knowledge meritorious,
yet lacked strength in brilliant colors.
Yánshòu continued his will,
unique in his exquisite sharpness,
excelling at depicting things and portraying forms,
was it not Méi Chéng's inherited technique?
Zhāng Héng, thorough and ample,
Cài Yōng, refined and elegant,
literature and history cultured,
gazing across generations.
Thus, bamboo and cypress differ in heart but share constancy,
gold and jade vary in substance yet are both treasures.
Liú Xiàng's memorials
were pointed in meaning but mild in tone;
Zhào Yī's cí and fu
were rich in ideas but loose in form;
Kǒng Róng, spirited in writing,
Mí Héng, sharp in thought for composition,
each had partial excellence.
Pān Xù relied on the classics to display talent,
thus surpassing all in edicts;
Wáng Lǎng expressed fervor to convey will,
also achieved beauty in prefaces and inscriptions.
However, before Qīng and Yuān,
many employed talent without pursuing learning;
after Xióng and Xiàng,
often cited texts to aid writing;
this is the great divide in approach,
a distinction that must not be confused.
The literary talent of Wèi Wén,
vast and pure in elegance,
was disparaged in traditional discussions,
said to be a thousand miles behind Cáo Zhí.
However, Zǐjiàn (Cáo Zhí) had swift thoughts and outstanding talent,
his poetry beautiful and his petitions extraordinary;
Zǐhuán (Cáo Pī) deliberated meticulously but with restrained force,
thus not competing to be the first to sing;
yet his Music Bureau poems are clear and soaring,
his "Diǎn Lùn" argumentative and essential,
each with its own strengths and weaknesses,
and there is no confusion about that.
But common opinions sway with bias,
echoing uniformly like thunder,
thus leading to Wén Dì's talent being diminished due to his high status,
while Sī Wáng's value was enhanced by his straitened circumstances,
which is not a sound judgment.
Zhòngxuān (Wáng Càn) overflowed with talent,
swift yet precise,
excelling in many forms of writing,
with few flaws in his diction;
selecting his poetry and fu,
he stands as the crown among the Seven Masters!
Chén Lín and Rú Xǔ were renowned for their edicts and proclamations;
Xú Gàn excelled in fu and essays;
Liú Zhēn had lofty emotions matched with literary grace;
Yìng Yáng, with his superior learning, achieved literary excellence;
Lù Cuì and Yáng Xiū,
possessed considerable skill in note-taking and records;
Dīng Yí and Hándān,
also contained the beauty of discourse;
they are worthy of note.
Liú Shào's "Zhào Dū",
could rival earlier masters;
Hé Yàn's "Jǐngfú",
shone upon later generations;
Xiūliǎn's (Yīng Xún) emotional style,
is marked by his "Bǎi Yī" expressing his will,
Jífǔ's (Yīng Zhēn) literary principles,
are perfected in color in "Lín Dān";
Jī Kāng followed his heart to express his arguments,
Ruǎn Jí channeled his spirit to compose poetry,
different voices yet harmonious in resonance,
different wings yet flying together.
Zhāng Huá's short pieces,
are elegant and clear,
his "Jiāo Liáo" conveying allegorical meaning,
akin to Hán Fēi's "Shuì Nán".
Zuǒ Sī, with his extraordinary talent,
delved deeply into profound thought,
exerted his sharpness in "Sān Dū",
and stood out in "Yǒng Shǐ",
sparing no effort.
Pān Yuè was quick-witted,
his diction naturally harmonious and fluent,
epitomizing beauty in "Xī Zhēng",
displaying surplus talent in elegies and laments,
not from external sources.
Lù Jī's talent sought to probe the depths,
his diction striving for breadth,
thus his thoughts could achieve cleverness,
but he could not control the complexity.
Shìlóng (Lù Yún) was clear and practiced,
using discernment to check disorder,
thus able to display fresh and clean literary grace,
adept in short pieces.
Sūn Chǔ composed his thoughts,
often straightforward and疏通;
Zhì Yú expressed his feelings,
always following rules with warmth and elegance;
his critiques and classifications,
were systematic.
Fù Xuán's writings,
often conveyed admonitory meanings;
Chángyú's (Fù Xián) memorials and petitions,
consistently upheld firmness and integrity;
both were solid talents like pillars,
not just flashy petals of flowers.
Chéng Gōng Zǐ'ān,
selected fu and occasionally achieved beauty;
Xiàhóu Xiàoruò,
had the form but all in miniature,
Cáo Shū was clear and refined in long pieces,
Jìyīng (Zhāng Hàn) was discerning and incisive in short verses,
each with their own strengths.
Mèngyáng (Zhāng Zǎi) and Jǐngyáng (Zhāng Xié),
equally talented and elegant,
can be said to be like the governments of Lǔ and Wèi,
brothers in literature.
Liú Kūn, elegant and vigorous with much style,
Lú Chén, emotional yet clear in reasoning,
also met their times and circumstances.
Jǐngchún (Guō Pú), resplendent and free,
deserved to lead the Mid-Jìn revival,
his "Jiāo Fǔ" was solemn and grand in view,
his "Xiān Shī" also soared ethereally to the clouds.
Yǔ Yuánguī's memorials and petitions,
were refined, detailed, and leisurely fluent;
Wēn Tàizhēn's notes and records,
followed reason with clarity and coherence;
both were skilled craftsmen with the brush.
Sūn Shèng and Gān Bǎo,
excelled in literature as historians,
their standards aimed at,
the aspirations of canonical teachings,
though their approaches differed,
their literary brilliance was somewhat similar.
Yuán Hóng started with high aspirations,
thus outstanding yet often biased;
Sūn Chuò moved in measured steps,
thus orderly but lacking vividness;
Yīn Zhòngwén's solitary inspirations,
Xiè Shūyuán's leisurely sentiments,
both dissolved the structure of diction,
into elusive and floating sounds;
though滔滔 in romantic style,
greatly diluted the literary intent.
The extraordinary talents of the Sòng period,
with literary works gathered like fish scales,
being close in time, are easy to understand,
and need no laborious evaluation.
Observing the forest of talents in the Later Hàn,
they can compare with those of Western Capital (Xī Jīng);
the literary garden of the Jìn era,
matches that of Yèdū;
yet when speaking of the Wèi period,
Yuánfēng is always mentioned as the foremost;
in praises since Sòng,
Jiàn'ān is also cited as an example;
Why is that?
Is it not because they were golden ages for literature,
and grand gatherings for recruiting talent?
Alas,
this is why the ancients valued the times!
The Eulogy says:
Talent is rare, indeed,
each nature endowed differently.
Once literature is woven together,
it condenses into brocade for a thousand years.
Lingering are the remaining colors,
the legacy flourishes greatly.
Do not call it杂乱,
it can be clearly appreciated.
Discernment, the Forty-Eighth
How difficult discernment is!
Sound is truly hard to know,
and true understanding hard to encounter;
to meet one who understands,
is it but one in a thousand years!
Since ancient times, those with discernment,
often despised their contemporaries and longed for the past,
as the saying goes: "What is daily before them is not used,
but from afar, hearing of it, they yearn."
When the "Chǔ Shuō" first appeared,
and "Zǐ Xū" was newly completed,
Qín Shǐ Huáng and Hàn Wǔ Dì,
regretted not being of the same time;
yet when they were contemporaries,
Hán Fēi was imprisoned and Sīmǎ Xiāngrú was轻视d,
is this not clear evidence of despising contemporaries!
As for Bān Gù and Fù Yì,
their writings were on par,
yet Bān Gù mocked Fù Yì, saying:
"Once he starts writing, he cannot stop himself."
And when Chén Sī (Cáo Zhí) discussed talent,
he also strongly criticized Kǒng Zhāng (Chén Lín),
Jìnglǐ (Dīng Yì) requested polishing,
and was praised as a fine example,
while Jìxù (Lǐú Xiū) loved to slander and reproach,
compared to Tián Bā,
the intent is also evident.
Thus Wèi Wén stated that "literati slight each other,"
which is no empty talk.
As for Jūnqīng (Lóu Hù) with his glib tongue,
who mistakenly wished to discuss literature,
claiming that "Sīmǎ Qiān, in writing his book,
consulted Dōngfāng Shuò,"
then Huán Tán and others,
looked at each other and laughed derisively;
he was but a gambler,
speaking lightly and deserving ridicule—
how much more so for literary scholars,
to speak recklessly!
Thus, to have clear and penetrating insight,
yet value the ancient and despise the modern—
these two rulers are examples;
to have truly great and profound talent,
yet exalt oneself and belittle others—
Bān and Cáo are examples;
to have learning insufficient for literature,
yet believe the false and be迷ed by the true—
Lóu Hù is an example;
the comment about the "sauce jar,"
is it not much to lament!
The qílín and phoenix are vastly different from deer and pheasants,
pearls and jade stand far apart from gravel and stones.
When the bright sun shines down upon them,
and clear eyes capture their forms.
Yet the Lǔ official mistook the qílín for a deer,
the Chǔ people took a pheasant for a phoenix,
the Wèi commoners regarded a luminous jewel as a strange stone,
and the Sòng visitor treated a Yān pebble as a precious pearl.
Even tangible objects are easily misjudged,
so egregiously can errors arise;
how much more difficult to discern literary sentiment,
who dares claim it is easy to distinguish?
Literary compositions are diverse and numerous,
substance and ornament interwoven,
readers often have personal preferences,
none can encompass all perfectly.
The passionate applaud stirring rhythms,
the reserved admire subtle depths,
the superficially clever are delighted by ornate beauty,
the eccentric are thrilled by the bizarre.
What matches their taste they sigh over and recite,
what differs they reject and discard,
each clinging to their partial understanding,
attempting to judge infinite variations—
this is what is called "facing east
and failing to see the western wall."
Only after playing a thousand tunes can one comprehend music,
after viewing a thousand swords can one recognize weaponry;
thus, to achieve comprehensive perception,
one must first broaden one's experience.
View towering peaks to comprehend small mounds,
taste ocean waves to understand tiny streams,
impartial to weight and lightness,
unbiased in love and hate,
only then can one balance principles like a scale,
and illuminate texts like a mirror.
Therefore, to assess literary sentiment,
first establish six perspectives:
first, examine the structure,
second, the use of language,
third, continuity and innovation,
fourth, the unconventional and orthodox,
fifth, allusions and meanings,
sixth, rhythm and melody.
Once these methods are applied,
strengths and weaknesses will emerge.
Writers express emotions through words when moved,
readers penetrate emotions through analyzing texts,
tracing the ripples to seek the source,
even the obscure will become clear.
Though we cannot see the faces of those from ancient times,
reading their texts reveals their hearts.
Is it that the writings are too profound?
No, the fault lies in our shallow perception.
When the mind dwells on mountains and rivers,
the qín expresses those feelings;
how much more when shaped by the brush tip,
can principles remain hidden?
Thus, the mind's illumination of truth
is like the eyes' perception of forms:
with clear vision, no form goes unrecognized,
with an acute mind, no principle remains unpenetrated.
Yet vulgar critics often err,
rejecting the deep and favoring the shallow—
this is why Zhuāng Zhōu laughed at "Plucking the Willow,"
and Sòng Yù lamented "White Snow."
Once Qū Yuán said:
"My substance and refinement are hidden within,
the crowd knows not my extraordinary brilliance."
Only a connoisseur can recognize uniqueness.
Yáng Xióng declared, "My heart loves profound, broad, and exquisite writing,"
his disdain for the superficial
is thus evident.
Only with deep insight into the arcane
comes joyful inner satisfaction,
like the spring terrace delighting the masses,
or music and food halting passersby.
It is said the orchid, national fragrance,
worn and adored, grows more fragrant;
so too, books, the nation's splendor,
savored and pondered, reveal their beauty.
O noble connoisseurs,
pray heed this.
Envoi:
A great bell weighing tons,
set by Kuí and Kuàng.
Fine books fill the chest,
judged by discerning critique.
Beware the seductive tunes of Zhèng,
lest they mislead the ear.
Only with this rule,
can one not stray from the path.
On Cultivating Talent - Chapter Forty-Nine
The "Zhōu Shū" discusses scholars,
comparing them to fine timber,
valuing both utility and literary grace.
Thus, the unhewn wood is carved and painted,
walls are raised and then adorned.
Yet recent writers
pursue ornament at the expense of substance,
so Wèi Wén declared, "Writers ancient and modern
often neglect minor conduct";
Wéi Dàn's critiques
further disparaged many talents.
Later generations echo mindlessly,
lumping all together uniformly—
alas, how lamentable!
A brief look at literary men's flaws:
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú eloped with a widow and accepted bribes,
Yáng Xióng was fond of drink and lacked foresight,
Féng Yǎn disregarded integrity,
Dù Dǔ made endless requests without shame,
Bān Gǔ flattered Dòu to wield power,
Mǎ Róng sided with Liáng and amassed wealth,
Kǒng Róng's arrogance led to his execution,
Mí Héng's folly brought about his death,
Wáng Càn was frail yet aggressively ambitious,
Chén Lín was hasty and careless,
Dīng Yí was greedy and sought goods,
Lù Suì sponged off others shamelessly,
Pān Yuè deceitfully prayed against Mǐnhuái,
Lù Jī fawned upon Jiǎ and Guō,
Fù Xuán was rigid and insulted his superior,
Sūn Chǔ was stubborn and sued his office,
all such cases
are blemishes on literary men.
If such flaws exist among literati,
they are found in military men as well.
Ancient generals and ministers
had many faults indeed:
like Guǎn Zhòng's theft,
Wú Qǐ's greed and licentiousness,
Chén Píng's stains,
Jiǎng and Guàn's slander and envy.
From then on,
instances are too numerous to count.
Kǒng Guāng, bearing high office,
yet flattered Dǒng Xián;
how much more so for Bān and Mǎ in low posts,
or Pān Yuè in humble positions!
Wáng Róng, founder of a state with high rank,
sold offices and vexed the people;
how much more for Mǎ and Dù in poverty,
or Dīng and Lù in destitution!
Yet Zǐxià remained a renowned Confucian without blame,
and Jùnchōng was unstained among the Bamboo Grove—
high reputation diminishes criticism.
Consider the loyalty of Qū Yuán and Jiǎ Yì,
the alertness of Zōu and Méi,
Huáng Xiāng's pure filial piety,
Xú Gàn's quiet reserve—
can it be said that literary men
are always flawed?
Humans are endowed with five talents,
each varying in strength and use;
unless one is a supreme sage,
perfection is hard to demand.
Yet generals and ministers, due to high status, are excused,
while literary men, due to low rank, are often criticized—
this is why great rivers surge mightily,
while tiny streams are scrutinized in inches.
The rise and fall of reputations
follows this pattern;
the openness or obstruction of positions
also has its reasons.
A scholar's advancement
depends on accomplishing tasks.
Lǔ's Jìng Jiāng,
merely a wise woman,
yet her weaving was likened
to governing a state;
how can a man of letters
be ignorant of governance?
Those like Yáng and Sīmǎ,
had literary skill but lacked substance,
hence they remained in low positions.
Once Yǔ Liàng's talent was pure and outstanding,
his achievements renowned,
so his literary art was not emphasized;
had he not held high office,
he would have been known for his writing.
The arts of war and letters
should complement each other.
Xì Hú studied the "Shū Jīng",
thus was made marshal—
how can loving letters mean neglecting arms?
Sūn Wǔ's "Art of War",
its words like pearls and jade—
how can practicing war mean ignorance of letters?
Thus the noble man conceals his talents,
awaiting the right time to act,
to unfold his endeavors and achievements.
He should indeed accumulate inner qualities to enrich his center,
and radiate brilliance to manifest outwardly,
with the substance of the pián and nán trees,
and the trunk of the yùzhāng tree.
In composing literature, he must aim to organize military and state affairs;
in bearing heavy responsibilities, he must serve as pillars and beams.
In obscurity, he cultivates himself to leave behind writings;
in prominence, he seizes the times to achieve merits.
Such a man of letters
corresponds to the timber fit for fine woodworking.
Eulogy says:
Observe those ancient cultivators,
possessing admirable literary virtue.
Their fame illuminates the southern Chǔ,
their brilliance stirs the northern Liáng.
If carved but not substantial,
who would take them as models of integrity?
Is it not that they glorify themselves,
but also bring honor to the state?
Preface to Intentions: Chapter Fifty
Now, Wénxīn
speaks of the mind's effort in writing.
In the past, Juānzǐ had "Mind of the Lute,"
Wángsūn had "Ingenious Mind,"
how beautiful is the word "mind" indeed!
Hence I use it.
Since ancient times, literary compositions
have taken form through elaborate ornamentation,
but does this mean adopting Zōu Shì's "Carving Dragons" in all its expressions?
The universe is vast and distant,
the multitude of talents diverse and mixed;
to stand out from the crowd,
relies solely on wisdom and art.
Time passes swiftly,
the spirit does not linger;
to elevate one's voice and spread one's substance,
creation is the means.
Modeling the appearance after heaven and earth,
endowed with nature from the five elements,
comparing the ears and eyes to the sun and moon,
equating the voice and breath with wind and thunder,
humans transcend all things,
being indeed spiritual.
Though the body is as fragile as grass and trees,
the name outlasts the solidity of metal and stone.
Therefore, the noble man in life
establishes virtue and sets forth words.
Is it that he loves argument?
It is by necessity!
At seven years of age,
I dreamed of colorful clouds like brocade,
and I climbed to pick them.
Upon passing thirty,
I often dreamed at night of holding ritual vessels of red lacquer,
following Zhòngní southward;
awakening at dawn,
I was then joyful and pleased.
How great is the sage, so hard to meet,
that he should appear in a dream to this humble one!
Since the beginning of humankind,
there has been none like the Master.
To expound the sage's intent,
nothing surpasses annotating the Classics,
yet scholars like Mǎ and Zhèng
have already elaborated them exquisitely.
Even with profound insights,
it is insufficient to establish a school.
Only the use of literature,
truly branches of the classics,
through which the five rites are accomplished,
and the six codes are put to use,
by which sovereign and minister achieve brilliance,
and military and state affairs are illuminated.
Examining their origin,
all stem from the classics.
But as we are far removed from the sages,
literary forms have disintegrated;
writers favor the unusual,
prizing frivolous and deceptive language,
adorning feathers with added painting,
embroidering sashes and aprons with patterns,
deviating ever more from the root,
heading towards error and excess.
The "Zhōushū" discusses diction,
valuing substance and essentials;
the master Confucius set forth teachings,
condemning heterodox views;
the difference in diction and teaching
should be embodied in the essentials.
Thus, taking up brush and mixing ink,
I begin to discuss literature.
A detailed survey shows many in recent times have discussed literature:
such as Wèi Wén's exposition of classics,
Chén Sī's preface to letters,
Yìng Yáng's literary discourse,
Lù Jī's "Rhyme-prose on Literature,"
Zhòng Zhì's "Genre Classifications,"
Hóng Fàn's "Literary Grove,"
each illuminates a corner or crevice,
rarely viewing the broad path.
Some critique the talents of their time,
others evaluate the writings of past masters,
some broadly outline the aims of elegance and vulgarity,
others summarize the ideas of specific works.
Wèi's classic is detailed but not comprehensive,
Chén's book argumentative but inappropriate,
Yìng's discourse ornate but sketchy,
Lù's rhyme-prose clever but fragmented,
"Genre Classifications" precise but impractical,
"Literary Grove" superficial and lacking focus.
Moreover, figures like Jūnshān and Gōnggàn,
Jífǔ and Shìlóng,
discuss literary ideas broadly;
often emerging intermittently,
they all fail to shake the leaves to seek the roots,
or observe the waves to trace the source.
Without recounting the admonitions of ancient sages,
they offer no benefit to the considerations of later generations.
Now, the creation of Wénxīn
is rooted in the Dào,
guided by the sages,
embodied in the Classics,
informed by the Apocrypha,
and transformed by the "Lí Sāo."
The pivotal points of literature
are thus thoroughly addressed.
As for discussing prose and verse,
categories are distinguished and classified,
tracing origins to mark periods,
explaining names to clarify meanings,
selecting texts to fix exemplars,
and setting forth principles to outline systems.
In the upper chapters,
the guiding principles are clear.
Regarding the analysis of emotion and ornamentation,
it must encompass and systematize,
elucidating spirit and nature,
mapping wind and force,
to include adaptation and interconnection,
and review sound and word,
observing rise and decline in "Shí Xù,"
praising and censuring in "Cái Lüè,"
lamenting in "Zhīyīn,"
standing firm in "Chéng Qì,"
cherishing the "Xù Zhì,"
to command all chapters.
In the lower chapters,
the detailed items are evident.
Positioning principles and fixing names,
clear in the numbers of the "Great Changes,"
those pertaining to literary use
are but forty-nine chapters.
Now, evaluating a single text is easy,
but synthesizing numerous writings is difficult.
Though I have lightly plucked the fine hairs
and deeply reached the marrow,
some subtle ideas and hidden sources,
seem near yet are far,
and what the words fail to record
are also beyond count.
When my evaluations are formed into text,
some agree with old discussions,
not due to echoing,
but because divergence is inherently impossible.
Some differ from previous theories,
not out of willful disagreement,
but because agreement is inherently impossible.
Agreement and difference
do not defer to ancient or modern,
but dissect the texture,
aiming solely for balance.
Holding the reins in the field of literary elegance,
circling the mansion of ornate splendor,
I have nearly covered it all.
But words cannot fully convey meaning,
a difficulty even the ancient sages faced;
my insight is but from a jar or tube,
how can it set the standard?
Vast are the past ages,
which have sunk my hearing;
distant is the future,
whose view will likely be clouded by this dust.
Eulogy says:
Life has its bounds,
but wisdom knows no shore.
Chasing after things is truly hard,
while following one's nature is quite easy.
Proudly facing the springs and rocks,
savoring the meanings in literature.
If writings indeed carry the heart,
then my heart finds its refuge.
